Ideo charitas dicitur nunquam excidere, quia habetur hic et in futuro, in praesenti vero habita amittitur, et amissa iterum recuperatur.

QUAESTIO CXIX. Scientia destruetur, etc. Quaeritur quomodo dicat scientiam destrui in futuro. Nunquid non habebimus cognitionem in futuro earum rerum, quarum nunc habemus? Habebimus quidem, et multo majorem quam habeamus in praesenti: quomodo ergo scientia destruetur? Solutio. Dicunt quidam quod scientia destruetur a sua partialitate et imperfectione, ut non sit partialis et imperfecta. Sed 536Ahoc est eam augeri et perfici, et non destrui, quia eodem modo potest dici de charitate, quod ipsa sit destruenda. Sicut enim imperfecte cognoscimus: ita imperfecte diligimus, et cum venerit quod perfectum est, evacuabitur quod ex parte est.

Solutio. Dicunt quidam, quod non scientia, sed modus ejus aenigmaticus et umbratilis destruendus est. Sed iterum eadem ratione et charitas videtur esse destruenda: cujus modus scilicet imperfectionis in futuro est evacuandus. Ad hoc respondetur quod verum est quod modus imperfectionis tolletur a charitate, sed non omnis modus. In futuro enim diligetur propter se, et propter Deum proximus, sicut in praesenti diligitur. Alii etiam dicunt quod actus scientiae in futuro destruetur. Charitas vero, 536Bquae nunc est, nec ejus actus, nec quidam modus in futuro destruetur: fides autem, et spes ex toto evacuabuntur: scientia vero ex parte destrueter: cujus actus et modus non erit.

QUAESTIO CXX. Sed est alia quaestio, quae nos magis urget: verum est, et negari non potest quin charitas in praesenti sit comparatione futuri imperfecta, sed Apostolus probat tali argumento, quod prophetiae evacuabuntur, et quod scientia destruetur: Ex parte scimus, et ex parte prophetamus: cum autem venerit, quod perfectum est, evacuabitur quod ex parte est: cum ergo charitas ex parte est, consimili argumento ipsa evacuabitur, cum venerit quod perfectum est. Solutio. Nos autem dicimus quod 536Calia ratione dicitur scientia, vel prophetia ex parte, alia ratione charitas imperfecta. Ex eo enim quod quidam cognoscunt, quidam non cognoscunt, prophetia vel doctrina habet locum in hoc praesenti, ubi alius alium docet et instruit. In futuro vero ubi omnes erunt docibiles Dei, quando omnes a maximo usque ad minimum cognoscent Deum plene et perfecte, tunc doctrina hominum non habebit locum: quando nemo dicet fratri suo: Cognosce Deum. Ideoque scientia, id est doctrina, evacuabitur. Charitas autem non sic dicitur ex parte esse. Non enim ideo habet esse, quia quidam diligunt, et quidam non diligunt: imo multo verius erit quando omnes diligent perfecte. Nota, aenigma est obscura similitudo, et sicut in praesenti omnis creatura est quasi 536Dquoddam speculum, in quo videtur Deus: sic in futuro ipse Deus erit speculum omnis creaturae, in quo omnia videbuntur verius, quam in semetipsis. Hinc est secundum quosdam quare scientia sit destruenda: quia umbratilis iste modus cognoscendi, quem nunc habemus, plena cognitione accedente non erit.

QUAESTIO CXXI. Charitati non possunt fides et spes deesse: fides vero et spes sine charitate esse possunt. Dicunt tamen quidam, ut supra dictum est, quod fides sine charitate esse non potest: quorum error hic destruitur. Cum enim dicit: Si habuero omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum: innuit manifeste, quod fides etiam perfecta potest haberi sine charitate. 537AEt expositor in praedictis verbis manifeste eos arguit dicens, quod fides et spes sine charitate esse possunt.

QUAESTIO CXXII. De spe vero quaeri potest quomodo ipsa sine charitate esse possit. Nonne spes est fiducia futurorum bonorum ex praecedentibus meritis veniens? Haec autem non potest esse sine charitate. Itaque videtur quod sine charitate spes esse non possit. Item si spes est, ut aliis videtur, exspectatio futuri commodi, jam praesumptio erit potius quam spes, si certus sum quod remunerabit, licet sint nulla merita. Ad hoc responderi potest, quod duplex est spes: remunerationis, et promerendi: spes vero promerendi sine charitate non esse potest, spes autem remunerationis (non) potest haberi sine 537Bcharitate.

QUAESTIO CXXIII. Qui loquitur lingua, non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo (I Cor. XIV). Quaeritur quid sit loqui lingua? Solutio. Alii dicunt quod loqui lingua est loqui parabolice; alii lingua incognita. Augustinus dicit quod prolatio signorum, quae spiritus in spiritu hominis informat, dicitur esse loqui lingua. Unde Apostolus ait: Spiritus loquitur mysteria (Ibid.). Idem enim dicit loqui lingua, et loqui spiritu. Spiritus sanctus in primitiva Ecclesia formabat ad conversionem fidelium signa coelestium secretorum in mentibus fidelium, et prolationem talium vocat loqui linguis Apostolus. Notandum vero quod illi qui linguis loquebantur, quandoque intelligebant, quandoque non intelligebant. Sed dicet 537Cquis: Si ille, qui loquitur lingua, intelligit quod dicit, jam hoc est non loqui lingua, sed prophetare. Solutio. Licet ipse intelligat, nisi ipse aliis exponat, non prophetat, sed tantum loquitur lingua. Nota quaedam fieri in Ecclesia ad solum decorem, non adeo ad necessitatem: inter quae continetur loqui linguis.

QUAESTIO CXXIV. Eritis loquentes in aera, etc. Ex his verbis arbitrantur quidam quod loqui linguis sit loqui diversis generibus linguarum, sed non est hoc verum: imo ad hoc inducit Apostolus istud, ut ostendat, loqui linguis sine interpretatione parvam habere utilitatem, sicut loqui omnibus generibus linguarum potius confusionem quam aedificationem 537Dfaceret his, qui nullam eorum intelligerent.

QUAESTIO CXXV. Si nesciero virtutem vocis. Quaeritur quid vocet virtutem vocis. Solutio. Vocis significationem, vocat vocis virtutem.

QUAESTIO CXXVI. Quaeritur etiam quare hujusmodi locutio lingua fieri dicatur. Solutio. Ideo hoc fit quia quod in lingua est, in voce et in prolatione est: quod vero in corde est, in intellectu est: quia in corde intelligentia est: unde quia haec locutio tantum in prolatione est, et non in intelligentia, ideo lingua fieri dicitur: spiritu etiam, et non mente. Est enim spiritus vis animae inferior mente, in qua imagines rerum confuse comprehenduntur. Est enim visibilium imaginaria et confusa comprehensio, sine discretione proprietatum eorum, quae 538Acomprehenduntur: qualis fuit illa Pharaonis de vaccis et spicis visio: ipse enim tantum imagines videbat. Joseph vero in intellectu de his habuit Dei revelationem.

QUAESTIO CXXVII. Quaeritur quid verba sic prolata significent: quando quis sic lingua loquitur, ut hoc exemplum ponamus: Exit qui seminat seminare semen suum. Nam si haec est vocis significatio, ipsa vera fuit: quaeritur ergo, si id ea dicitur, quod ea proprie significatur: si dicatur ita esse, infertur, ergo quoddam falsum ea significatur. Ad hoc respondent quidam dicentes: Non est vocis significatio quaerenda in hujusmodi, sed rerum tantum, quod pertinet ad allegoriam. Alii dicunt, ut licentius loquantur, quia proprie quidem falsum significat: 538Bnon tamen ea falsum dicitur: quia non ibi dictum terminatur: non enim est finis locutionis illa prima vocis significatio, sed secunda, quae allegorica dicitur. Potest autem dici, quod locutio ipsa neque verum neque falsum significat: res enim ibi tantum significant verum, quod ibi mystice intelligitur. Nec nego quin ibi sit vocis significatio, sed tantum incomplexe, quia haec vox, homo, significat hominem, et sic de caeteris; sed non significant complexe; non enim conjuncte significant, ut verum vel falsum significetur, sed ut res significent illas: quibus verum significatur. Vel potest dici, quod propositio ipsa ex rerum proprietate, quae significantur: ad illud significandum quod mystice intelligitur 538Cassumitur, ut haec vox, semen, verbum Dei significat, ex proprietate rei quam significat.

QUAESTIO CXXVIII. Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris, etc. (I Cor. XV.) Quaeritur an Christus secundum carnem moriendi habuit necessitatem? Quod autem habuit moriendi necessitatem, videtur velle auctoritas super locum illum. Quemadmodum statutum est hominibus semel mori: post hoc autem judicium: sic Christus semel oblatus est (Hebr. IX); sic, id est eadem necessitate et jure naturae; quo caeteri moriuntur. Item dicit auctoritas, quia voluit oblatus est (Isai. LIII). Igitur sola voluntate, quomodo ergo necessitate? Solutio. Constat quod in Christo nulla erat causa moriendi, quia nullum peccatum: tamen, ut volunt quidam, inter 538Dcaeteras poenalitates, etiam necessitatem moriendi voluntarie suscepit, et sic haec necessitas non impedit voluntatem, quam, sicut quando voluit, accepit: sic eam, quando voluit, deposuit: si enim, inquiunt, aliquod majus beneficium non esset collatum carni assumptae, necessario subjaceret legi naturae: quam etiam necessitatem quidam intelligunt per mortalitatem.

QUAESTIO CXXIX. Ego sum minimus apostolorum, etc. Quaeritur quomodo Apostolus se dicat minimum apostolorum, cum majoris meriti sit meritis aliorum: plus enim omnibus loboravit. Solutio. Hoc dicit secundum priorem statum, non secundum praesentem, in quo non minimus apostolorum fuit, sed maximus. Sed objicitur: Non enim 539Adicit: Ego fui minimus, sed ego sum minimus apostolorum: igitur cum non sit inter minimos, sed potius inter primos, videtur quod mentiatur, et sic ad mortem peccare: quia os, quod mentitur, occidit animam (Sap. I). Solutio. Sensus est: Ego sum minimus apostolorum, id est me aliis non praefero, sed potius alios mihi: nimirum, omnia enim peccata sua, praeterita vel praesentia, occulta vel manifesta, habebat ante oculos suos: aliorum vero simplicitatem et innocentiam consideravit, et sic secundum hanc considerationem humiliora de se sentiebat: sicut enim superbus si qua bona habet, illa semper attendit, et aliorum infirmitates, unde se solum magnum arbitratur, alios vilipendens: sic humilis suas infirmitates sine intermissione videt, bona vero 539Baliorum perpendit: hinc est quod sancti, cum sint majores, se humiliores sentiunt, nec est fallens opinio, quia bona, quae habent, non sua, sed Dei munera esse judicant, mala vero, quibus subjacent, sua esse sciunt.

QUAESTIO CXXX. Gratia Dei sum id quod sum, etc. Quaeritur de qua gratia loquatur. Siquidem de gratia Dei operante, et cooperante, sive gratia praeveniente, et gratia subsequente, jam in superioribus dictum est: gratia enim praeveniens, vel operans eadem est: quae operatur in nobis sine nobis, scilicet praeparando, et sanando liberum arbitrium, ut bonum velit, quam notat Apostolus dicens: Gratia Dei sum id quod sum: gratia vero subsequens, vel 539Ccooperans una et eadem est, quae operatur in nobis, non sine nobis, subsequendo, et adjuvando, ne frustra velimus, quam notat Apostolus dicens: Et gratia ejus in me vacua non fuit, quia omnibus plus laboravi: non autem ego, sed gratia Dei mecum. Ex hoc itaque, quod dicit: Ego sum id quod sum gratia Dei, destruitur error Pelagianorum, qui dicebant liberum arbitrium ad salutem promerendam sufficere. Item ex eo quod supponit, et gratia ejus in me vacua non fuit, hominem ostendit ex libero arbitrio aliquid posse, quod quidam haeretici negant dicentes, quod homo nil promereri potest. Apostolus vero demonstrat hominem ex se quidem nil posse, sed tantum ex gratia superveniente: oportet enim hominem gratia praeveniri: deinde liberum arbitrium, 539Djam a gratia praeventum ipsi gratiae cooperari debet: cujus natura talis est ut relucere et cooperari possit, sicut radio solis oculus tactus videre potest. Quod ergo homo operatur, ex gratia est cui cooperatur. Quaedam enim gratia, ut jam dictum est, operatur sine adjutorio hominis, quia compungit mentem, et excitat, homo vero sine gratia, nec consentire potest gratiae, nec aliud quidquam efficere, sed gratiae trahenti et ducenti innititur, et sic gratia adjutus promeretur. Ex quo patet quod non tantum gratia est, quando homo aliquid boni facit, sed etiam ex libero arbitrio, licet totum sit opus gratiae, vel per se, vel cum homine operantis. Sunt itaque quaedam ex sola gratia, quaedam ex gratia et homine.

540AQUAESTIO CXXXI. Si resurrectio mortuorum non est, nec Christus resurrexit. Quaeritur de hypothetica an sit vera, et quomodo sit intelligenda. Solutio. Vera est, et sic intelligitur: Si impossibile esset mortuos resurgere, ut quidam haeretici dicebant, nec Christum surrexisse est possibile; vel si sancti non essent resurrecturi, nec verum esset quod Christus resurrexit; quia totum quod fecit in carne, moriendo, patiendo, resurgendo, pro nobis fecit.

QUAESTIO CXXXII. Si Christus non resurrexit, inanis est fides nostra. Quaeritur quomodo dicat Apostolus inanem esse fidem nostram: et miserabiliores sumus omnibus hominibus (I Cor. XV), si non erit resurrectio mortuorum vel corporum. Nam cum 540Banima immortalis, et ipsa sola capax sit visionis Dei, et sic sola habere beatitudinem possit, nonne beati esse possumus sine corporum resurrectione? Et ad idem:

QUAESTIO CXXXIII. Quaeritur ad quid erit corporum resurrectio, cum eis ibi opus non erit, ubi Christus erit omnia in omnibus, nec ipsa beatitudinem suscipere possint, quae erit solius animae? Solutio. Videndum est diligenter quid dicatur, et secundum quid. Quod enim ait: Miserabiliores sumus omnibus hominibus, non secundum animam, sed secundum corpus dicit. Hic enim majorem miseriam aliis passus est Apostolus. Est autem corporum resurrectio, ut et secunda gloriemur stola: claritas enim illa, 540Cquae in corpore erit: ad augmentum beatitudinis ipsius erit, ut quod prius habuit ad miseriam, jam habeat ad gloriam et decorem. Probat Apostolus resurrectionem mortuorum per resurrectionem Christi: quae ideo tantum facta est, ut resurrectio corporum crederetur, et fieret: Cum tradiderit regnum Deo et Patri (Ibid.), id est cum Ecclesiam, in qua modo regnat per fidem, per cognitionem, quam habuit de Filio, ad Patris cognitionem et visionem perducet.

QUAESTIO CXXXIV. Donec ponat omnes inimicos sub pedibus ejus. Quaeritur quomodo dicat quod oportet Christum regnare: Donec ponat, etc. (Ibid.) Nonne in aeternum regnabit, et praecipue inimicis subditis? Solutio. In locis similibus, donec, ponitur 540Dpro in aeternum: si enim tunc, quando habet adversarios, regnat, constat quod regnabit omnibus sibi subjectis, et sic in aeternum regnabit.

QUAESTIO CXXXV.-- Tunc, et ipse Filius subjectus erit illi, qui subjecit sibi omnia. Quaeritur secundum quam naturam Filium subjectum Patri dicat. Nam si secundum divinam, eo minor erit: quod falsum est, quia secundum divinitatem aequalis est Patri. Item si secundum humanam hoc sit dictum, tunc secundum eam omnia sunt subjecta ei: et secundum humanam est Dominus omnium: quare et Creator, et sic secundum eamdem videtur esse aequalis Patri; secundum quam minor eo est: unde legitur: Aequalis Patri secundum divinitatem; minor Patre secundum humanitatem. Solutio. Potest 541Ahoc sane intelligi secundum utramque naturam, scilicet divinam et humanam, secundum humanam omnia sunt subjecta ei, secundum quam ad aequalitatem Patris sublimatus est, dum verbo consubstantiali Patri, in unam personam, humana natura unita est, secundum quam plenitudinem donorum et ipse accepit; de qua plenitudine nos omnes accepimus (Joan. I), et sic ei subjecti. Item secundum divinam naturam quidam sic intelligunt, quod subjectus est Filius Patri, quia ab eo habet esse, a quo habet quidquid habet. Juxta illud: Doctrina mea non est mea (Joan. VII). Item: Pater major me est (Joan. XIV). Quod nonnulli secundum divinam naturam intelligi volunt. In hujusmodi verbo notatur distinctio, quia Filius a Patre, non Pater a Filio 541Best; unde Pater principium Deitatis dicitur, quia a nullo est, et ab ipso tam Filius, quam Spiritus sanctus est. Est enim Pater principium, non de principio Filius principium de principio; Spiritus sanctus ab utroque procedens, sed hujusmodi nonnisi convenienti et loco et tempore dicenda sunt, ne infirmi scandalum incurrant.

QUAESTIO CXXXVI. In dispari claritate erit par gaudium. Quaeritur si dispar claritas, quomodo gaudium par possit esse? Nonne juxta quantitatem claritatis, erit quantitas gaudii! Nonne ipsa claritas erit ipsum gaudium? Item si unus altero beatior, alter altero majus gaudium habebit, quomodo ergo par gaudium erit? Item gaudium omnium nonne 541Cerit singulorum? quomodo ergo in dispari claritate erit par gaudium? Si idem nummus omnibus dabitur, quomodo dispar claritas? si par gaudium erit, ergo gaudium Petri erit gaudium Martini. Solutio. Aliud est gaudium experientiae, aliud voluntatis; ut gaudium Petri renumerationis est, et experientiae, Martino vero non experientiae, sed affectus est. Tantum enim placet illi bonum Petri, quantum ipsi Petro, non tamen in se sentit, et experitur tantam beatitudinem, quantam Petrus sentit. Est itaque differens beatitudo secundum quantitatem, licet sit eadem secundum qualitatem. Veluti ergo de sanitate alicujus convalescentis ex infirmitate, tantum gaudeo, quantum ipse, affectu, et si non experientia, quia sanitatem in me non sentio, quam ipse experitur. 541DSicut duo eodem lecto conteguntur, alter tamen plus calet: sic in una visione Dei, unus intensius gaudebit, quam alter. Sed nullus inferior, nulli majori invidebit, nec majus gaudium superioris sibi desiderabit, quia unusquisque tantum habebit, quantum volet, alioquin non esset beatus. Ibi vita sine morte, notitia sine errore, amor sine offensione. Ibi videbitur finis desideriorum nostrorum scilicet Deus sine fine, amabitur sine fastidio, laudabitur sine fatigatione.

QUAESTIO CXXXVII. Seminatur corpus animale, etc. Quaeritur an corpus ab anima, an anima a corpore habeat animalitatem, id est sensualitatem? Solutio. Nec corpus animalitatem, nisi-ab anima habere potest; nec animalis, id est, sensualitatem 542Ahabens, esset anima non corpori conjuncta. Videtur itaque animalitas nosci ex utriusque conjunctione, anima tamen sola sentit per corpus, corpus vero ea suscipit, non etiam sentit. Prius enim homo sic creatus est, ut ex creatione passibilis esset, nunquam tamen pateretur, nisi peccasset. Unde et dictus est immortalis fuisse ante peccatum, quia poterat non mori, poterat enim non peccare, quia si non peccaset non moreretur.

QUAESTIO CXXXVIII. Solet item quaeri, cum dictus sit mortalis, et quodammodo immortalis homo ante peccatum, an utrumque habuit ex natura, an neutrum, an alterum tantum. Solutio. Salva reverentia secretorum, sine praejudicio melioris sententiae dicimus quod naturaliter fuit homo ante peccatum mortalis et passibilis; 542Bbeneficio vero ligni vitae fieret immortalis: unde doctores non dicunt simpliciter illum tunc fuisse immortalem; sed addunt quodam modo, et determinant quomodo: mortalem vero simpliciter eum pronuntiant fuisse, juxta hoc dictum est: Primus homo factus est in animam viventem, id est in animam, quae corpus vegetaret et vivificaret, non sicut cibis non indigeret.

QUAESTIO CXXXIX. Haec autem dico, fratres, quod caro et sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt; neque corruptio incorruptelam. Quaeritur igitur quae corpora habituri sumus. Solutio. Eadem corpora, quae nunc habemus: post resurrectionem habebimus, sed immutata non secundum substantiam, sed 542Csecundum qualitatem: haec dissolubilia; illa vero indissolubilia; sed bonorum impassibilia, malorum vero passibilia: unde ipsa tanquam in morte perpetua erunt. Quod autem indissolubilia erunt, decet Apostolus, dicens: Caro, et sanguis regnum Dei non possidebunt (Ibid.). Quod autem impassibilia corpora habituri sunt, insinuat Apostolus, dicens: sed omnes immutabimur (Ibid.).

QUAESTIO CXL. Canetenim tuba, etc. Quaeritur, quid nomine tubae significetur? Solutio. Dicunt doctores, quod aliquod evidens et praeclarum signum, sic vocat Apostolus, quo mysterium futurae resurrectionis implebitur: quae tuba alibi vocatur clamor, alibi vox archangeli vel vox Christi.

542DQUAESTIO CXLI. Quaeritur etiam de voce tubae, an futura sit materialis? Solutio. Patet quod vox materialis erit ministerio angeli facta; quia sicut per tubam convocabatur populus Judaeorum ad festum vel ad bellum, sic tunc ad judicium vocabuntur, vel aliquod evidens signum, quo idem fiat, quod voce fieri solet.

QUAESTIO CXLII. Absorpta est mors in victoria. Quaeritur quae mors, et in qua victoria sic absorpta? mortis enim nomine quandoque diabolus, qui est auctor mortis, quandoque peccatum, quod separat a Deo, quandoque dissolutio animae et corporis significatur. Solutio. Potest sane intelligi et de diabolo, et de peccato, et dissolutione animae et corporis. Constat quod in victoria Dominicae resurrectionis sit absorptus 543Adiabolus: ne dominetur, sicut ante, quando timore mortis compellebantur homines ad quodlibet scelus; nunc autem sancti mortem contemnunt: maxime autem in futura generali omnium resurrectione omnis mors absorbebitur, quando hoc mortale induet incorruptelam.

QUAESTIO CXLIII. Virtus vero peccati lex. Qualiter hoc sit intelligendum: ex his, quae dicta sunt, super epistolam ad Romanos, facile potest perpendi: lege enim data, et carnalis concupiscentia invaluit, et praevaricatio accessit. Lex enim prohibendo auget concupiscentiam, nisi Spiritus sanctus infundat charitatem.

QUAESTIO CXLIV. Itaque fratres stabiles estote, et immobiles. Quaeritur in quo haec duo differunt. Solutio. 543BStabiles in fide, ne per se moveantur pede superbiae; immobiles in tentationibus, ne manu peccatorum impellente fidem deserant. Tria sunt genera tentationum: unum violentum, aliud fraudulentum, tertium violentum et fraudulentum. Primum fit per apertas persecutiones; secundum per falsos fratres et haereticos; tertium fiet per Antichristum. Omne 544Agenus autem tentationum immittit diabolus: unde et leo dictus est aperte saeviendo, draco occulte et latenter seducendo: unde scriptum est: Sub lingua ejus labor, et dolor (Psal. X).

QUAESTIO CXLV. De Apollo notum facio vobis, quod multum rogavi eum, ut veniret ad vos, sed non fuit voluntas ejus, ut nunc veniret (I Cor. XVI). Quaeritur uter irrationabiliter egerit, an Paulus rogando, ut iret? an Apollo non acquiescendo quia videtur aut hic non rogasse quod decuit, aut ille omisisse quod facere debuit? Solutio. Verum est quod uterque rationabiliter egit, quia Apostolus rogavit, ut hoc faceret; unde Apollo, quia sic petebatur, videbat magis dimittendam Apostoli petitionem, quare 544Bnon acquievit.

QUAESTIO CXLVI. Salutate invicem in osculo sancto. Quaeritur quare adjecit, sancto? Solutio. Est osculum lasciviae, est osculum proditionis, ut Judae, est osculum sanctitatis et concordiae, ut quod interius appareat, scilicet vinculum charitatis, etc. De hoc ergo dicit, ut caetera excludat.

II. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

  • 513

513AQUESTION I. Paul, called to be an Apostle, etc. (I Cor. I.) This Epistle, which is addressed to the Corinthians, was not written by the Apostle in the second place, as in the body of the epistles it is arranged in the second place. For both epistles sent to the Corinthians were written before 513Bthat which is to the Romans. Which is clear from this, that in the Epistle to the Romans he says that he will set out for Rome after he has assigned the collection made by the Achaeans for the poor who are at Jerusalem. Of which collection, to be made, he makes mention in these. But it is not without a rational cause that that to the Romans is set before the others in the body of the epistles, but on account of the dignity of the Romans. Or rather because in it first is taken away and destroyed that vice which is pride. But the Corinthians, converted to the faith by the Apostle, but afterward in manifold ways subverted and seduced by false apostles, were erring in the virtues of the sacraments, and especially in the virtue of baptism, thinking that, when conferred by an evil man, it had no virtue, a greater from a better, a lesser from a less good. 513CThey also thought little of the Apostle, and held him in contempt: he who had not come to them in the words of human wisdom, but in the simplicity of faith for the instruction of the little ones. Concerning the resurrection also they did not think rightly, saying that it had already taken place: some also among them altogether denied it. Certain ones also wished to hold the law together with the Gospel as though necessary to salvation. In marriage also they sinned, as in many other things, and made schisms: in which the Apostle intends to correct them. For after pride is cut down in us, it remains that we cut down also the other vices. From these things, then, it appears what is the matter of this epistle, what the intention, what the mode and order of proceeding. But the special matter of this 513Depistle is the state of the Corinthians, in which they then were, when the Apostle wrote to them from Ephesus. But the intention is to recall them from contentions to the unity of faith. But the mode is such, that he instructs, rebukes, confirms, praises, according to the qualities of persons. The order is such: he sends beforehand a salutation, after the manner of those writing epistles, lest at the outset he seem to have chided them. Then he sets before them concerning good things, that others may be conformed to them, and thus he comes to reproving contention. He begins therefore from the salutation, saying, Paul, using a name of humility against pride; Apostle, which is a name of dignity and office.

QUESTION II. Through the will of God, etc. It is asked what he here calls the will of God. For the will of God is sometimes called his counsel, sometimes 514Ahis precept, sometimes his disposition, sometimes his approbation, sometimes his permission. Solution. He calls the will of God his good pleasure.

QUESTION III. Grace to you, and peace from God. It is asked what the grace of God is. Solution. The grace of God is said to be 514BGod giving freely, and grace, that is, divine inspiration, namely the operation of God, from which the soul is moved to love God and neighbor.

QUESTION IV. To them that wait for the revelation, etc. It is asked whether to every just man it is revealed at once after his death concerning his salvation. For it seems not: for since that revelation is a full knowledge, which is eternal beatitude, it seems, if this be granted, that no one is in purgatorial punishments: for can anyone be at once in punishment and in glory? Solution. The perfect pass at once to the knowledge of the highest good, in which is eternal beatitude. But the less perfect, before they come to eternal beatitude, pass through purgatorial punishments, yet certain of their 514Crest at last. But that there are purgatorial punishments, Augustine makes manifest, saying: The mildest purgatorial punishment is heavier than any temporal punishment whatever that is among us: and so there cannot be at once punishment and glory in such a fire.

QUESTION V. It is asked how that is to be understood which is read: The angels shall tremble in the day of judgment; for if then there will be trembling in them, how are they blessed? Solution. That trembling notes veneration of a higher power, not that the punishment of fear can be there where there is eternal beatitude. It is to be noted that not every mortal sin is called a crime, but only that which is worthy of accusation and damnation.

QUESTION VI. Unto the day of the coming of the Lord, etc. It is asked whether the Lord will come on a day to judgment; 514Dbecause often the time of his coming is called a day. Solution. The time of the coming of the Lord is called a day, not for the illumination of the air, but for the revelation of hidden things: for all things which now lie hidden will then be laid open. But it is not known whether he will come by day or by night. For not only by the name of day, as above, but also by the name of night is the time of judgment designated, as it is written in the Gospel: At midnight there was a cry made: Behold, the bridegroom cometh (Matth. XXV); but it is called night on account of its exceeding hiddenness: the day of judgment is so called on account of the discerning of the good and the wicked.

QUESTION VII. Now this I say, that every one of you saith: I am of Paul, etc. It is asked whether the Apostle speaks truly, saying, Now this, etc., when 515Anone of them said this. For they did not glory in the true apostles, but in the false. Whence in what follows he is about to say: But these things, brethren, I have transferred in a figure to myself, and to Apollo (I Cor. IV). Solution. The Apostle speaks truly, and the sense of the words is: Now this I say, that every one, etc., that is, this which I say is like that which every one of you says. But he did not wish to designate those in whom they gloried by their proper names, lest he should seem to envy them; and that in greater matters he might show that in lesser ones there is no glorying.

QUESTION VIII. Augustine says that Christ retained to himself the power of baptizing, which, if he willed, he could have given to his servants. It is asked, therefore, what that power is, which Christ retained to himself, and could have given to his servants, 515Band yet did not give. Whether it is the power of outwardly dipping bodies; but this he gave to the apostles, on whom he conferred the ministry of baptizing; but if he calls the power of baptizing the inward washing of souls, this power God alone can have, whose alone it is to infuse himself into souls, and to wipe away the stains of sins: how then could he give this to his servants? Solution. In answering this question many labor, not knowing what Augustine signified by the name of power. But we say that he calls power a dignity: by which, through the invocation of the name of Christ, or of the whole Trinity, baptism is given: which dignity he could have given to his chief servants, so that baptism might be designated by their name, and be called the baptism of Paul, the baptism 515Cof Peter, and baptism designated by their names might have as great a force as it has when designated by the name of Christ himself: yet he did not wish to give this to them, lest anyone place his hope in man.

QUESTION IX. Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? etc. What it is to be baptized in the name of Paul is wont to be asked. Solution. The faithful are not baptized in the name of Paul; because those who are baptized are not bidden to believe in Paul, but in Christ, nor is the name of Paul invoked over them or over the element, that the sacrament may be made, but the name of Christ, who alone baptizes in the Spirit.

QUESTION X. Lest the cross of Christ should be made void by the wisdom of speech. It is asked how by the wisdom of speech 515Dthe cross of Christ should be made void. Solution. The wisdom of the world, which is called the wisdom of speech, because it is commended by no virtue, but by the composition of words alone, supposes that natural genius suffices for knowing, and free will for living rightly: which if it were so, the cross of Christ would be made void, that is, Christ would have died in vain.

QUESTION XI. I will destroy the wisdom, etc. Is not all wisdom from God? how then is it said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise? Does God destroy that which is from himself? Solution. Their wisdom in themselves is not the wisdom of God; because they ascribe it to themselves, and abuse it: whence while they think to comprehend the highest things, they become vain in their thoughts, and thus from their wisdom incur damnation to themselves. Therefore their false 516Aopinion, by which they believed that God could not do anything against the accustomed course of nature, and by which they supposed that free will sufficed for salvation, is called by the prophet the wisdom of the wise, which God destroys by acting against it, according to the reasons above, working our salvation in the midst of the earth.

QUESTION XII. The world by wisdom knew not God. It is asked how this is true which he here says, since elsewhere it is written of the wise of the world: When they had known God, they glorified him not as God (Rom. I): how are both true, the world knew not, and when they had known God? etc. Solution. That: When they had known God, etc., is understood of the possibility of knowing. But this, 516Bthe world knew not God, is taken of the act of knowing. Or rather that, when they had known God, is understood of a few of the wiser and more excellent. But this, the world knew not, is expounded of all, or the greater part. Whence he here says the world: by which name the whole, or the greater part, is wont to be understood. Or the world, that is, the wise of the world, even if they had known God according to the works of restoration, in power, not in piety; in majesty, not in humility. It is to be noted that there are theophanies in creatures, that is, divine apparitions, as in the world, whose greatness demonstrates the highest power of God; but the fullness or beauty of the world demonstrates the wisdom of God; but the usefulness of the world intimates the benignity of God: in power the Father, in wisdom the Son, in 516Cbenignity the Holy Spirit is understood.

QUESTION XIII. He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord, etc. It is asked what it is to glory in oneself, or of oneself. Solution. He glories in himself, or of himself, who thinks that to be of himself which is of God, and therefore attributes praise to himself, who, so far as in him lies, takes from God what is his own: for God alone is the author of good things. Whence it follows that whoever says any good to be of himself, in a certain manner makes himself God. He also glories in himself who, although he know that what he has is from God, yet turns back to himself the end of it, which he ought to refer to God.

QUESTION XIV. It is asked also what it is to glory in the Lord. Solution. He glories in the Lord who by the grace 516Dof God alone judges himself worthy of glory.

QUESTION XV. And I came not to you in loftiness of speech, or of wisdom, etc. (I Cor. II.) It is asked how the Apostle says that he came not to the Corinthians in wisdom, but preached to them Christ, and him crucified: as though it were less difficult to understand that God assumed in the flesh died, than that God is one in essence, and three in persons? Solution. In Christ there are two natures, human and divine: but those things which are according to the human nature are more akin to us than those which are according to the divine nature: wherefore by us they are more easily believed and understood. But those which are according to the divine nature, as concerning the three persons, and the same essence, and the like, are more remote, 517Aand therefore more difficult to understand. Whence he well said that he came not to them in wisdom, when he discoursed to them of the death of Christ; because he preached those lesser things, and not those loftier ones.

QUESTION XVI. Is it not required, in order that anyone be perfect, that he believe God to be one and three? And thus the Apostle seems to have handed down to them an imperfect doctrine, not preaching those loftier things, and thus to have deceived them. Solution. Faith is spoken of in two ways: either when it is simply set forth what is to be believed; or when the distinction of the things which are believed is set out distinctly — what is to be believed, and how, and why. But thus the Apostle set before them, generally and without distinction of the several articles, what they ought to believe. For thus it behooves that in the first place 517Bbelievers be initiated, and afterward that the advancing be perfected.

QUESTION XVII. We speak wisdom among the perfect. It is asked whom the Apostle here calls perfect. For some are perfect in faith and in knowledge; others perfect in knowledge, and less in faith; others perfect in faith, and less in knowledge. In faith and knowledge the apostles are perfect; perfect in knowledge, and less in faith, are certain clerics, who are less constant in faith than the country folk; in faith and not in knowledge are very many country folk, who have attained little of knowledge, and yet believe perfectly. Solution. It seems to us that the Apostle was speaking wisdom among those perfect in knowledge, because those who are perfect in faith alone seem incapable of the higher things: yet deservedly to such faithful ones many things are often revealed: 517Cand therefore, according to some, he speaks among those perfect in faith.

QUESTION XVIII. Neither of the princes of this world, which is brought to nought [who are brought to nought]. It is asked how the wisdom of the philosophers is brought to nought, since it seems to be itself a comprehension of the truth. Solution. It is brought to nought when it is shown to be false or nothing: for they thought, as has already been said, that God could do nothing against nature. And so, among the great and many things which they truly comprehended, they asserted many false ones, and that truth which they had from God they attributed not to God but to themselves, whence their wisdom was turned into darkness.

QUESTION XIX. Which none of the princes of this world. It is asked first whom he calls the princes of the world? Solution. Either the wise of the world, or the demons, or even 517Dthose learned in the law.

QUESTION XX. It is asked, therefore, secondly, how that is true, that none of the demons knew him, since it is written of those who said: Jesus, thou Son of David, why art thou come to torment us before the time? (Matth. VIII.) And again: And there were many devils going out, and crying: Thou art the Son of God; and he suffered them not to speak, for they knew him to be the Son of God (Marc I). Solution. The demons are said to have known on account of their supposing: who rather supposed Christ to be God than truly knew it: for God always left the devil in doubt, so that always after some humble things he did lofty ones, and after the sublime returned to the humble: whence after that notable 518Amiracle concerning Lazarus, when the devil altogether thought him to be God, he allowed himself to be seized, bound, scourged: whence again the devil judged him to be a mere man; but when he was now led to the governor, and the Jews themselves confirmed in evil, it was in some manner revealed to him that through him he would lose his own right, and he wished to persuade Pilate through his wife to release him.

QUESTION XXI. Likewise it is asked, thirdly, concerning the Jews, how it is true that they did not know him, since it is written of them in the Gospel parable: Behold the heir; come, let us kill him (Marc. XII). And elsewhere: That through envy they had delivered him up (Matth. XXVII): but if they knew him, and yet killed him, incredible cruelty was in them. Likewise, if they knew him to be God, they knew him to be immortal, and thus unable 518Bto die: how then did they seek his death, if they knew that he could not die? Solution. Some say that the Jews knew Christ, which they could not deny. Or in truth some of them knew him to be that one who had been promised in the law and the prophets. But they did not believe him to be God; yet that they killed him whom they knew to be just, was envy. Whose nature is such, that against its own goods it seeks the harm of others: therefore they were utterly ignorant of the dispensation of the divine counsel.

QUESTION XXII. That we may know the things that are given us. It is asked what it is to know the things that are given us. Solution. To know from whom they are given, and not to be ungrateful to the giver: for he is said truly to have who knows whence he has; he does not have, who knows not whence he has, and is ungrateful 518Cto him from whom he has: for no one is blessed by the gifts of God who is ungrateful to the giver.

QUESTION XXIII. Comparing spiritual things with spiritual. It is asked whom he calls spiritual: for some are perfect in life, and not in understanding; others in understanding, and not in life. Solution. Those whom above he named perfect, here he calls spiritual.

QUESTION XXIV. It is asked whom he calls the animal man. For a man is animal according to life, and according to understanding. Solution. He calls animal the man intent upon earthly wisdom, who, considering earthly things, reckons the things that are of God to be foolish.

QUESTION XXV. But the spiritual man discerneth all things that are necessary to salvation, and he himself is judged of no man. 518DFor the animal man cannot understand what he doeth, or why. It is objected. Peter was rebuked by Paul, therefore a spiritual man is judged by a spiritual man. Solution. The spiritual man is judged of no man, that is, he is shown by no one to be damnable and worthy of damnation: for although he sin in something, yet this is not damnable to him.

QUESTION XXVI. I could not speak to you as to spiritual, etc. (I Cor. II). Was not the Apostle spiritual, both in life and in knowledge, and thus able to speak spiritual things, which he also did? Whence above: We speak wisdom among the perfect (I Cor. II); how then does he say, I could not speak to you as to spiritual? Solution. He does not say this as though he did not inwardly have the faculty of teaching greater things, but because they themselves were not fit hearers; yet often, when the perfect and imperfect 519Aare mingled, the same things are said, even if they are not understood in the same way.

QUESTION XXVII. I have planted, Apollo watered, but God now gave the increase. It is asked how the Apostle divides between himself, and God, and Apollo, since Paul or Apollo does nothing except from God and through God, and thus whatever either Paul or Apollo works, God also works. Solution. The Apostle divides, that he may show what God works through Paul himself, and through Apollo, and through himself: for the Apostle, by preaching, was working unto the faith of Christ, which God also did through Paul. For in vain would the Apostle speak outwardly, unless the Holy Spirit were within, working, and moving the mind.

QUESTION XXVIII. He that watereth, and he that planteth, are one. 519B It is asked how one, since they are divided both in substance and in accident? Solution. They are one, that is, indifferent. For neither does Paul confer more from that which is Paul's than Apollo from that which is Apollo's. For in the conferring of gifts this one does no more than that one: for God alone confers the gifts; yet Paul labors more than Apollo, and a greater gift is conferred through the office of Paul than of Apollo, because through the faith which is from preaching one comes to baptism. Or, through the sacraments themselves no more is conferred from this one than from that one, or through this one than through that one.

QUESTION XXIX. For we are God's helpers, etc. Does God need anything? How then were the apostles God's helpers? Solution. They are called God's helpers because God works through them, although he could work that same thing 519Cthrough himself.

QUESTION XXX. As a wise architect, I have laid the foundation, etc. It is asked what he calls the foundation. Solution. The faith of Christ, which works through love, which they obtained from the preaching of Paul himself: this foundation remaining, no one can perish, although some stains adhere, which are purged by fire. For although here they possessed some worldly things by desire, yet they did not prefer these to God, but God to all. But to prefer God to all is, if the option or choice were given of dying or of denying Christ, to choose to die rather than to deny Christ. Upon this foundation one builds this, another that.

QUESTION XXXI. It is asked, what is to be understood by wood, hay, 519Dand stubble? Solution. Some say that by these three is understood venial sin: but how do these build upon this foundation, since rather any sin whatever pertains to destruction than to building? Likewise, how shall he who builds these be saved yet so as by fire, since faith without works is dead? Likewise, if any man have all faith, so as to remove mountains, and have not charity, it profiteth nothing (I Cor. XIII): therefore, if there is no salvation without charity, how can anyone be saved building these three alone upon this foundation?

QUESTION XXXII. Others say otherwise, that by wood, hay, stubble are understood good works, but imperfect ones. According to which opinion it is asked how a good work is to burn, or how 520Ait suffers loss? Solution. Not the good work, because it is good; but because it is imperfect it will be purged of its imperfection, and especially of certain carnal affections which the builders of such things have, which seem to be venial sins.

QUESTION XXXIII. All things are yours; and you are Christ's; and Christ is God's, etc. It is asked according to which nature we are Christ's, that is, whether we are his according to the human nature, or according to the divine. Solution. It can be said that we are his not only according to the divine nature, according to which he is our Creator, but also we are his according to the human nature, according to which he is our Redeemer; but he himself, according to both natures, is of God the Father, from whom he has whatever 520Bhe has; but in one way and in another: for according to that which he is God, he has by nature all things which are the Father's; and all the same things he has according to that which he is man, but by grace: this is the norm of right faith.

QUESTION XXXIV. I am conscious to myself of nothing, etc. (I Cor. IV). It is asked how the Apostle says that he is conscious to himself of nothing, and yet is not hereby justified: and John in his Epistle says: If our heart do not reprehend us, we have confidence toward God (I Joan. III). And Paul himself elsewhere: For our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience (II Cor. I): wherefore we ought to think ourselves just, and thence to have glory, if our conscience does not reprehend us. For what is a greater perfection of justice than to have so pure 520Ca conscience? Solution. Something can always lie hidden from us: and therefore, in order that we may have true justice, it does not suffice that our conscience does not gnaw at us: yet we can glory in this, that our conscience is clean and pure.

QUESTION XXXV. Likewise it is asked how the Apostle was not conscious to himself, since he knew that he was not without sin. Whence John: If we say that we have no sin, we are liars, and the truth is not in us (I Joan. I). And the child, whose life is of one day upon the earth (Job II), is not without sin. Whence he himself says: And I do that which I will not (Rom. VII). Solution. The Apostle was of such perfection that whatever his conscience dictated to him was to be done, 520Dthis he did. Whence, if at any time as a man he had sinned, either through ignorance, or by stealth, or by frailty, the force of divine love consumed the whole like stubble.

QUESTION XXXVI. Judge not before the time, etc. It is one thing to judge concerning ambiguous matters, which is forbidden, because damnable: it is another to suspect, which is of human infirmity, of which perhaps no one is free. But since the Apostle forbids judging, and the Lord himself forbids the same in the Gospel, what is it that elsewhere the Lord says: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep (Matth. VII). And how they may also be discerned, he himself adds, saying: By their fruits you shall know them (ibid.). Hence he seems to intimate that we ought to judge concerning such. Solution. 521AIt is one thing to discern the evil, that they may be guarded against; another to judge them worthy of damnation: whom we do not definitely know whether they are good or evil.

QUESTION XXXVII. Likewise it is asked how false prophets can be discerned from their works, since they do all the same things that the good also do: for by fruits are understood works. Solution. By the virtue of perseverance the false are proved and discerned from the true.

QUESTION XXXVIII. It is asked whether that is true which the Apostle says: You are now filled (I Cor. IV), since he speaks ironically: which does not seem to be, since the contrary is true. Solution. As often as such a kind of speech occurs, as to the surface of the word and the first signification of the utterance, what is said is false: yet he himself who speaks does not lie; 521Bbut rather speaks the truth, which happens from the nature of the trope.

QUESTION XXXIX. Not to confound you. Is it not good to bring it about by a word that a sinner be confounded, and blush for his fault, and thus be corrected: how then does the Apostle say, I say not this, to confound you? Solution. Confusion is twofold. There is a confusion which is unto death, from which some are made worse; and there is a confusion which is of correction, when one blushes from correction over his sins, that a man may abstain the more.

QUESTION XL. Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity? It is asked how the Apostle divides, saying, whether with a rod, or in charity. Solution. The name "charity" is here, from the adjunct, restricted to the sweet and delightful things 521Cwhich come from charity; but sometimes charity signifies all things, hope thou, and the sweet things, which pertain to salvation.

QUESTION XLI. The expositor says that in those who are punished by an inflicted penalty, sin is diminished: but it is asked how this is true, since they bear the inflicted penalty unwillingly, and in this are contrary to justice, and thus sin the more, and thus their sin is increased in this, that they are punished. Solution. It can be said of such, that at least they avoid, through the penalty which they suffer, the sins into which they would fall if they lived longer: for if they bore the penalty willingly, even the sin already committed would be forgiven.

(I COR. V). I have judged to deliver such a man 521Dto Satan, etc. From this place of the Apostle the Church takes the sentence of anathema, that is, of separation; and separation is made now of known and manifest persons, now of unknown; but whether of these or of those, they are first to be summoned before the Church. Some also are to be awaited longer, and more often admonished, according to the diversity and quality of persons and of sins, as if a king, through whose anger slaughter threatens the Church. But after they have been separated, if they are known, in no way is one to communicate with them: if unknown, if anyone communicate unknowingly, he does not sin; but if he suspect, if he can avoid it without scandal, let him avoid; if he cannot, let him communicate. But this vengeance ought to be done for the sake of the common utility, both of him and of others.

522AQUESTION XLII. It is asked, then, whether to excommunicate someone is good, which seems so, because just. Solution. It is good, that is, expedient, yet not in itself and from its own quality is it good: but when such a thing is called just, it is understood thus, that is, requited according to desert, not that it is informed by the quality of justice.

QUESTION XLIII. Likewise it is asked whether to be excommunicated is good. Solution. According to the aforesaid reasoning it seems to be good, because excommunication seems to be expedient not only to the rest but even to him: for if he should resist the admonition of the Church, he would sin.

QUESTION XLIV. But it is asked, if it happen that he be excommunicated who did not deserve it, but someone is struck with the sentence of excommunication out of the hatred or 522Benvy of a prelate, whether he ought to resist, or to yield. Solution. If without scandal he can resist, let him resist, and by good zeal repress the swelling of his prelate; if without scandal he cannot, let him yield, and for God's sake patiently endure: whence the sentence of a prelate is always to be feared, not always to be held. When someone is excommunicated, he is delivered into the power of Satan, that he may vex his flesh, so that at last he may thus come to his senses: yet Satan does not always vex. For the crafty enemy spares one, that he may gain many, or that he may keep him for himself.

QUESTION XLV. Purge out the velus leaven, etc. It is asked what he calls the old leaven? Solution. Vain boasting, or the oldness of life, which is to be purged by 522Cnewness of life.

QUESTION XLVI. Such cannot be gained to Christ, etc. This is from the gloss. It is asked: Since the human mind is prone to evil rather than to good, and especially when it is urged to return to accustomed things, why did the Apostle grant to those newly converted to the faith to have table and conversation in common with the gentiles, since Christians would more easily come to idolatry by the persuasion of the gentiles than the gentiles come to the faith by the admonition of Christians? Solution. In the primitive Church those converted to the faith, fervent with charity, could not easily be torn from the foundation: which the Apostle knowing, granted to it only fellowship with the gentiles.

QUESTION XLVII. If he who is named a brother among 522Dyou is a fornicator, etc. Since there is now so great a multitude in the Church, it is asked whether we act against the precept of the Apostle when we take food with such, or whether all such are to be cast out of the Church and cut off with the sickle of anathema. Solution. So indeed it would be to be done, if it could be done without scandal: but yet, because so great and so many would rather make a schism, since they spurn correction and amendment, they are tolerated: and therefore nothing else remains but that Rachel weep for her children. It is to be noted that of fornications some are bodily, others spiritual: bodily is every use of those members apart from the lawful; spiritual is that which separates the soul from God, and takes it away, as a bride from the bridegroom.

QUESTION XLVIII. Know you not that the saints shall judge this 523Aworld? (I Cor. VI.) Here the Apostle shows that it is lawful for the saints to judge concerning secular matters: but if this is so, how does he afterward subjoin: there is now plainly a fault among you, that you have lawsuits among yourselves (Ibid.): if it is lawful to judge, how is this a fault? Solution. It is lawful for the saints to have causes under discipline, but it is not lawful to contend among themselves.

QUESTION XLIX. It is asked how this is true, that it is lawful to demand back one's own, since the Lord says: If anyone take away what is thine, ask it not again? (Luc VI.) Solution. To demand back one's own, although it be not evil, yet is an occasion of evil: therefore the Lord counsels not to demand back one's own, for the sake of avoiding contentions. This is what the Apostle says: All things are lawful to me, but all things are not expedient (I Cor. X).

523BQUESTION L. It is asked in what manner the saints are to judge in the future? And it is said, not only by the comparison of a better deed, but also by authority and power. Whence not without reason it is asked what that power is, since it is written: The Father judgeth no man, but hath given all judgment to the Son (Joan. V). Solution. As Daniel says: The judgment sat, and the books were opened, namely of the eternal reasons, according to which the judgment shall be made, and the books of consciences, concerning which the judgment shall be made (Dan. VII). These books of the eternal reasons and of consciences will be open and manifest to those who are to judge with the Lord. And this revelation of hidden things, according to some, is their power and authority: according to others, the saints are therefore said to be about to judge with the Lord because by their comparison the evil 523Cwill appear damnable. Whence it is read that the saints shall judge the nations.

QUESTION LI. It is asked whether it is a precept, or a counsel, or a permission, this which he says concerning judgments? Now it is a counsel concerning the highest things, as that: Concerning virgins I have no precept; but I give counsel (I Cor. VII). A precept concerning middle things, as: Thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not commit adultery (Exod. XX), etc.; a permission concerning the lowest things, as concerning the taking of food. But it seems that it is a precept: for if I do not demand back my own, I foster in error him who has taken it away; wherefore for the sake of the common utility I ought to demand it back: wherefore I demand it back from precept; because every evil is to be fled from precept. Solution. It is a permission to demand back; but a counsel 523Dnot to demand back. The Apostle therefore shows what is lawful to the weak; but the Lord shows what befits the perfect, namely not to demand back: but to contend, and to carry on lawsuits before a judge, especially an unbeliever, is altogether a fault.

QUESTION LII. He who is joined to a harlot is made one body. It is asked concerning this unity, what it is, and according to what it is to be understood. Solution. He notes that such are one not only by bodily conjunction, but in the ardor of lust, and this is most foul, thus to be made one body with a harlot, who ought to be one spirit cleaving to God.

QUESTION LIII. For they shall be, he says, two in one flesh. It is asked how the Apostle brings forward this authority, which is concerning that conjugal union which is holy, 524Ato show this foul union, which is between the fornicator and the harlot, since in no way can that union which is there be this. Solution. The sense is: If in that conjugal union one body is made of both, much more is this made one flesh on account of the greater delight of the vice.

QUESTION LIV. Bear God, etc. What is it to bear God? Solution. To live soberly, and justly, and piously. They therefore bear God who live well in him: for this is to put on his image and the form of justice, just as they trample God under foot who by living ill deny him; but they lay God down who grow lukewarm in charity and are made more lax and remiss.

QUESTION LV. The gloss says: It is graver to sin against God than against the neighbor; but do not those who sin against the neighbor 524Boffend God? How then is this distinguished, both the one and the other? Solution. To sin against God is, through contempt in those things which pertain specially to him, as in the sacraments, and faith, and the like, to offend God. To sin against the neighbor is to injure him by some wrong, which is less grave than the first. Or, to sin against God is to violate the mind inwardly. To sin against the neighbor is outwardly to injure a man by word or example: not therefore is everyone who offends him said to sin against God.

QUESTION LVI. Now concerning the things whereof you wrote to me, etc. (I Cor. VII.) He treats of marriage in three ways: according to precept, according to permission, according to counsel, which several things let the diligent reader distinguish in their places. What marriage is must be seen, 524Cwhat the efficient cause, what the cause on account of which it is contracted, who are the legitimate persons, and what are the goods of marriage. And so marriage or matrimony is the marital conjunction of male and female, retaining, between legitimate persons, an undivided manner of life. This definition befits only the marriage of the faithful. According to others: Marriage is the power of lawfully being joined, contracted from lawful consent. The efficient cause is the material consent expressed through words of the present. The consent, which is in the soul, ought to be shown before the Church, without which there is no marriage, whence it is read: Matrimony is made not by the union of bodies, but by the will of souls. The cause on account of which it is contracted is the procreation 524Dof offspring, and the avoidance of fornication. The legitimate persons are those whom neither a vow of continence, nor blood, nor order, nor disparity of worship, nor condition, nor frigidity of nature impedes. Three are the goods of marriage: faith, offspring, sacrament — namely inseparability, which is twofold, of the sacrament and of matrimony itself: for this third good, namely the sacrament, is not marriage itself, although it is itself a sacrament, as is that also: but whether both are of the same thing can be asked, which here we defer to resolve for the sake of brevity, whose traces we follow: for in the [treatises on] sacraments and the sentences of our elders we pursue these things more diligently.

QUESTION LVII. But this I say by way of indulgence. It is asked what indulgence is, or is called? 525ASolution. Indulgence is the concession of a laxer life; so that what would be unlawful and a sin, where there was no concession, becomes lawful. For the carnal union of man and woman would be a sin, unless it had taken up the state of the married, and thus through concession the unlawful becomes lawful, which is wont to be done for the sake of avoiding a graver sin.

QUESTION LVIII. But I would that all of you were as myself. It is asked how the Apostle says that he wishes all chaste, since he knew that God does not: for if this were so, how would the propagation of the human race come about? Solution. There is an implicit condition, as if he said, I wish, and it is good, or it would please me, that all were such: perhaps, if all were good who now are, the number of the predestined would be filled from them.

525BQUESTION LIX. Let not the husband put away, etc. It is asked whether a husband can put away his wife, if she be convicted of adultery? Solution. He can put her away. Likewise it is asked whether he, or she, can be joined to another while the other is living. Some say that he cannot.

QUESTION LX. It is asked whether marriage still remains, namely after divorce; if it remains, then the husband has power over the body of his wife, and conversely. Solution. It remains, and he has the power; but he cannot use this power, unless a reconciliation has been made.

QUESTION LXI. It is asked au among unbelievers, or between a believer and an unbeliever, there is matrimony: which does not seem to be, since it is written that no marriage which was not made in God is ratified. Solution. 525CThey say that there is marriage among unbelievers, as between Priam and Hecuba, and between Philip and Herodias. Whence John reproved Herod for adultery; for it is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife (Matth. XIV): because, if there was adultery and marriage there, as Chrysostom says.

QUESTION LXII. But if the unbeliever depart, let him depart. It is asked, if between a believer and an unbeliever there is marriage, how the Apostle says: If he will depart, let the unbeliever depart, and let the believer be joined to another (I Cor. VII), when above he says that she who is dismissed should remain unmarried: for if it is a true marriage, how can it be dissolved? If it is not a marriage, how does he persuade them to remain together, since every union apart from the lawful is fornication? Solution. The believer has power 525Dover the body of the unbeliever, but not conversely; because, as is read, the injury done to the Creator dissolves the right of matrimony: the believer therefore can both remain and depart. Because also that debt which was owed was previously paid; but the power which she had, she did not lose. But the unbeliever departing, if he join himself to another, commits adultery.

QUESTION LXIII. Concerning the marriages of the ancients it is wont to be asked whether they were true marriages, seeing how one having several wives conducted himself toward each by marital law. How was there lawful consent there, retaining an undivided manner of life. Solution. Some say that they were not marriages, but held the place of marriage. But others say that there were true marriages among some, and that there are among the Jews and unbelievers: 526Afor he who says that the marriage of such is not ratified does not deny it to be a marriage, but asserts it not to be ratified.

QUESTION LXIV. It is asked whether marriage is a greater good than virginity. And it seems that it is; because there are greater straits, and pains, and labors in marriage than in virginity, and to each one the reward will be rendered according to his labor. Solution. It does not follow, if the labor is greater here than there, that therefore the glory is greater. For virginity is a greater good in itself than marriage. Yet certain married persons are not of less merit than certain virgins.

QUESTION LXV. Be not made the servants of men. Above he said: Wast thou called being a servant? care not for it 526B(I Cor. VII): how then does he here forbid that we be servants of men? Solution. He warns that men be not served for the sake of men: which is done when the hope of salvation is placed in them, as those who said: I am of Paul, but I of Apollo (I Cor. I).

QUESTION LXVI. But he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body, etc. From these words fornication seems graver than the other sins: for where there is greater delight and greater contempt, there is also greater offense. Solution. A certain delight, from the penalty inflicted for original sin, is present in our members: which although it be greater in delight than the other sins, yet does not seem to be greater than all other sins in guilt or fault. Likewise they wish to prove by the authority of Jerome that fornication is graver than the other sins. For he says: 526CAs much delight as preceded in the deed, so much bitterness of mind ought to follow in the satisfaction, and thus it seems that where there is greater delight, there is greater fault. Solution. This, as I judge, is not said in comparison with all the others; but in any kind whatever the quantity of the crime is understood according to the quantity of the delight.

QUESTION LXVII. Each one hath his first gift, etc. It is asked how this is true, since there are many to whom nothing has been given whereby they can be saved? Solution. He speaks only of the faithful, of whom there are diverse grades, as continence, marriage, virginity: in which they can be saved, as if he said: He who would not contain, let him descend to the marriage 526Dgranted to him by God, that in it he may be saved.

QUESTION LXVIII. For the figure passeth away. It is asked how this is true, since it is written: The earth standeth for ever (Eccle. I). Solution. He does not say the world passeth away; but the figure of the world, that is, the form and appearance which it now has, will change into a better form: yet if anywhere it be read that the world passeth away, this is to be understood according to form, not according to substance, which will always be.

QUESTION LXIX. He that joineth not, doth better. On account of a greater aptitude for meriting. But it is asked how there is a greater aptitude for meriting in virginity than in marriage: since the fight is greater here than there? For if there is greater difficulty of meriting in marriage, there seems to be a greater reward. Solution. In virginity, 527Awith less labor, greater profit, and therefore a greater aptitude for meriting. In marriage, great labor, and little profit: in which grade it is a great thing at least to stand.

QUESTION LXX. But I think that I also have the Spirit of God. It is asked what spirit of God the Apostle says he had, that the Corinthians might acquiesce in his counsel? For if we say charity, it does not suffice. For he could have charity, and not knowledge, like very many; if knowledge, it does not suffice: for many have knowledge, but their life does not answer to their words. Whence the counsel of such can deservedly be reproved. Solution. By the Spirit of God he understands both knowledge and charity; because in both the Apostle excelled. Whence also in his counsel one ought to acquiesce. 527B

QUESTION LXXI. Knowledge puffeth up, etc. (I Cor. VIII.) Of itself, without charity, not from its own quality; but by occasion, as the law works wrath. But the same seems able to be said of charity. For many, remaining in the advance of charity and of the other virtues, sometimes grow proud, and thus fall. As therefore the occasion of transgressing is taken from knowledge, so it seems to be taken from charity, which is not to be granted. For from charity no one takes an occasion of evil. For it dealeth not perversely; it is not puffed up (I Cor. XIII). Solution. Knowledge is such a thing that it puffs up: and yet it is from God, just as riches offer an occasion of evil, and yet are from God; just as also wood is apt for burning, yet is not burned unless fire be applied; 527Cso also knowledge never puffs up unless the heart of man be kindled. But can charity ever be so kindled? For can anyone have charity, and be proud?

QUESTION LXXII. An idol is nothing. It is asked how this is true, since anything artificial is something. Augustine says: The matter is from God, but the folly of men gave the form. But again, since it is written: Every substance, every form, every conjunction, and every joining is made by God: how is the form of the idol not from God, since it is something? Origen says: An idol is nothing, that is, it has the likeness of no thing that exists. Or an idol is nothing, that which they think to be the idol, that is, a person made of the image and 527Dof a presiding spirit: Or (which is better) an idol is nothing in the world, that is, it has no power in the things of the world, to change them for better or worse. Whence things sacrificed to idols, as far as concerns themselves, it is lawful to eat; but not in the presence of a weak person, lest he do this with veneration of the idol.

QUESTION LXXIII. There is no God but one. Is not the Father God, and the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, and the Father is not the Son, or the Holy Spirit? How then is there but one God? Likewise the Father is unbegotten God, and the Son is begotten God, how then is there one God? Solution. There is one God in nature, not in person: but what is the sense of these words, God one in nature, not in person? A great question among the moderns. But to speak what I feel, many seem to me to savor of the Sabellian heresy, being ignorant of the manifold signification of this word, unus, or unum, or even singulus, or 528Asubstantia. For these three words are taken otherwise in theology, otherwise in the common usage of speaking, concerning which one must treat by itself.

QUESTION LXXIV. It is asked whether the Son, or the Holy Spirit, is to be called our Father? Solution. Not simply, lest the unbegotten person be understood: but it can be so with such a determination, namely according to the grace of regeneration: for the whole Trinity in common by its grace regenerates us into sons of adoption.

QUESTION LXXV. Likewise it is asked whether God the Trinity is that Father who is eternally Father, or another. 528BSolution. Not that one, nor another, but one and the same with the same.

QUESTION LXXVI. It is asked whether the angels are to be called gods, as holy men are called gods, as that: I have said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the most High (Psal. LXXXI). Solution. The angels are not to be called gods, lest they seem to be worshipped with that service which is called latria. In three ways is one called God: substantively, as the Trinity; by adoption, as the saints; by appellation, as the gods of the nations.

QUESTION LXXVII. For their conscience, being weak, is defiled. It is asked how he says that their conscience is defiled: for if they believed themselves to do this for God, namely to eat things sacrificed to idols with veneration, would they not, if they left this off, 528Csin, since all that is not of faith is sin? Whence also Paul, if he did not persecute the Church, then when he believed that it was to be persecuted for God, would sin. Solution. Because they did this to a creature, as to the Creator, they had no excuse on account of ignorance: for so perverse and blinded was their mind, that they thought a wooden or stone image to be God, whence fittingly the Apostle says: Their conscience, being weak, is defiled (I Cor. VIII), not that it is defiled on account of God. Note that it is lawful for a preacher to take necessary things from his subjects, yet let him do this without scandal.

QUESTION LXXVIII. Doth God take care for oxen? 528D(I Cor. IX.) Does not God take care of all things? and if of all, how does he not take care of oxen? Solution. One is the care of providence, which is had generally of all things; another is the care of precept, which God does not have concerning oxen. For he does not give precepts to men, that he may teach them how they ought to nourish oxen; for this care he has concerning men alone.

QUESTION LXXIX. I became to the Jews as a Jew. It is asked how, as a Jew? or truly a Jew? Solution. He truly used the rites of the Jews, as Augustine says; not by dispensation, as Jerome says. But it would be done by dispensation, if it were evil, and yet were done for a time for the sake of a greater good, namely, that through that feigning they might be converted to the true 529Afaith of Christ. But those two pillars of the Church were diverse in this: yet we do not say that either of them lied, since to believe this or that is no peril of faith: concerning which controversy it shall be spoken in what follows.

QUESTION LXXX. All ate the same spiritatem food (I Cor. X). It is asked, how the same? Solution. The same in signifying, or the same in effecting. For that sibus was of the same efficacy as this, as they hold: yet certain sacraments of the Old Testament have their virtue and efficacy from the sacraments of the New Testament: just as from the body of Christ, which is a sacrament, the manna taken by the faithful had its virtue.

QUESTION LXXXI. Neither let us tempt Christ, as 529Bsome of them. God tempts, that he may prove; the devil tempts, that he may cast down; man tempts, that he may explore and know. And so temptation is threefold. The first is of proving, which is good, as that of Job. The second is of deceiving, which is the trying of the mind unto deceiving. The third is of distrust and despair, as that of the Jews saying: Can God prepare a table in the desert? (Psal. LXXVII.) It is asked, therefore, how the Jews are said to have tempted Christ, since they seem to have worshipped only God the Father and God the Trinity. Solution. The Jews are therefore said to have tempted Christ, because all the preceding things figured Christ; hence it is that this temptation was rather said to be of Christ than of the Father, although it is not more of the Son than of the Father, although it is so said.

529CQUESTION LXXXII. And they perished by the destroyer, that is, by the angel striking them outside the borders of the promised homeland. But if it be asked whether that angel was good or evil, we answer that the evil are sometimes punished by the good, sometimes by the evil; but the good are not punished except by the evil.

QUESTION LXXXIII. Upon whom the ends of the ages are come. But were the ages ended at the coming of Christ; but if they are not ended, how is it the end of the ages? Solution. They are ended in us, because, whereas there preceded diverse states of life, in all of which there was a variation and a certain expectation of the coming of Christ, but we expect no other state of life, because between this life and the future there is nothing 529Dintermediate; but to those who still expect the Messiah, the end of the ages has not yet come, as to the wretched Jews.

QUESTION LXXXIV. God is faithful, who will not suffer, etc. It is asked how he says that God does not permit anyone to be tempted above that which he can bear, since many fall from temptation, and are separated from God, and thus are overcome by the devil, and so are tempted more than they can endure. Solution. As long as they are with God, he does not suffer them to be tempted above that which they can. But that some of them yield is because they are unwilling to resist temptation when they can; whence it is just that they be tempted to that degree, their fault demanding it. But God sometimes permits someone to be tempted for the sake of proving, and for the preservation of virtues: which temptation is of providence, 530Aas with Paul, to whom there was given a sting of the flesh (II Cor. XII), for the preservation of humility.

QUESTION LXXXV. The chalice of benediction, which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ. It is asked concerning the name of this sacrament, why it is called the Eucharist. Solution. The sacrament of the body and blood of Christ is called, on account of its excellent virtue, the Eucharist, that is, good grace, in which sacrament there is not only an increase of virtue and grace, but he himself is received who is the fountain and origin of all virtue and grace. In which sacrament there are three things: namely, the visible species of bread and wine, and the body and blood of Christ, and spiritual grace. The first is the sacrament of the second, the second is the reality of the first and the sacrament of the third, the third is the virtue of the first and the reality of the second. 530BAnd so the first is only a sacrament, the second is both sacrament and reality, but the third is only reality. The first sacrament therefore has two realities, one signified and contained, namely the true body and blood of Christ; the other signified and not contained, namely the unity of the Church.

QUESTION LXXXVI. It is asked likewise why, after the sacrament of the typical lamb, the Lord gave his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood? Solution. That he might show that the legal sacraments, among which the chief was the sacrament of the Paschal lamb, ought to cease, and that the sacrament of the new law be substituted: among which the Eucharist holds the first place: therefore also that he might imprint this sacrament more closely, 530Cand commend it more tenaciously to the memory of the disciples.

QUESTION LXXXVII. Then it is asked why he gave this sacrament under another species, and not under its own? Solution. That faith might have merit, which is of invisible things, because faith has no merit when human reason offers proof; and lest the eye shudder at what the hand holds, and lest we be insulted by unbelievers.

QUESTION LXXXVIII. Likewise it is asked why under this species rather than under another. Solution. Because a thing of this species has an express likeness with both realities of this sacrament, because, as bread is from many grains, and wine from many grapes, so the material body of Christ is from many members, and the spiritual from many 530Dfaithful. And as in bread and wine there is a full and principal refreshment of bodies, so in this sacrament there is a full and principal refreshment of souls, because through the eating of the flesh one comes to the taste of the divinity.

QUESTION LXXXIX. Likewise it is asked: since the whole Christ is received under either species, why is it received not under one only, but under a twofold species? Solution. Therefore under two species, that it may be shown that he assumed the whole man, that he might heal the whole man; for he assumed body for the sake of body, soul for the sake of soul, and bread is changed into flesh, and wine into blood. Therefore indeed it is received under two species, that the taking-up of soul and body in 531AChrist, and the liberation of both in us, may be signified.

QUESTION XC. Likewise, since flesh and blood are under either species, it is asked whether the substance of either species is changed into the flesh and blood of Christ? Solution. Although either be under either species, yet the substance of bread alone is changed into flesh alone, and the substance of wine alone into the substance of blood alone.
