Nor ought they to be called two sacraments, but one. Nor is the sacrament therefore said to be repeated, because the benediction is not repeated over the same species. Nor ought other substances to be offered in the sacrifice of truth, because from others the body and blood of Christ cannot be consecrated, but from a grain of wheat reduced into bread, and from wine.

531BQUESTION XCI. It is asked why water is put with wine in the chalice of the Lord. Solution. The water signifies the people: whence neither ought the wine, by which Christ is signified, to be offered without water, because Christ suffered only for the people, nor water without wine in any way; because the people is not redeemed except through Christ.

QUESTION XCII. But it is asked whether the sacrifice becomes void if the water be omitted. Solution. If anyone, not intending to introduce heresy, has omitted the water through forgetfulness or ignorance, it does not seem to be void: whence neither do the Churches of the Greeks add water. But water alone can in no way be offered in sacrifice, nor bread except of grain, that is, of wheat, nor the grain except reduced into bread.

531CQUESTION XCXIII. But it is wont to be asked whether the water with the wine is changed into blood. Solution. Some say that it is changed; but to us it seems that it is not changed: which we received from master Achard.

QUESTION XCIV. It is asked whether Judas received the body of the Lord in the dipped morsel. Solution. Not then, but before with the others.

QUESTION XCV. It is asked concerning the accidents, which remain in species, taste, weight, and form, in what subject they are. Solution. Many doctors agree in this, that they are without a subject, just as the substances of flesh and blood are there without accidents of this kind.

QUESTION XCVI. It is wont also to be asked concerning the breaking 531Dand partition which is there, in what thing it takes place; because there is no other substance than the substance of flesh and blood, which remains whole. Solution. The body of Christ remains whole in itself, and yet is broken and divided in the sacrament.

QUESTION XCVII. It is asked whether the evil man receives the true body of the Lord and the true blood. Solution. He truly receives both, but to his own harm; because unworthily — for he is unworthy who receives otherwise than Christ instituted, or who is in mortal sin.

QUESTION XCVIII. Likewise it is asked whether Christ is immolated daily. Solution. He who was once slain on the altar of the cross is immolated daily in memory of his passion in the sacrament, nor is it repeated from his infirmity, but from ours, who daily sin, and obtain the remission of venial sins, 532Aand an increase of virtues if we participate worthily. It is objected concerning that which Augustine says, that the good man receives the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament; but the evil man only the sacrament, and not the reality of the sacrament, and it has already been said above that the evil man receives the true body and the true blood: therefore the evil man receives not only the sacrament, but also the reality of the sacrament, which is to be believed without doubt. Solution. In the aforesaid words Augustine calls the sacrament the true body and true blood of Christ; he calls the reality the spiritual grace, which the good man alone and not the evil receives.

QUESTION XCIX. It is asked what kind of body Christ gave to his disciples, mortal or immortal? If mortal, how could it without injury be ground 532Bor broken by the teeth; if immortal, then he gave such as it was not yet. Solution. Soundly we say that he gave such as he willed, to whom nothing was impossible. Yet some assert that he gave a mortal one, which, as we do not assert, so we do not deny.

QUESTION C. It is asked what is the virtue of this sacrament? Solution. The remission of venial sins, the perfecting of virtues, and it is instituted for the increase of virtues, and as a medicine of daily infirmity.

QUESTION CI. It is asked whether one ought to communicate daily. Solution. Augustine says: to receive the Eucharist daily I neither praise nor blame: yet if anyone is in the disposition of sinning, he is more burdened by receiving than 532Cpurified; and if anyone is gnawed by mortal sin, let him make satisfaction with tears; and if for the rest he have the will of not sinning, let him approach securely.

QUESTION CII. It is wont to be asked whether depraved priests can confect this sacrifice? Solution. Although some be depraved in life, if they are within by name and by sacrament, it is believed that they truly consecrate: but those who are excommunicated, and manifestly marked with heresy, do not seem able to do this. In this sacrament three things must be observed, namely form, order, and intention: the form instituted by the Lord; the order, that he be a priest; the intention, that he intend to do this.

QUESTION CIII. It is asked whether the body of the Lord is touched or received by brute animals? Solution. In no way is it received either by a mouse, or by another little beast.

532DQUESTION CIV. What then does the mouse receive, which eats it? Solution. God knows — perhaps nothing but the accidents which are there.

QUESTION CV. Eat not for the sake of him who judged, and for conscience' sake, namely of the weak, etc. It is asked how he says: Eat not for the sake of the unbeliever, or the weak believer, is it not better to eat for the sake of both than to abstain? For if one abstains, the unbeliever is offended. But the weak is rather to be left to himself, as was said above: He that is weak, let him eat herbs (I Cor. XIV). For in this opinion, he who thinks that thou dost venerate the idol, if thou eatest things consecrated to the idol, he is to be left to himself: for although he judge that thou sinnest by eating, yet thou dost not eat with veneration of the idol, 533Anor is he himself, by thinking this, turned away from the faith, but rather by zeal for the faith believes thee to err in this that thou eatest, and therefore is indignant. Solution. It is better to instruct by abstaining him who ate, than by eating to foster him in error. Likewise, if thou shouldst eat in the presence of a weak brother, he himself would be scandalized, and from the scandal would perish. Therefore one ought rather to abstain than to eat.

QUESTION CVI. Whether you eat, or drink, etc. It is asked how it can be fulfilled, that we do all things to the glory of God, since we do many things naturally, which we do not do for this, that we may please God? Solution. Let all our works be done so circumspectly, that nothing be done against God.

QUESTION CVII. As I also please all men in all things. Elsewhere he says: If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ 533B(Galat. I). Was he, pleasing all men in all things, not the servant of Christ? Solution. That which he says: If I yet pleased men, is understood thus: If I pleased men so far as in me lies, so as to put the cause and end in man, I should not be the servant of Christ. But he who pleases for the sake of the truth, not he himself, but rather the truth itself pleases.

QUESTION CVIII. If any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the Church of God. Here we have authority that the customs of holy Church are to be held, even if we are ignorant of the reason why they were thus established by her: for God does not permit his Church to err in those things which pertain to himself. Note: The Church is called the convocation of the faithful, and the house in which one assembles to receive the Eucharist, 533Cnot only for the commemoration of the death of Christ, but also that we may be conformed to Christ in morals and life.

QUESTION CIX. The man is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the image and glory of the man, etc. It is asked how the man is the image of God and not the woman, since in Genesis it is written of both, that they were made to the image of God? (Gen. I.) Solution. One is the image common to man and woman, of which it is treated in Genesis; another is that which befits the man alone and not the woman. The first consists in the natural power of knowing God; the second is understood in this, that, as from God are all things, so from one man are all men. Or it is to be taken morally: that by the man reason be understood; by 533Dthe woman, sensuality, and according to this the man and not the woman is the image of God.

QUESTION CX. There must be heresies, etc. Concerning the authority of the Church. It is asked who is to be called a heretic? Solution. A heretic properly is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage, and especially of glory, or of his own principality, invents false and new and depraved sects, alien from the truth, or holds, follows, and defends sects invented by others.

QUESTION CXI. But let a man prove himself, etc. If anyone is in mortal sin, let him not approach, but say: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof (Matth. VIII). What then is it for anyone to prove himself, but to see whether his conscience gnaws at him concerning a mortal sin, and whether he is in the purpose of remaining still in 534Asin? But the priest ought to admonish him who is in mortal sin, though not manifest, not to approach; yet he cannot withdraw communion from him. But if public report or a crime accuse him, let him in no way approach, lest the priest give it to him. For if, either for favor of him, or convicted by money, he gives to such a one, so far as in him lies, he kills Christ: which is greatly to be feared.

QUESTION CXII. Now there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit, etc. (I Cor. XII.) Since the works of the Trinity are undivided, it is asked why he attributes graces to the Holy Spirit, ministrations to the Son, operations to the Father? Solution. In grace especially appears benignity, which pertains to the property of the Holy Spirit: therefore he attributes graces to the Holy Spirit. In ministrations 534Bindeed wisdom shines, which is wont to be referred to the Son. In operations, power, which is specially of the Father: therefore he refers operations to the authority of the Father.

QUESTION CXIII. To one is given the word of wisdom, etc. It is to be noted that wisdom and knowledge are taken here otherwise than there: O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God (Rom. XI). For when he says: O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God, by wisdom and knowledge he calls the divine essence. But when he says, to one is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge, by wisdom he calls the knowledge of eternal things, but by knowledge, the knowledge of human things.

QUESTION CXIV. All these things one and the same Spirit worketh. It is asked why the Father is not called gift, 534Cas the Son or the Holy Spirit, since he gives himself, as also do the other persons: for to no one is the Son or the Holy Spirit given without the Father. Solution. On account of the authority of the origin, lest he be understood to be from another, who is from none.

QUESTION CXV. For as one body, etc. It is asked whether the good alone participate in these gifts? Or also the evil? But that even the evil have these gifts of the Spirit is plain from that which is read in the Gospel, that they will say to the Lord in the day of judgment: Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name, and cast out devils? (Matth. VII) to whom the Lord will say: Amen I say to you, I know you not, etc. (Matth. XXV.) Likewise John the evangelist, when he saw a certain man, who did not follow the Lord, casting out devils in the name 534Dof Christ, wished to forbid him; to whom the Lord said: Forbid not; he that is not with me is against me (Marc. IX). From which it is plain that the evil also often use these gifts, and thus it seems that they are of the body of Christ, and are his members; but the same, since they are evil, are members of the devil. Solution. The Apostle does not say that all having the gifts of the Holy Spirit are established in the unity of the body; or the Church is taken broadly, namely the multitude of all participating in the sacraments of the Church. Among whom are certain rotten members, and many grains with chaff, which are said to be in the body, but not of the body. Whence John: They went out from us, but they were not of us (I Joan. II). Note that the Apostle says all the members of the body, since they are many, are one body. This I say on account of 535Acertain ones unwilling to concede that all the parts of some whole joined together receive the name of the whole, since it is also said in the creed of Athanasius, soul and flesh are one man.

QUESTION CXVI. If I should have all faith, but charity, etc. (I Cor. XIII.) Here the Apostle manifestly shows that faith, and the other gifts, cannot be had without charity. It is asked therefore, first of all, of what faith he here treats — whether of the catholic faith, or of another? But not of another, because by another mountains cannot be transferred from place to place, as by this of which he here treats: therefore he here treats of the catholic faith. Whence it is established that it can be had without charity, and thus can be had by the wicked, which many deny. But according to these, the catholic faith is a faith working 535Bthrough love. Of whom it can be asked whether they call it one thing, or two — faith working through love — but this whole cannot be one? For he who has faith thus not only believes, but also loves. But these two cannot be in the wicked; yet so far as it is simply in faith, this whole can be even in the wicked, even in the devil. For what does this good man believe that this evil man does not believe? Does not this evil man, or even the devil, believe that Christ died, and was raised again from death, and the other things which are to be believed, which are necessary to faith? But it is objected, according to this, that the devil has the catholic faith, and thus becomes a catholic. Solution. "Catholic" is said in two ways: both he who lives in catholic wise, imitating the life of Christ; and he is called catholic who believes all 535Cthings that are to be believed, whether he have charity or not. Certain ones concede that even the devil, according to the other acceptation, can be called catholic — which sounds grievously to our ears, especially since that knowledge which he has of Christ is rather from subtlety of nature than from the inspiration of the Christian faith.

QUESTION CXVII. Charity is the proper fountain of good things, etc. It is asked whether charity can be had by those who are to be damned. Are they not strangers, who do not share in the proper fountain of good things? Solution. Charity is called the proper fountain of good things for this reason, that no one can at once have charity and be evil.

QUESTION CXVIII. Charity never falleth away, etc. 535DIt is asked whether charity, once had, is never lost. For if it never falls away, and is never lost, then those who are to be damned can never at any time have charity. Solution. Charity is said never to fall away for this reason, that it is had both here and in the future; but had in the present it is lost, and once lost is again recovered.

QUESTION CXIX. Knowledge shall be destroyed, etc. It is asked how he says that knowledge is destroyed in the future. Shall we not have in the future the knowledge of those things of which we now have it? We shall indeed have it, and much greater than we have in the present: how then shall knowledge be destroyed? Solution. Certain ones say that knowledge shall be destroyed as to its partiality and imperfection, so that it be not partial and imperfect. But 536Athis is for it to be increased and perfected, and not destroyed; because in the same way it could be said of charity, that it is to be destroyed. For as we know imperfectly, so we love imperfectly; and when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.

Solution. Certain ones say that not knowledge, but its enigmatic and shadowy mode is to be destroyed. But again, by the same reasoning, charity too seems to be destroyed: whose mode, namely of imperfection, is in the future to be done away. To this it is answered that it is true that the mode of imperfection shall be taken away from charity, but not every mode. For in the future the neighbor shall be loved for his own sake, and for God's sake, as he is loved in the present. Others also say that the act of knowledge shall be destroyed in the future. But charity, 536Bwhich now is — neither its act, nor any mode of it — shall be destroyed in the future; but faith and hope shall be wholly done away; but knowledge in part destrueter: of which there shall be neither act nor mode.

QUESTION CXX. But there is another question, which presses us more: it is true, and it cannot be denied, that charity in the present is imperfect in comparison with the future; but the Apostle proves by such an argument that prophecies shall be done away, and that knowledge shall be destroyed: We know in part, and we prophesy in part: but when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away: since therefore charity is in part, by a like argument it too shall be done away, when that which is perfect is come. Solution. But we say that 536Cknowledge, or prophecy, is said to be in part by one reason, and charity imperfect by another reason. For from the fact that some know, and some do not know, prophecy or doctrine has place in this present, where one teaches and instructs another. But in the future, where all shall be taught of God, when all from the greatest to the least shall know God fully and perfectly, then the teaching of men shall have no place: when no one shall say to his brother: Know God. And therefore knowledge, that is, doctrine, shall be done away. But charity is not in this way said to be in part. For it does not have being for this reason, that some love and some love not: nay, it shall be much more truly when all shall love perfectly. Note: an enigma is an obscure likeness; and as in the present every creature is as it were 536Da kind of mirror in which God is seen, so in the future God himself shall be the mirror of every creature, in which all things shall be seen more truly than in themselves. Hence it is, according to some, why knowledge is to be destroyed: because this shadowy mode of knowing, which we now have, when full knowledge comes will be no more.

QUESTION CXXI. Faith and hope cannot be lacking to charity; but faith and hope can exist without charity. Yet certain ones say, as was said above, that faith cannot exist without charity: whose error is here destroyed. For when he says: If I should have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing: he manifestly intimates that even perfect faith can be had without charity. 537AAnd the expositor, in the aforesaid words, manifestly refutes them, saying that faith and hope can exist without charity.

QUESTION CXXII. But concerning hope it can be asked how it can exist without charity. Is not hope a confidence of future goods, coming from preceding merits? But this cannot be without charity. And so it seems that hope cannot exist without charity. Likewise, if hope is, as it seems to others, the expectation of a future advantage, it will now be presumption rather than hope, if I am certain that he will reward, though there be no merits. To this it can be answered that hope is twofold: of reward, and of meriting: but the hope of meriting cannot exist without charity, while the hope of reward can (not) be had without 537Bcharity.

QUESTION CXXIII. He that speaketh in a tongue, speaketh not to men, but to God (I Cor. XIV). It is asked what it is to speak in a tongue. Solution. Some say that to speak in a tongue is to speak in parables; others, in an unknown tongue. Augustine says that the utterance of signs, which the Spirit forms in the spirit of man, is said to be speaking in a tongue. Whence the Apostle says: The Spirit speaketh mysteries (Ibid.). For to speak in a tongue and to speak in the spirit he says to be the same. The Holy Spirit, in the primitive Church, formed for the conversion of the faithful the signs of heavenly secrets in the minds of the faithful, and the utterance of such things the Apostle calls speaking in tongues. But it is to be noted that those who spoke in tongues sometimes understood, sometimes did not understand. But 537Csomeone will say: If he who speaks in a tongue understands what he says, then this is not to speak in a tongue, but to prophesy. Solution. Although he himself understand, unless he expound to others, he does not prophesy, but only speaks in a tongue. Note that certain things are done in the Church only for adornment, not so much for necessity: among which is contained speaking in tongues.

QUESTION CXXIV. You shall be speaking into the air, etc. From these words certain ones judge that to speak in tongues is to speak in diverse kinds of languages; but this is not true: nay, the Apostle brings this in to show that to speak in tongues without interpretation has little usefulness, just as to speak in all kinds of languages would make rather confusion than edification 537Dfor those who understood none of them.

QUESTION CXXV. If I know not the power of the voice. It is asked what he calls the power of the voice. Solution. He calls the signification of the voice the power of the voice.

QUESTION CXXVI. It is also asked why speech of this kind is said to be done by the tongue. Solution. This is so because what is in the tongue is in the voice and in the utterance; but what is in the heart is in the understanding; because in the heart is intelligence: whence, because this speech is only in the utterance, and not in the intelligence, it is therefore said to be done by the tongue; by the spirit also, and not by the mind. For the spirit is a power of the soul lower than the mind, in which the images of things are confusedly apprehended. For it is an imaginary and confused apprehension of visible things, without discernment of the properties of those things which 538Aare apprehended: such as was that vision of Pharaoh concerning the cows and the ears of grain: for he saw only images. But Joseph had in his understanding the revelation of God concerning these things.

QUESTION CXXVII. It is asked what words thus uttered signify, when someone thus speaks in a tongue — to set down this example: He that soweth went forth to sow his seed. For if this is the signification of the voice, it was true: it is asked therefore whether that is said by it which is properly signified by it: if it be said to be so, it is inferred, therefore, that something false is signified by it. To this certain ones respond, saying: The signification of the voice is not to be sought in such things, but only that of the things, which pertains to allegory. Others say, to speak more freely, that it does indeed properly signify something false; 538Byet a falsehood is not spoken by it: because the statement is not there terminated; for the end of the speech is not that first signification of the voice, but the second, which is called allegorical. But it can be said that the speech itself signifies neither true nor false: for the things there signify only the truth, which is there mystically understood. Nor do I deny that there is there a signification of the voice, but only incomplexly, because this word, "man," signifies a man, and so of the rest; but they do not signify complexly; for they do not signify conjointly, so that the true or the false is signified, but so that they may signify those things by which the truth is signified. Or it can be said that the proposition itself, from the property of the things which are signified, is taken up 538Cto signify that which is mystically understood, as this word, "seed," signifies the word of God, from the property of the thing which it signifies.

QUESTION CXXVIII. Christ died for our sins, etc. (I Cor. XV.) It is asked whether Christ, according to the flesh, had the necessity of dying? That he had the necessity of dying seems to be the intent of the authority upon that passage: As it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment: so also Christ was offered once (Hebr. IX); so, that is, by the same necessity and law of nature by which the rest die. Likewise the authority says, because it was his own will he was offered (Isai. LIII). Therefore by will alone: how then by necessity? Solution. It is established that in Christ there was no cause of dying, because no sin; yet, as certain ones will have it, among 538Dthe other penalties, he took up voluntarily also the necessity of dying; and thus this necessity does not impede the will, which, as he received it when he willed, so he laid it down when he willed: for if, they say, some greater benefit had not been conferred upon the assumed flesh, it would necessarily be subject to the law of nature — which necessity also some understand by mortality.

QUESTION CXXIX. I am the least of the apostles, etc. It is asked how the Apostle calls himself the least of the apostles, since he is of greater merit than the merits of the others: for he labored more than all. Solution. He says this according to his former state, not according to the present, in which he was not the least of the apostles, but the greatest. But it is objected: For he does not 539Asay, I was the least, but I am the least of the apostles: therefore, since he is not among the least, but rather among the first, it seems that he lies, and thus sins unto death: because the mouth that belieth killeth the soul (Sap. I). Solution. The sense is: I am the least of the apostles, that is, I do not prefer myself to others, but rather others to myself: for indeed all his sins, past or present, hidden or manifest, he had before his eyes; but the simplicity and innocence of others he considered, and thus, according to this consideration, he felt more humbly of himself: for as the proud man, if he has any goods, always attends to them, and to the infirmities of others, whence he judges himself alone great, despising others; so the humble man without ceasing sees his own infirmities, but weighs the goods 539Bof others: hence it is that the saints, though they be greater, feel themselves the more humble, nor is it a deceiving opinion, because the goods which they have they judge to be not their own, but the gifts of God; but the evils to which they are subject they know to be their own.

QUESTION CXXX. By the grace of God I am what I am, etc. It is asked of what grace he speaks. Indeed, of operating and cooperating grace, or preventing grace and subsequent grace, it has already been said in what precedes: for preventing, or operating, grace is one and the same, which works in us without us, namely by preparing and healing free will, that it may will the good, which the Apostle notes, saying: By the grace of God I am what I am; but subsequent, or 539Ccooperating, grace is one and the same, which works in us, not without us, by following after and helping, lest we will in vain, which the Apostle notes, saying: And his grace in me hath not been void, because I have laboured more than all: yet not I, but the grace of God with me. From this therefore, that he says: I am what I am by the grace of God, the error of the Pelagians is destroyed, who said that free will suffices for meriting salvation. Likewise, from the fact that he adds, and his grace in me hath not been void, he shows that man can do something from free will, which certain heretics deny, saying that man can merit nothing. But the Apostle demonstrates that man of himself can indeed do nothing, but only from grace supervening: for it is needful that man be prevented by grace; then free will, 539Dalready prevented by grace, ought to cooperate with grace itself: whose nature is such that it can shine back and cooperate, as the eye touched by the ray of the sun can see. What therefore man works, is from grace, with which he cooperates. For a certain grace, as has already been said, works without the help of man, because it pricks the mind and rouses it; but man without grace can neither consent to grace, nor effect anything else, but leans upon grace drawing and leading, and thus, helped by grace, merits. From which it appears that it is not grace only when man does anything of good, but also from free will, although the whole is the work of grace, either by itself, or working with man. And so there are certain things from grace alone, and certain things from grace and man.

540AQUESTION CXXXI. If there be no resurrection of the dead, then Christ is not risen again. It is asked concerning the hypothetical, whether it be true, and how it is to be understood. Solution. It is true, and is thus understood: If it were impossible for the dead to rise, as certain heretics said, neither is it possible that Christ rose; or if the saints were not to rise, neither would it be true that Christ rose; because all that he did in the flesh — by dying, by suffering, by rising — he did for us.

QUESTION CXXXII. If Christ be not risen again, our faith is vain. It is asked how the Apostle says that our faith is vain, and we are more miserable than all men (I Cor. XV), if there will be no resurrection of the dead, or of bodies. For since 540Bthe soul is immortal, and it alone is capable of the vision of God, and thus it alone can have beatitude, can we not be blessed without the resurrection of bodies? And to the same:

QUESTION CXXXIII. It is asked, to what end will be the resurrection of bodies, since there will be no need of them where Christ will be all in all, nor can they themselves receive the beatitude which will be of the soul alone? Solution. It is to be seen diligently what is said, and according to what. For that which he says: We are more miserable than all men, he says not according to the soul, but according to the body. For here the Apostle suffered greater misery than others. But the resurrection of bodies is, that we may glory also in the second robe: for that brightness 540Cwhich will be in the body will be for the increase of beatitude itself, so that what before it had for misery, it may now have for glory and adornment. The Apostle proves the resurrection of the dead by the resurrection of Christ: which was done for this reason alone, that the resurrection of bodies might be believed, and might come to pass: When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father (Ibid.), that is, when he shall lead the Church — in which he now reigns through faith, through the knowledge which it had of the Son — to the knowledge and vision of the Father.

QUESTION CXXXIV. Till he put all his enemies under his feet. It is asked how he says that Christ must reign: Till he put, etc. (Ibid.) Will he not reign forever, and especially when his enemies are subdued? Solution. In like places, "till" is put 540Dfor "forever": for if he reigns then, when he has adversaries, it is established that he will reign when all are subject to him, and thus he will reign forever.

QUESTION CXXXV.-- Then the Son also himself shall be subject unto him that put all things under him. It is asked according to what nature he says the Son is subject to the Father. For if according to the divine, he will be less than him: which is false, because according to the divinity he is equal to the Father. Likewise, if this be said according to the human, then according to it all things are subject to him: and according to the human he is Lord of all: wherefore also Creator; and thus according to the same he seems to be equal to the Father, according to which he is less than him: whence it is read: Equal to the Father according to the divinity; less than the Father according to the humanity. Solution. This can 541Awell be understood according to both natures, namely the divine and the human: according to the human all things are subject to him, according to which he was exalted to the equality of the Father, when the human nature was united in one person to the Word consubstantial with the Father, according to which he himself also received the fullness of gifts; of which fullness we all have received (Joan. I), and thus are subject to him. Likewise, according to the divine nature, certain ones understand it thus, that the Son is subject to the Father, because from him he has being, from whom he has whatever he has. According to that: My doctrine is not mine (Joan. VII). Likewise: The Father is greater than I (Joan. XIV). Which some will have understood according to the divine nature. In a word of this kind a distinction is noted, because the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son 541B; whence the Father is called the principle of the Deity, because he is from none, and from him is both the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the Father is a principle not from a principle; the Son a principle from a principle; the Holy Spirit proceeding from both. But things of this kind are to be said only at a fitting place and time, lest the weak incur scandal.

QUESTION CXXXVI. In unequal brightness there will be equal joy. It is asked, if the brightness is unequal, how can the joy be equal? Will not the quantity of joy be according to the quantity of brightness? Will not the brightness itself be the joy itself? Likewise, if one is more blessed than another, the one will have greater joy than the other: how then will the joy be equal? Likewise, will not the joy of all 541Cbe that of each? How then, in unequal brightness, will there be equal joy? If the same coin be given to all, how is the brightness unequal? If the joy will be equal, then the joy of Peter will be the joy of Martin. Solution. One thing is the joy of experience, another that of the will; as the joy of Peter is of remuneration, and of experience, but for Martin it is not of experience, but of affection. For the good of Peter pleases him as much as it does Peter himself, yet he does not feel and experience in himself so great a beatitude as Peter feels. And so the beatitude is different according to quantity, although it be the same according to quality. Just as, therefore, at the health of someone recovering from infirmity I rejoice as much as he does, by affection, though not by experience, because I do not feel in myself the health which he experiences. 541DAs two are covered by the same bed, yet one is warmer: so in the one vision of God, one will rejoice more intensely than another. But no inferior will envy any greater, nor will he desire for himself the greater joy of the superior, because each one will have as much as he wills, otherwise he would not be blessed. There is life without death, knowledge without error, love without offense. There will be seen the end of our desires, namely God without end, he will be loved without weariness, he will be praised without fatigue.

QUESTION CXXXVII. It is sown a natural body, etc. It is asked whether the body has animality, that is, sensuality, from the soul, or the soul from the body? Solution. Neither can the body have animality except from the soul; nor would the soul be animal, that is, having 542Asensuality, unless joined to a body. And so animality seems to be known from the conjunction of both; the soul alone, however, feels through the body, but the body receives it, and does not itself feel. For man was first so created that from creation he was passible, yet he would never have suffered, unless he had sinned. Whence he is also said to have been immortal before sin, because he was able not to die, for he was able not to sin, since, if he had not sinned, he would not die.

QUESTION CXXXVIII. It is likewise wont to be asked, since man before sin was said to be mortal, and in a certain manner immortal, whether he had both from nature, or neither, or one only. Solution. Saving the reverence due to hidden things, and without prejudice to a better opinion, we say that man before sin was naturally mortal and passible; 542Bbut by the benefit of the tree of life he would become immortal: whence the doctors do not say simply that he was then immortal, but they add "in a certain manner," and determine in what manner; but mortal they pronounce him simply to have been, according to this that is said: The first man was made into a living soul, that is, into a soul which should quicken and vivify the body, not so as to have no need of foods.

QUESTION CXXXIX. Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God; neither shall corruption possess incorruption. It is asked therefore what bodies we are going to have. Solution. The same bodies which we now have we shall have after the resurrection, but changed not according to substance, but 542Caccording to quality: these dissoluble, but those indissoluble; but those of the good impassible, but those of the wicked passible: whence they will be as if in perpetual death. But that they will be indissoluble, the Apostle teaches, saying: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God (Ibid.). But that they are going to have impassible bodies, the Apostle intimates, saying: but we shall all be changed (Ibid.).

QUESTION CXL. Canetenim the trumpet, etc. It is asked, what is signified by the name of the trumpet? Solution. The doctors say that the Apostle so calls some evident and manifest sign, by which the mystery of the future resurrection will be fulfilled: which trumpet is elsewhere called a cry, elsewhere the voice of an archangel or the voice of Christ.

542DQUESTION CXLI. It is asked also concerning the voice of the trumpet, whether it will be material? Solution. It is manifest that there will be a material voice made by the ministry of an angel; because as by the trumpet the people of the Jews was called together to a feast or to war, so then they will be called to judgment; or some evident sign, by which the same is done that is wont to be done by the voice.

QUESTION CXLII. Death is swallowed up in victory. It is asked, what death, and in what victory it is thus swallowed up? For by the name of death is signified sometimes the devil, who is the author of death, sometimes sin, which separates from God, sometimes the dissolution of soul and body. Solution. It can well be understood both of the devil, and of sin, and of the dissolution of soul and body. It is established that in the victory of the Lord's resurrection the devil 543Ais swallowed up: that he may not domineer, as before, when by the fear of death men were driven to any crime whatever; but now the saints despise death: but chiefly in the future general resurrection of all shall all death be swallowed up, when this mortal shall put on incorruption.

QUESTION CXLIII. And the strength of sin is the law. How this is to be understood may easily be weighed from those things which were said upon the Epistle to the Romans: for the law being given, both carnal concupiscence grew strong, and transgression came on. For the law by forbidding increases concupiscence, unless the Holy Spirit infuse charity.

QUESTION CXLIV. Therefore, brethren, be ye steadfast and unmovable. It is asked in what these two differ. Solution. 543BSteadfast in faith, lest of themselves they be moved by the foot of pride; unmovable in temptations, lest by the impelling hand of sins they forsake the faith. There are three kinds of temptations: one violent, another fraudulent, the third violent and fraudulent. The first is done through open persecutions; the second through false brethren and heretics; the third will be done through Antichrist. But every 544Akind of temptation the devil sends: whence he is also called a lion, by raging openly, and a dragon, by seducing secretly and stealthily: whence it is written: Under his tongue is labour and sorrow (Psal. X).

QUESTION CXLV. Concerning Apollo, I make known to you, that I greatly besought him to come unto you, but it was not his will to come now (I Cor. XVI). It is asked which of the two acted unreasonably — whether Paul in asking that he should go, or Apollo in not consenting? Because it seems either that this one did not ask what was fitting, or that the other omitted what he ought to have done. Solution. It is true that both acted reasonably, because the Apostle asked that he should do this; whence Apollo, because he was thus asked, saw that the Apostle's petition should rather be set aside, wherefore 544Bhe did not consent.

QUESTION CXLVI. Salute one another with a holy kiss. It is asked why he added, "holy"? Solution. There is a kiss of wantonness; there is a kiss of betrayal, as of Judas; there is a kiss of holiness and concord, so that what is within may appear outwardly, namely the bond of charity, etc. Of this therefore he speaks, that he may exclude the rest.

III. IN EPISTOLAM II AD CORINTHIOS.

  • 543

543C(II COR. I.) Paulus apostolus, etc. Haec est secunda epistola, quae Corinthiis destinatur. Scribit autem aliquando duas, aliquando unum epistolam tantum Apostolus; sed nec, cum unam, aliquid diminutum et imperfectum, nec cum duas aliquid superfluum dicit, ut hic videri potest. Nam haec epistola, quae sequitur, consummatio et confirmatio est praecedentis. In hac enim secunda, monet eos corrigi, qui nondum per praecedentem epistolam erant correcti. Notat eos, quod in eleemosynis erant parci. Correctum fornicatorem praecipit recipi. Unde patet quae hujus materia epistolae sit, quae etiam intentio. Est autem materia specialis status Corinthiorum, in quo tunc erant. Intentio vero ad unitatem et integritatem fidei revocare. In hoc autem 543Dstatu speciali generalem Ecclesiae statum signat, et informat, et omnes ad unitatem fidaei invitat. Praemittit more suo, et aliorum scribentium epistolas, salutationes eorum, quibus scribit, captando benevolentiam: unde et dicit, Paulus apostolus, conjungendo nomen humilitatis et nomen dignitatis, ut dignitatis excellentiam humilitas comes temperet, sine qua omnis virtus cassa et inanis. Item Jesu Christi, Jesus est nomen personae. Fuerint autem plures hoc nomine dicti, ut Jesus Nave, Jesus magnus sacerdos, sed et omnes nuncupative. Christus vero solus substantive, quia et nomen, et rem habuit: qui Salvator mundi vere fuit. Interpretatur enim Jesus Salvator. Christus vero nomen personae, 544Cquod utramque complectitur naturam. Est enim nomen officii, ut sacerdos, miles, et interpretatur unctus. In Veteri Testamento duae ungebantur personae, regalis et sacerdotalis; Christus vero unctus est unctione regali, qui secundum divinam naturam suos regere potuit; secundum vero naturam humanam offerendi potestatem accepit, qui semetipsum obtulit Deo Patri: unde ex officio regali et sacerdotali Christus dicitur. Voluntas Dei multis modis accipitur, ut jam superius dictum est, et iterum dicere non erit superfluum. Dicitur enim voluntas Dei ipsa dispositio, et beneplacitum. Unde: Omnia quaecunque voluit fecit (Psalm. CXXXIV). Dicitur etiam voluntas Dei, consilium, vel praeceptum: unde dicitur: Deus vult omnes salvos fieri (I Tim. II), id est, 544Dconsulit et praecipit ea facere: per quae salventur, ut sunt prohibitio, vel permissio, et si qua hujusmodi.

QUAESTIO I. Cum ego voluissem hoc, nunquid levitate usus sum? Quaeritur ergo utrum Apostolus mentitus fuerit, promittendo se venturum, cum non venerit: ipse enim dixit, veniam, et non venit: ergo apud ipsum erat est, et non, id est, affirmatio et negatio de eodem, et sic mendacium, et sic reus mendacii. Solutio. Mendacium est falsa vocis significatio cum intentione fallendi: unde qui dicit falsum, quod putat verum: non est judicandus mendax, cum potius fallatur, quam fallat. Quicunque vero cum intentione fallendi verum dicit vel falsum, reus est 545Amendacii: unde colligitur, quod aliquis dicens verum, reus est mendacii, sive mentitur: et quod aliquis dicit falsum, non tamen mentitur vel reus est mendacii.

QUAESTIO II. Quaeritur autem de iis, qui pie mentiuntur, an mendacii rei sint, ut obstetrices illae Aegyptiae? Nam ex intentione fallendi falsum pronuntiabant. Solutio. Qui sic mentiuntur peccant, et dum vitae aliorum provident, contra conscientiam suam agentes, veritatem offendunt, et animae propriae periculum incurrunt.

QUAESTIO III. Item de iis quaeritur qui joco falsum dicunt. Solutio. Aliquando sic jocari malum est, aliquando non; si vero ex consuetudine, sic peccatum est.

545BQUAESTIO IV. Aliis quidem odor mortis in mortem, etc. (II Cor. II.) Quaeritur an odor mortis sit bonus an malus, cum Apostolus dicat se esse odorem, aliis in mortem, aliis in vitam: si enim bonus quomodo in mortem. Item si malus, quomodo bonus Deo? Solutio. Apostolus non erat nisi odor bonus, et tamen hoc odore bono alii moriebantur, id est, occasionem per invidiam sumebant, sicut lex bona, et tamen occasio mali quia praevaricationis.

QUAESTIO V. Non quod sufficientes simus, etc. (II Cor. III). Hic quaeritur quomodo dicat Apostolus, quod sufficientes non sumus aliquid a nobis cogitare, cum mala ex nobis et cogitare, et facere possimus. Item cum quaedam naturaliter possimus facere, quae neque ad praemium neque ad poenam 545Csunt, haec autem sunt illa quae a prima creatione data sunt nobis, ut digitum erigere, curvare, deponere, et hujusmodi. Solutio. Apostolus hic agit de bonis illis, quae meritum habent apud Deum, quae nullo modo possunt sine gratia superveniente et juvante fieri. Unde Misericordia ejus praeveniet me (Psal. LVIII), et misericordia ejus subsequetur (Psal. XXII). Gratia enim praevenit voluntatem, ut velit, et subsequitur, ne frustra velit. Unde Apostolus hic destruit errorem illorum, qui dicebant initium boni naturaliter non posse esse sine gratia, sed boni consummationem esse ex nobis: in hoc quod dicit, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Ex libero enim arbitrio facultatem bene operandi habemus, non tamen hac facultate uti possumus nisi 545Dgratia adjuvante. Est enim liberum arbitrium per culpam ita depressum, ut potentia sua uti non possit, nisi erigatur a gratia et adjuvetur, sicut cum potestatem equitandi habeam, non tamen hujus potentiae exercitium habere possum absque equo.

QUAESTIO VI. Littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat, etc. Quaeritur quomodo littera dicatur occidere: nunquid talia praecipit, quae observata occidant? quomodo ergo stabit quod alibi dicit Apostolus, quod lex sancta est, et mandatum sanctum, bonum et justum, si praecepta occidant? Item si dicatur quod littera sine spiritu, id est sine gratia, occidat, idem de Evangelio dici posse videtur. 546AItem si dicatur littera ideo occidere, quia non possunt omnia ad litteram ibi observari: non pereat, qui ea observaverit. eodem modo dici potest de Evangelio. Nam si hoc, nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, et biberitis ejus sanguinem, etc. (Joan. VI), ad litteram observatur, id est, ut littera sonat, ut sic manducare, et bibere intelligamus, hic, sicut alibi, stultum et damnabile est. Solutio: Littera sine spiritu occidit, id est, sine gratia, quia occasio mortis est, sicut scientia absque charitate inflat. Littera vero Evangelii non absque spiritu est. Vel ut alibi jam dictum est: Per litteram, sive legem, intelligitur mandatum sine gratia: quod semper occidit: quia concupiscentiam augens superaddit praevaricationem. Per Evangelium, 546Bmandatum cum spiritu, id est gratia, intelligitur: unde Apostolus vocat legem ministrationem mortis: Evangelium, ministrationem justitiae.

QUAESTIO VII. Et non sicut Moysi ponebat velamen, etc. Quaeritur de velamine, an excaecet. Solutio. Aliud est velamen figuratum, quod est lectio Moysi: quod figuratum est per velamen, quod Moyses loquens filiis Israel posuit super faciem suam. Aliud est velamen caecitatis, quod est positum super cor Judaeorum: utrumque velamen aufertur per Christum. In cujus rei figura velum templi scissum est in passione Christi.

QUAESTIO VIII. Nos autem omnes revelata facie gloriam Dei speculantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur, 546Cetc. Quaeritur quid gloriam, et quid imaginem vocet? Solutio. Gloriam Dei, quam speculamur, et imaginem, in quam transformamur, idem vocat, scilicet Christum, qui est gloria, et imago Dei increata, sicut vir est gloria, et imago Dei creata.

QUAESTIO IX. Qui est imago Dei invisibilis (II Cor. IV). Quaeritur cur Filius dicatur imago Patris. Solutio. Ut ostendatur sic esse ex Patre, ut per omnia ei similis et aequalis ostendatur.

QUAESTIO X. Si autem quaeratur cur Spiritus sanctus, cum sit ex Patre, et similis et aequalis per omnia, non dicatur imago Patris sicut Filius. Respondetur quia imago, aequalitas, et similitudo magis pertinent ad proprietatem Filii, quam ad 546Dproprietatem Spiritus sancti. Ea enim quae nascuntur, non quae procedunt, solent esse similia. Notandum quod ad imaginem et aequalitatem sequitur similitudo: quia ubicunque imago, vel aequalitas est, ibi est similitudo, sed non convertitur. Item nec imago infert aequalitatem, nec infertur ab ea, quia et imago sine aequalitate, et aequalitas sine imagine esse potest.

QUAESTIO XI. Habentes eumdem spiritum fidei. Dicit expositor super hunc locum, quod tempora variata sunt, non fides, quia quidquid nos credimus, et illi antiqui crediderunt, et e diverso. Unde sic objicitur: Abraham credidit Christum nasciturum, et nos credimus natum: sed aliud est esse 547Anasciturum, aliud natum: ergo aliud credidit ille, et aliud nos? Solutio. Quidquid credimus nos, et antiqui, etc., id est, res eaedem subjectae sunt nostrae fidei, et illorum: non tamen sequitur quod idem, quod est modo praeteritum, esse in tempore eorum praeteritum; vel quod tunc futurum, modo sit futurum. Item si opponitur: Abraham credidit Christum nasciturum, sed modo falsum est Christum nasciturum: ergo Abraham credidit falsum. Solutio. Ut nobis videtur, quid interpretatur quale. Cum enim dicitur: Abraham credidit Christum nasciturum, sensus est, fidem habuit de Christi nativitate, quae tunc futura erat; sed in assumptione, cum dicitur, modo falsum est Christum nasciturum, sensus est: nativitas Christi non est futura: unde 547Bex illis duabus nullo modo sequitur Abraham falsum credidisse.

QUAESTIO XII. Sed licet is, qui foris est, noster homo. Quaeritur an duo homines sint homo exterior, et homo interior, et an idem sit homo exterior, et homo vetus, et homo interior, et homo novus. Solutio. Sicut homo vetus, et homo novus, non sunt duo homines, sed unus, licet secundum aliud vetus, secundum aliud novus dicatur, sic homo exterior, et homo interior non duo homines, sed unus et idem secundum diversa sic dictus est. Nec idem est homo vetus, et homo exterior; nec idem est homo novus, et homo interior. Vetus enim homo consistit in culpa, et poena, quae duo non solum inveniuntur in homine exteriore, sed etiam in homine interiore. Homo 547Cvero novus intelligitur secundum justitiam et gloriam: quae duo etiam ad hominem interiorem pertinent. Homo vero exterior dicitur, quidquid habemus commune cum brutis: homo interior, quod nobis commune est cum angelis.

QUAESTIO XIII. Qui dedit nobis pignus spiritus, etc. (II Cor. V). Quaeritur quomodo Spiritus sanctus dicatur pignus, et cujus rei sit arrha? Solutio. Spiritus sanctus amor est, et ex amore, quem habemus erga Deum, certi sumus de promissione ipsius; et quia hanc certitudinem habemus ex Spiritu sancto, ideo Spiritus sanctus quasi arrha, et pignus nobis datus est a Deo. Est autem pignus certitudo rei creditae, vel promissae, vel credendae. 547DScientes ergo timorem Domini hominibus suademus. Timor in quinque species dividitur, ut jam in epistola ad Romanos dictum est, nec opus est recedere.

QUAESTIO XIV. Sive enim mente excedimus, etc. Quaeritur qui sint mentis excessus. Solutio. Duo sunt excessus, vel pavor, vel intentio ad superna: ita ut quodam modo a memoria labantur inferiora. In hoc mentis excessu fuerunt omnes sancti: quibus arcana Dei mundum excedentia revelata sunt.

QUAESTIO XV. Pro omnibus mortuus est Christus. Quaeritur quomodo pro omnibus mortuus sit Christus: cum ejus mors non omnibus prosit: damnandis enim non prodest, sed tantum electis. Solutio. 548ASecundum Hieronymum sic intelligitur, pro omnibus salvandis. Universitas enim quandoque restringitur, et hoc modis pluribus. Quandoque enim colligit signum universale singula generum, quandoque genera singulorum, quandoque neutrum, sed partem majorem, vel digniorem ipsius universitatis. Vel secundum Augustinum, mortuus est pro omnibus Christus, quia hoc ejus mors promeruit, ut per ipsum omnes salvarentur, nisi in ipsis remaneret: sufficiens enim erat ad omnium salutem.

QUAESTIO XVI. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. Quaeritur quomodo Pater in Filio, vel Filius in Patre dicatur esse: vel quomodo illud 548Bsit intelligendum: Qui videt me, videt et Patrem (Joan. XIV). Solutio. Ideo alter in altero esse vel videri dicitur, quia una est substantia eorum naturaliter. Quod addo, ut haeresim Sabellianam excludam. Ibi est unitas, ubi nulla diversitas, sed omnimodo indifferentia, et aequalitas, et identitas. Unde Hilarius ait: Pater videtur in Filio propter unitam naturae similitudinem: sic enim detestamur pestem Arianorum, quod nihilominus exsecramur insaniam Sabellianorum, sic Deum trinum confitemur, quod unum, et sic unum, quod trinum. Multi enim in diebus nostris sunt Sabelliani, quantum ad intellectum, qui confitentur tres personas: sed cum dicitur, quod tres personae sunt una substantia, non aliud intelligunt, quam Sabellius intellexit: 548Cquod inde contingit, quia non animadvertunt multiplicem hujus nominis, substantia, significationem. Dicit enim Hilarius quod cum dicitur: Pater et Filius sunt una substantia, talis locutio habet et fidei conscientiam, et fraudem paratam. Deinde aperit utrumque dicens: Si singularem Deum Patrem, et Filium significes, falsa est intelligentia: si autem dicas ideo Patrem et Filium unam substantiam, vel unum simpliciter, ut intelligas unum, par et indifferens, per omnia aequale, ex nulla parte dissimile, vera est intelligentia. Quibus verbis manifestissime distinguit, inter unitatem personalem, et unitatem naturalem: Pater enim et Filius unum sunt in natura, non in persona.

548DQUAESTIO XVII. Ecce nunc dies salutis, etc. (III Cor. VI). Quaeritur cur tempus gratiae dies salutis dicitur, cum etiam in tempore legis naturalis et scriptae multi salvarentur? Solutio. Ideo dies salutis hoc tempus gratiae dicitur, quia in hoc tempore hostia oblata est, per quam solam introitus patet in regnum, per quam etiam illi, qui praecesserunt, salutem meruerunt. Unde etiam tempus gratiae dicitur, propter majores vires nobis datas per fidei, et dilectionis manifestationem: unde et vires diaboli sunt imminutae, et quia nunc omnia gratis, non causa alicujus terreni commodi fiunt, et quia illa, quae in aliis temporibus sunt promissa, hoc tempore sunt adimpleta.

549AQUAESTIO. XVIII. Charitate non ficta, etc. Quaeritur quae charitas dicatur ficta. Solutio. Quae non perseverat, vel quae non est sufficiens ad salutem, vel simulata, scilicet aliquod signum dilectionis exterius ostensum, cum intus non sit in corde, et haec charitas non est charitas.

QUAESTIO XIX. Quasi morientes, et ecce vivimus. Quaeritur juxta haec quomodo jugum Domini sit suave, et onus leve, cum sancti tot et tanta dura et difficilia patiantur, et quomodo laborantes et onerati ad se venientes requiem inveniant, cum non a labore ad requiem, sed potius a requie ad laborem videantur transire. Solutio. Sanctis gravia et aspera sustinentibus adest Spiritus sanctus, qui in exterioris hominis corruptione interiorem hominem revocat, 549Bde die in diem, et gustata requie spirituali, spe futurae beatitudinis omnia aspera relevat, et sic in tot duris levius est onus Christi. Omnia enim saeva et immania, facilia et prope nulla facit amor Dei et Domini nostri Jesu Christi.

QUAESTIO XX. Ut fiat aequalitas, sicut scriptum est: Qui multum non abundavit, etc. (II Cor. VIII.) Quaeritur an minores qui (quasi provinciales) ministrant stipendia militibus Christi, sint illis in meritis aequales: quod videtur Apostolus velle dicens, ut fiat aequalitas. Solutio. Ista aequalitas non est pietatis, sed quia utrique sustentant, et sustentantur ab invicem. Minores enim majores in carnalibus sustentant, et sustentantur in spiritualibus. Et majores minores, id est spiritales, carnales sustentant in 549Cspiritalibus, et sustentantur in carnalibus ab eisdem.

QUAESTIO XXI. Providemus enim bona non solum coram Deo, etc. Quaeritur quomodo dividat Apostolus, scilicet coram Deo, et coram hominibus, cum non possit fieri coram Deo, nisi etiam fiat coram hominibus? Nec tamen semper exigitur opus exterius, videlicet cum deest facultas. Semper autem exigitur, ut munda sit conscientia. Solutio. Ut Apostolus ostendat conscientiam non posse esse mundam, nisi etiam bona provideantur coram hominibus, ideo distinguit inter haec duo.

QUAESTIO. XXII. Quaeritur: Quid est providere bona coram Deo? Solutio. Sic mentem aptare, ut 549Dnihil fiat contra Deum, quod fieri nequit, nisi scandalum vitetur fratrum exterius, vel ideo dividat inter praedicta, ut ostendat quaedam esse quae licet fieri quantum ad Deum pertinent, quia in se bona sunt, quamvis aliter videatur hominibus, ideoque possunt praetermitti. Quod ergo expedit et decet, illud fiat quod expedit nobis ad meritum, quod decet ad exemplum caeteris. Ergo propter conscientiam bona providere debemus coram Deo. Propter famam providemus etiam bona coram hominibus: qui enim conscientiae fidens famam negligit, crudelis est, quod facit qui non curat, an quod facit placeat, an displiceat, et propter scandalum fratrum nihil dimittit.

QUAESTIO XXIII. Qui parce seminat, parce et metet. 550A(II Cor. IX.) Quaeritur de pauperibus, qui parce seminant, vel nihil, an ideo parce et ipsi metent. Solutio. Non parce seminat ille qui parum largitur, si animus promptus sit dare, si plus haberet. Parce ergo seminare dicendus est, qui parvam habet dilectionem, sive plus, sive minus det: et hic parce metet, id est, parvam percipiet retributionem in vitam aeternam.

QUAESTIO XXIV. Non enim audemus nos inserere, etc. (II Cor. II.) Id est, non usurpamus nobis potestatem, sed potestate nobis a Deo data utimur. Quaeritur itaque quid sit usurpare potestatem. Solutio. Ille usurpat sibi potestatem, qui non electus, vel non vocatus, sumit sibi honorem, qui ingerit se, et non accepta potestate vult dominari.

550BQUAESTIO XXV. Nos autem non in immensum gloriamur. Quaeritur: Quid est in immensum gloriari? Solutio. Plusquam debet, et in eo quod non debet quis gloriari, quod facit ille qui extendit se in id in quod jus non habet. Abuti autem potestate est adulari, et vitia peccantium palpare. Uti potestate est peccantes arguere, et caetera quae ad aedificationem pertinent facere.

QUAESTIO XXVI. Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Quaeritur quid sit in Domino gloriari, cum alibi dicat: Absit mihi gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini nostri Jesu Christi (Galat. VI). Et illud: Non solum gloriamur in spe filiorum Dei, sed etiam in tribulationibus nostris (Rom. V). Nunquid idem est in Domino, et in cruce Domini, et in tribulationibus gloriari? 550CQuid est gloriari? Solutio. Gloriari est gaudere laude, et gloria se dignum judicare. In Domino gloriari est totam fiduciam non sibi, sed Domino tanquam auctori attribuere, et in Christo exsultare gaudio spirituali. In cruce Domini gloriari duobus modis potest intelligi. Ille enim recte in cruce Domini gloriari dicitur, qui cum gaudio, et spe futurae vitae imitatur Domini passionem, et hoc est gloriari in tribulationibus. Dicitur etiam aliquis gloriari in cruce Domini, qui non judicat se dignum salute, nisi per passionis Dominicae meritum, dicens cum apostolo Petro: Quia non est aliud nomen sub coelo in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri (Act. IV), haec dico absque praejudicio melioris sententiae.

550DQUAESTIO XXVII. Aemulor enim vos Dei aemulatione, etc. (II Cor. XI.) Quaeritur: quid est aemulatio? Solutio. Aemulatio est motus mentis in bonum vel in malum propter alienum statum. Quando est in bonum, tunc est amoris; quando est in malum, tunc est livoris.

QUAESTIO XXVIII. Quaeritur item: quid est aemulari Dei aemulatione? Solutio. Diligere ad honorem Dei, vel ea aemulatione quam Deus inspirat.

QUAESTIO XXIX. Despondi enim vos uni viro virginem castam exhibere Christo. Quaeritur de hac desponsatione Apostoli cum non omnes qui sunt in Ecclesia sint virgines, ut conjugati, quomodo ergo potest eos qui non sunt virgines exhibere virginem, quasi unam, insuper castam? Solutio. Duplex est virginitas: 551Acorporis et mentis: carnis virginitas est corpus intactum, mentis virginitas est integritas hominis interioris incorrupta. Haec autem exigitur ab omni fideli, sine qua illa quae est carnis non prodest. Virgo autem una omnes dicuntur propter unitatem integrae fidei, solidae spei, sincerae dilectionis. Casta, non habens aestum malae voluntatis.

QUAESTIO XXX. Satanas transfigurat se in angelum lucis, etc. Quaeritur an periculosum sit credere Satanam esse angelum lucis, cum ea dicit, vel facit, quae congruunt bonis. Solutio. Si tunc quando dicit vel facit ea quae conveniunt, non est error periculosus; cum autem suas fallacias incipit ducere ne quis post eum eat, opus est vigilantia: quod non fit sine Deo.

551BQUAESTIO XXXI. [ In fame, et siti, etc. Quaeritur ubi est promissio Dei dicentis: Primum quaerite regnum Dei, et haec omnia adjicientur vobis (Matth. VI). Videtur enim promissio titubasse, cum Apostolus dicat se laborasse in fame, et siti, frigore et nuditate. Solutio. Novit ille medicus, cui semel nos totos commisimus, et a quo promissionem praesentis vitae et futurae habemus, quando haec adjutoria apponat, vel subtrahat sicut nobis expedire judicat?

QUAESTIO XXXII. Per fenestram in porta a fratribus. Quaeritur an hoc factum sit laudabile, an dignum reprehensione: quod videtur quibusdam, quia Dei auxilio non est liberatus. Solutio. Ante non est necessarium suffragium Dei quam defecerit humanum auxilium; nec debet aliquis exspectare 551CDei auxilium, dum habet quod faciat, ne videatur tentare Deum.

QUAESTIO XXXIII. Et sic effugi manus ejus. Quaeritur an Apostolus fecerit fugiendo, ut bonus pastor, an ut mercenarius. Nonne lupo veniente oves deseruit, et fugit? et sic videtur quod non bonus pastor, sed mercenarius fuerit. Solutio. Quando aliquis pastor specialiter a persecutoribus quaeritur, licet ei cedere, et rabiem persecutorum declinare, et fugiendo utilitati totius gregis se custodire, et interim caeteri qui ita non requiruntur, conservis suis cibaria praebeant. Cum autem, omnium commune instat periculum, ii, qui aliis indigent, non deserantur ab iis quibus indigent.

QUAESTIO XXXIV. Sive in corpore, sive extra corpus, 551Dnescio, Deus scit, etc. (II Cor. XII.) Quaeritur quomodo Apostolus dubitaverit an in corpore, an extra corpus sit raptus cum nemo in hac vita existens Deum sicuti est videre possit; unde dicit Moysi: Non videbit me homo, et vivet (Exod. XXXIII). Item si extra corpus sit raptus, ita scilicet quod anima separata a corpore fuerit, nunquid corpus ejus interim fuit mortuum? Item si intellectuali visione Deum vidit, tunc eum vidit vere, et illam cognitionem habuit, in qua summa est beatitudo et sic in beatitudine fuit; sed beatitudo semel habita nunquam amittitur; aut si jam susceptam Deus ei abstulit, videtur quod injuste Deus egerit. Solutio. Utrumque contingere potuit: vel quod anima a corpore 552Aseparata Deum in se viderit vel anima, libera a sensibus corporis in ipso corpore sic Deum contemplaretur; et quoniam alterum istorum recte contingere potuisset dubitando dicit Apostolus sive in corpore, sive extra corpus. Unde quodcunque horum fuerit, salva erit auctoritas illa: Non videbit me homo, et vivet, quia utroque modo exuisse hominem potuit. Si autem extra corpus fuit, tunc corpus mortuum fuit, et ab anima separatum, et iterum anima redeunte vivificatum. Cum autem plenam Dei cognitionem habuit, et sic in beatitudine fuerit, si iterum eidem eadem gloria subtracta fuit, non est mirum, nec incredibile, quia sic Deus servo suo dilectissimo beatitudinem et gaudium futurum, quod accepturus erat praeostendere potuit, 552But firmius in ejus dilectione et servitio perduraret, et tempus ipsum recipiendi vehementius desideraret: quemadmodum in monte transfiguratus gloriam humanitatis tribus discipulis suis ostendit.

QUAESTIO XXXV. Per tertium vero coelum, et paradisum, in quem raptus est, idem intelligit, videlicet plenam divinitatis intelligentiam, vel cognitionem. Nota de tribus coelis quadripertitam sententiam. Secundum primam sententiam primum coelum est aereum, unde aves coeli. Secundum est firmamentum, unde et vocavit firmamentum coelum. Tertium est empyreum, quod statim ex quo factum angelis est repletum, ubi angeli, et animae sanctae fruuntur contemplatione Dei. Secundum secundam sententiam primum coelum est corporalis visio, qua 552Ccoelum, et terra, et omnia oculis conspicua cernuntur. Eadem visione quandoque Dei munere videntur quaedam, ut Elisaeus currus ignitos (IV Reg. II), et Balthasar manum scribentem, in pariete, mane, thecel, phares (Dan. V). Secundum coelum est visio imaginaria, vel spiritalis, qua videntur non corpora, sed imagines eorum: sicut solent in somnis, vel in exstasi, ut Pharao spicas (Gen. XLI), et Petrus discum (Act. X). Tertium visio intellectualis, qua non corpora, nec imagines corporum videntur, sed incorporalia, et immaterialia instinctu mentis conspiciuntur, ut substantia, Deitas et omnis animae affectio. Tertia sententia tres coelos triplicem angelorum hierarchiam secundum Dionysium vocat. Prima in ascensu est quae continet angelos, et archangelos, 552Det virtutes. Secunda potestates, principatus et dominationes; tertia thronos et cherubim, et seraphim. Hanc itaque tertiam hierarchiam in ascensu, et primam in descensu, vocat Apostolus tertium coelum, sive paradisum: ad quod cum dicit se raptum, ostendit quod Deum vidit immediate facie ad faciem. Quarta sententia est, quod primum coelum dicitur cognitio coelestium corporum, secundum coelestium spirituum, tertium cognitio Deitatis.

QUAESTIO XXXVI. Scio hujusmodi, etc. Quaeritur quomodo hominem raptum dicat sive in corpore, sive extra, cum homo in corpore et anima subsistat, quomodo ergo dicit hominem posse extra corpus rapi. Solutio. Veritas hominis ibi consistit, ubi est 553Aimago, et similitudo Dei. Unde est illud: Mens cujusque, ipse est quisque. Nomine itaque hominis, vocat hominem interiorem.

QUAESTIO XXXVII. Datus est mihi stimulus carnis meae angelus, etc. Quaeritur a quo sit ei datus stimulus iste, an a Deo, an a diabolo. Si a Deo, quomodo angelus Satanae dicitur, quasi ab eo missus? Item si a diabolo missus, quomodo verum est quod sequitur: Ne magnitudo revelationum extollat, etc. Nunquid ideo Satanas per angelum missum a se Apostolum colaphizabat, ne in superbiam extolleretur? Solutio. Et a Deo, et a diabolo missus est ille qui Apostolum vexabat, sed propter aliud a Deo, et propter aliud a diabolo. A Deo ideo missus est, ne magnitudo revelationum extolleret eum. A diabolo ideo, ut eum ad 553Bdefectum traheret. A Deo etiam ideo missus est, ut virtus in infimitate perficeretur.

QUAESTIO XXXVIII. Propter quod ter Dominum rogavi, etc. Diabolus expetivit Job tentandum, et exauditus est (Job I). Apostolus petivit ut angelus Satanae recederet ab eo, et non est exauditus. Ubi est ergo divina justitia? Nunquid justum fuit diabolum exaudiri, et non Apostolum? Solutio. Deus eos quos sanare disposuit, non semper exaudit ad voluntatem, sed ad sanitatem. Quosdam vero iratus quandoque exaudit ad voluntatem, ut diabolum.

QUAESTIO XXXIX. Item cum sciret Apostolus hanc infirmitatem sibi datam ad profectum, et ad humilitatis conservationem, quaeritur an rationabiliter petierit 553Cut ab eo talis tentatio recederet. Solutio. Licet hoc sciret, tamen humane casum ex afflictione timebat, 554Aet sic ex timore humiliabatur; humilitas vero expellebat morbum superbae elationis, et hac dispensatione divinae providentiae, datus est ei stimulus ille.

QUAESTIO XL. Et non egerunt poenitentiam, etc. Quaeritur an poenitentia sit necessaria emendanti mores in melius; et quibus modis agitur poenitentia. Solutio. Non sufficit mores in melius mutare, et a malis recedere, nisi per poenitentiae dolorem, et humilitatis gemitum, et cordis contriti sacrificium satis fiat de culpa. Item notandum est quod tribus modis agitur poenitentia: ante baptisma, et post baptisma, pro gravioribus, et quotidie pro levioribus et crebris, juxta illud: Vitasti grandia, vide ne opprimaris arena.

QUAESTIO XLI. Oramus Deum, ut nihil mali faciatis 554B(II Cor. XIII). Hic innuit Apostolus quod sola gratia Dei declinatur a malo, dicendo: Oramus, etc. Nil enim valet exterior plantatio et irrigatio sine interiori incremento: quod dat Deus sola gratia. Quaeritur ergo cur in sacris Scripturis saepe praecipitur nobis et declinare a malo, et facere bonum: cum ad neutrum istorum sufficiat liberum arbitrium, cum solius gratiae opus sit proprium tam hoc quam illud. Solutio. Voluntas nonnihil facit, sed sola non facit. Ideo cum praecipitur, ut fiat hoc vel illud, liberum arbitrium debemus agnoscere; cum autem oratur, gratiae beneficium postulatur. De gratia et libero arbitrio jam in superioribus dictum est, et similiter quid per se gratia sine voluntate operetur, 554Cet quid sine illa non operetur; nec opus est ut eadem iterum repetantur.

III. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

  • 543

543C(II COR. I.) Paul an apostle, etc. This is the second epistle, which is addressed to the Corinthians. Now the Apostle sometimes writes two, sometimes one epistle only; but neither, when he writes one, does he say anything diminished and imperfect, nor, when he writes two, anything superfluous, as here can be seen. For this epistle, which follows, is the consummation and confirmation of the preceding. For in this second one he admonishes those to be corrected who had not yet been corrected through the preceding epistle. He marks them, that in almsgiving they were sparing. He commands the corrected fornicator to be received. Whence it appears what is the matter of this epistle, and also what the intention. The matter is the special state of the Corinthians, in which they then were. But the intention is to recall them to the unity and integrity of faith. But in this 543Dspecial state he signifies and forms the general state of the Church, and invites all to the unity of faith. He sends beforehand, after his manner, and that of others writing epistles, salutations of those to whom he writes, courting benevolence: whence also he says, Paul an apostle, joining a name of humility and a name of dignity, that humility as companion may temper the excellence of dignity, without which every virtue is empty and vain. Likewise, of Jesus Christ: Jesus is a name of the person. Now many were called by this name, as Jesus son of Nave, Jesus the great priest, but all by way of designation. But Christ alone substantively, because he had both the name and the thing: who was truly the Savior of the world. For Jesus is interpreted Savior. But Christ is a name of the person, 544Cwhich embraces both natures. For it is a name of office, like priest, soldier, and is interpreted anointed. In the Old Testament two persons were anointed, the royal and the priestly; but Christ was anointed with a royal anointing, who according to the divine nature was able to rule his own; but according to the human nature received the power of offering, who offered himself to God the Father: whence from the royal and priestly office he is called Christ. The will of God is taken in many ways, as was already said above, and to say it again will not be superfluous. For the will of God is called the disposition itself, and the good pleasure. Whence: Whatsoever he pleased he hath done (Psalm. CXXXIV). The will of God is also called counsel, or precept: whence it is said: God will have all men to be saved (I Tim. II), that is, 544Dhe counsels and commands them to do those things by which they may be saved, such as prohibition, or permission, and the like.

QUESTION I. Whereas when I was thus minded, did I use lightness? It is asked therefore whether the Apostle lied, in promising that he would come, when he did not come: for he himself said, I will come, and he did not come: therefore with him there was "it is" and "it is not," that is, affirmation and negation of the same thing, and thus a lie, and thus he is guilty of lying. Solution. A lie is a false signification of the voice with the intention of deceiving: whence he who says something false which he thinks true is not to be judged a liar, since he is rather deceived than deceives. But whoever, with the intention of deceiving, says what is true or false, is guilty 545Aof lying: whence it is gathered that someone saying what is true is guilty of lying, or lies; and that someone says what is false, and yet does not lie or is not guilty of lying.

QUESTION II. But it is asked concerning those who lie piously, whether they are guilty of lying, as those Egyptian midwives? For from the intention of deceiving they pronounced something false. Solution. Those who thus lie sin, and while they provide for the lives of others, acting against their own conscience, they offend the truth, and incur the peril of their own soul.

QUESTION III. Likewise it is asked concerning those who speak falsehood in jest. Solution. Sometimes so to jest is evil, sometimes not; but if from habit, then it is a sin.

545BQUESTION IV. To some indeed the odour of death unto death, etc. (II Cor. II.) It is asked whether the odour of death is good or evil, since the Apostle says that he is an odour, to some unto death, to some unto life: for if good, how unto death? Likewise, if evil, how good to God? Solution. The Apostle was nothing but a good odour, and yet by this good odour some were dying, that is, they took occasion through envy, as the law is good, and yet an occasion of evil, because of transgression.

QUESTION V. Not that we are sufficient, etc. (II Cor. III). Here it is asked how the Apostle says that we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, since we can both think and do evil of ourselves. Likewise, since certain things we can do naturally, which are neither for reward nor for punishment 545C— and these are those which were given us from the first creation, as to raise a finger, to bend it, to lay it down, and the like. Solution. The Apostle here treats of those goods which have merit with God, which can in no way be done without grace supervening and helping. Whence His mercy shall prevent me (Psal. LVIII), and his mercy shall follow me (Psal. XXII). For grace prevents the will, that it may will, and follows after, lest it will in vain. Whence the Apostle here destroys the error of those who said that the beginning of good cannot naturally be without grace, but that the consummation of good is from ourselves: in this that he says, but our sufficiency is from God. For from free will we have the faculty of working well, yet we cannot use this faculty except 545Dby the help of grace. For free will is through fault so depressed that it cannot use its own power, unless it be raised up by grace and helped, as, when I have the power of riding, yet I cannot have the exercise of this power without a horse.

QUESTION VI. The letter killeth, but the spirit quickeneth, etc. It is asked how the letter is said to kill: does it command such things as, when observed, kill? How then will that stand which the Apostle says elsewhere, that the law is holy, and the commandment holy, good and just, if the precepts kill? Likewise, if it be said that the letter without the spirit, that is, without grace, kills, the same can seem to be said of the Gospel. 546ALikewise, if it be said that the letter kills for this reason, that not all things can be observed there according to the letter: let him not perish who has observed them. In the same way it can be said of the Gospel. For if this, except you eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, etc. (Joan. VI), be observed according to the letter, that is, as the letter sounds, so that we understand eating and drinking thus, this, as elsewhere, is foolish and damnable. Solution: The letter without the spirit kills, that is, without grace, because it is an occasion of death, as knowledge without charity puffs up. But the letter of the Gospel is not without the spirit. Or, as was already said elsewhere: By the letter, or law, is understood the commandment without grace: which always kills: because, increasing concupiscence, it adds on transgression. By the Gospel 546Bis understood the commandment with the spirit, that is, grace: whence the Apostle calls the law the ministration of death: the Gospel, the ministration of justice.

QUESTION VII. And not as Moses put a veil, etc. It is asked concerning the veil, whether it blinds. Solution. One thing is the figured veil, which is the reading of Moses: which was figured by the veil that Moses, speaking to the children of Israel, put over his face. Another thing is the veil of blindness, which is placed over the heart of the Jews: both veils are taken away through Christ. In figure of which thing the veil of the temple was rent in the passion of Christ.

QUESTION VIII. But we all, beholding the glory of God with open face, are transformed into the same image, 546Cetc. It is asked what he calls glory, and what image? Solution. The glory of God, which we behold, and the image, into which we are transformed, he calls the same, namely Christ, who is the glory, and the uncreated image of God, as man is the glory, and the created image of God.

QUESTION IX. Who is the image of the invisible God (II Cor. IV). It is asked why the Son is called the image of the Father. Solution. That it may be shown that he is so from the Father, as to be shown through all things like and equal to him.

QUESTION X. But if it be asked why the Holy Spirit, since he is from the Father, and like and equal through all things, is not called the image of the Father as the Son is. It is answered that image, equality, and likeness pertain more to the property of the Son than to 546Dthe property of the Holy Spirit. For those things which are born, not those which proceed, are wont to be alike. It is to be noted that upon image and equality follows likeness: because wherever there is image, or equality, there is likeness, but it is not converted. Likewise, image neither infers equality, nor is inferred from it, because there can be image without equality, and equality without image.

QUESTION XI. Having the same spirit of faith. The expositor says upon this passage that the times are varied, not the faith, because whatever we believe, those ancients also believed, and conversely. Whence it is thus objected: Abraham believed that Christ was to be born, and we believe that he is born: but it is one thing to be 547Aabout to be born, another to be born: therefore he believed one thing, and we another? Solution. Whatever we believe, and the ancients, etc., that is, the same things are subject to our faith and to theirs: yet it does not follow that the same thing which is now past was past in their time; or that what was then future is now future. Likewise, if it is objected: Abraham believed that Christ was to be born, but now it is false that Christ is to be born: therefore Abraham believed something false. Solution. As it seems to us, the "what" is interpreted by the "of what kind."
