The solution of this question the Apostle sets down, saying: The law was set because of transgression, which can be understood in two ways, namely for the restraining of transgression, that at least through fear men might cease to transgress, so that at some time they might do the same voluntarily; or the law was set because of transgression, that is, that it might make men transgress, and thus they might be humbled, and seek a physician, and implore the help of grace. It was given therefore that it might humble the proud, and betray [their] weakness, 559Dand [be] a scourge to the hard and a sign of things to come.

QUESTION XIX. It is asked why the law was not given immediately after the fall of man? or why the Son himself did not come at once? or why he permitted so many men to perish? Solution. By great counsel this was done, that after the fall of man the law was not immediately given, or the Son sent. For unless the pride of man first made trial of the powers of his own choice, it would arrogate sufficiency to [its] liberty, and would judge that the law was given superfluously, and that the Son came in vain. Nor did all, who then were, perish: just as neither are all, who now are, made saved. And so this was done, that man might recognize the disease of his own weakness, and implore the grace necessary for him. For in the natural law he was left to himself, 560Athat thus he might make trial of the powers of nature, and was convicted of ignorance, and confessed [it], because the light of his eyes failed: yet still he believed that he had a virtue, by which he could fulfill whatever was necessary for salvation. Whence also he said: There is not lacking one who fulfills, but there is lacking one who commands. As if he said: I need knowledge, not virtue. And so the law was given, which might illuminate ignorance, but not aid weakness: which uncovered sin, but did not consume it, by the giving of which the disease grew strong, and concupiscence was increased, not by the fault of the law, but of nature, and by the instigation of the devil, that thus, the insufficiency of both laws being recognized, and his own weakness, [man] might cry to the physician, and seek the help of grace: and thus, with weaknesses multiplied, they hastened to the physician, who coming in the form 560Bof a servant healed the wounds of the sick. For this is that Samaritan, who drew near to the wounded man, who fell among robbers, and bound up his wounds: whom the priest, and the levite, that is the law and the priesthood, passed by (Luc. X): because the law brought no one to perfection (Hebr. VII). This is Elisha, who after sending the staff not effective of health, came to raise up the dead son of the Shunammite (IV Reg. IV). This is the Angel of great counsel, who descended into the pool, and when the water was moved one was healed (Joan. V). This is the omnipotent Word, who came from the royal seats, while a middle silence held all things (Sap. XVIII). Note that there are three silences. The first silence is the ignorance of languor, which was under the natural law. The second silence is the despair of salvation, 560Cwhich was under the written law, and this silence is the middle one. The third silence is the attainment of health: which will be in the glory of eternal beatitude. While therefore all things held a middle silence, that is, despaired of salvation: the Son of the most high King descended from the light of heaven to the darkness of the world or of hell. And coming he spoke peace, gave grace, set forth mercy, promised pardon. And thus, the middle silence being broken, the sick began with pure faith, and true confession, as with great cries to demand a remedy, and to hasten to the physician, by whom the sick might be healed, and [their] wounds cured.

QUESTION XX. The law was set in the hand of a Mediator. It is asked why Christ is called a Mediator? Solution. 560DBecause he mediates us, that is, reconciles [us] to God.

QUESTION XXI. But since not only the Son reconciles us to himself, but also God the Father, as the Apostle says: God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (II Cor. V), it is asked why the Son alone is called the Mediator of God and men. Solution. The whole Trinity by the exercise of [its] power reconciles us to itself: but the Son alone by the fulfilling of obedience, and by the undertaking of the sacraments, justifies and reconciles us. Whence not undeservedly he alone is called Mediator.

QUESTION XXII. Since Christ [is] God, and man, the mediator of God and men, it is asked according to which nature, whether according to the divine, or according to the human, or according to both, he is Mediator. Solution. The authors say that he is not mediator according to 561Athat which is God, but only according to that which is man, drawing near to us by mortality, [and] to God by justice.

QUESTION XXIII. But scripture hath concluded all under sin. It is asked what he calls scripture. Solution. The law, which elsewhere he calls the letter, here the Apostle names scripture: because it only commands, [and] does not help: it convicts of disease the sick man, who seemed to himself whole, and thus by showing sins, and not taking [them] away, concludes all under sin. The law was given therefore, that grace might be sought: and grace was conferred, that through it the law might be fulfilled: to this accords what he says elsewhere: God hath concluded all in unbelief, that he might have mercy on all (Rom. XI).

QUESTION XXIV. As many of you as have been baptized 561Bin Christ, have put on Christ. It is asked concerning him, who feignedly approaches baptism, whether he is baptized in Christ, and has put on Christ. For if it be said so, it follows that he is conformed to Christ: but if he is not baptized, [and] if he repent of his feigning, he will be able to be baptized, but this is not granted him: it is established therefore that if baptized. Solution. To be baptized in Christ, and to put on Christ is understood in two ways, either by the reception of the sacrament, which is common to good and bad; or by inward sanctification, and conformity of life, which belongs to the good alone.

QUESTION XXV. It is asked how Christ is the garment of the saints, and whether the saints are the garment of Christ? Solution. Christ is called the garment of the saints, and the saints also the garment 561Cof Christ. But in one way and another. For Christ is called the garment of the saints through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, protecting them from the heat of vices: but the saints [are] the garment of Christ, as it were having him within themselves, and surrounding [him]. Also they honor him by their holy manner of life: as the wicked, by living wickedly, blaspheme [him].

QUESTION XXVI. If you [be] Christ's, then [you are] Abraham's, etc. Christ is called the seed of Abraham, and the faithful are called the seed of Abraham. Whence it is asked whether according to the same signification both Christ and the faithful are called the seed of Abraham? Solution. Christ is the seed of Abraham corporally, because born of his stock: the faithful are the seed of Abraham spiritually, that is, just through 561Dfaith, as he was.

QUESTION XXVII. We were serving under the elements of the world (Galat. IV). If then the Jews also served under the elements, in what did they differ from the pagans? Solution. The Jews under the elements served God, not the elements themselves: but the pagans exhibited divine worship not to God, but to the elements themselves.

QUESTION XXVIII. When the fullness came, etc. It is asked why the coming of the Savior is called the fullness of time? Solution. For this reason, because at this time are fulfilled the things which in preceding times had been foretold, and it would seem more properly said the time of fullness, than the fullness of time, and the end of the age is called the same.

QUESTION XXIX. He sent his Son, etc. It is asked 562Awhence and whither the Son was sent. Hear: I came forth from the Father, and came into the world (Joan. XVI).

QUESTION XXX. But someone will say: Was he not in the world, and the world was made by him (Joan. I). Was he then sent thither, where he was before? Solution. He was before in the world by power, and by essence, but he began to be otherwise in the world, made visible through the undertaking of the servile form. As therefore when he came forth from the Father, he did not desert the Father; so he came into the world, in which he was before. But why the mission of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, since it is the work of the Trinity, is attributed to the Father, has already been said in what precedes.

QUESTION XXXI. Made of a woman. Since the Lord was born of a virgin, it is asked why the Apostle asserts [him] made of a woman? Solution. He used the Hebrew 562Bmanner of speech, which puts woman for female, as Eve in Genesis, not yet having suffered intercourse, is called a woman. Note that the expositor says that the Creator, who always was, was made, that he might be a creature; because he was made man, that he might become what he was not; not that what he was might perish; this I say on account of certain [persons], who deny that he was made anything.

QUESTION XXXII. Made under the law, that he might redeem them, who were under the law, etc. Did he not by his death redeem both those who were under the law, and those who were without the law? How then does the Apostle say Christ [was] made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, as though he redeemed them through the observance of the law? Solution. He was made under the law, that he might fulfill it, and having fulfilled [it] make it cease; and thus also 562Credeem the Jews from the prevarication of the law. For unless he kept the law, in which the promise was made, who would believe that he was the seed of Abraham promised to Abraham, in whom not only the Jews, but also all the nations should be blessed?

QUESTION XXXIII. That we might receive the adoption of sons. What does he call adoption; whether the gratuitous goods pertaining to present justice, or to future glory, through which we are made sons? Solution. Some think a distinction is to be made between the sons of adoption and the sons of grace, but I judge them to be the same.

QUESTION XXXIV. God sent the spirit of his Son, etc. Note that the Trinity is here manifestly signified. There are some, who say, that as the eternal generation of the Word 562Dis from the Father alone, so also is his temporal mission; because according to these, for the Father to send the Son, is [for the Son] to be from the Father, and to appear to us in the flesh assumed. Similarly they assert concerning the Holy Spirit, that as his eternal procession is from the Father, and the Son, and not from himself, so also [is] the temporal: but Augustine manifestly says that the temporal mission both of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is the work of the Trinity; whence the Son himself says that he was sent by the Holy Spirit.

QUESTION XXXV. Crying: Abba, Father. It is asked why the Apostle set down two words signifying the same thing; for one seems to be set down superfluously. Solution. He does this for this reason, that he might intimate two peoples joined by one faith. For the Hebrew name signifies the Jews, the Greek word the gentile people; 563Athe same signification of both words figures the unity of faith and of the Spirit.

QUESTION XXXVI. To those, who by nature are not gods. Here he intimates that the nature of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is one. For if the Son is not by nature God, then [he is] neither to be worshipped, nor adored. But it is objected to us thus: Is not the humanity of Christ worshipped and adored? and yet it is not by nature God. Solution. That which is assumed is adored not on its own account, but on account of the one assuming; therefore we adore the humanity of the Savior not alone and bare, but united to the Godhead.

QUESTION XXXVII. But rather, being known by God. Does not God know all things from eternity? How then is God said then as if first to know us, when we begin to believe in him? Solution. By a tropical 563Bmanner of speech what we do by God's authorship, is attributed to him; whence it is said: He asketh for the saints, because he maketh them ask, so [he is said] to know us, because he bestoweth on us the knowledge of himself, and to rest, because he maketh us rest in himself.

QUESTION XXXVIII. How are you turned again to the weak and needy things? The Galatians did not before keep the law, how then does he say: you are turned again to the needy things, etc. Solution. That he might show that legal observance after the coming of Christ differs little, or nothing, from idolatry. Or he says this for this reason, because they wished not only to keep the law, but were also turned to their former errors; thus by a double error they had been deceived by the false [apostles].

QUESTION XXXIX. And the seventh of the seventh decade, 563Cwhich is called jubilee. What is this that the expositor says? was not the fiftieth year called jubilee in the law? how then is the seventh year of the seventh decade called jubilee? for the seventh of the seventh decade is the sixty-seventh. Solution. The children of Israel, sometimes oppressed by captivity, could not keep the jubilee year in its order. But in the sixty-sixth year license of returning was given by Cyrus, and Darius, and in part they returned, and kept the sixty-seventh year for the jubilee. But someone will say that before the seventy years were fulfilled, they did not return from captivity. Solution. Not indeed generally and wholly did they return before the seventieth year; yet in the 563Dsixty-sixth year, as we said before, license of returning was granted to some, which is signified by the Alleluia, which is sung on the Saturday after Good Friday, which is the sixty-sixth day of Septuagesima. But since some were still detained in captivity, there follows the tract, which is a sign of labor, as the Alleluia is a sign of joy. But on the following Saturday there is sung also a second [Alleluia] together with the first Alleluia, prefiguring the general return of the Jews which is [at] the completed seventy years.

QUESTION XL. If it could have been done, you would have plucked out, etc. Was not that able to be done which the Apostle says? Solution. Holy Scripture says that thing cannot be done, which is not justly done; whence Job says: Would that I could kill myself (Job X). And the Lord to Lot: I cannot 564Ado anything, until thou enter thither (Gen. XIX). He said that he could not [do] what without doubt he could through power, but not through justice.

QUESTION XLI. Abraham had two sons. Did he not have more sons of Cetura after the death of Sara? How then does the Apostle say he had two, as though not more than two? Solution. If more than two, then two; for he does not say only two, but yet rather speaks of these than of the others, because Scripture follows out the particulars concerning these, intimating that something excellent is prefigured.

QUESTION XLII. But these are the two testaments. Concerning this and like expressions it is asked how they are true. Is not the figure one thing, the truth another; the signifier one thing, the signified another? how 564Bthen is the name of truth predicated of the name of figure, when it is said: These are the two Testaments, and the rock was Christ? (I Cor. X.) Solution. This word, to be, in places of this kind, is set for to signify.

QUESTION XLIII. Likewise why holy Scripture in such a place uses the substantive verb, can be asked. Would it not be plainer, if it were said: But these signify the two testaments, and the rock figured Christ? Solution. It belongs to words to signify, to things to be, properly. But in theology not only do words have signification, but also things are set for the signification of other things, that is, certain things are signified by other things. As often, therefore, as holy Scripture wishes to show, what thing has to signify what thing, it does not say: this signifies that; but this is that, as the rock 564Cwas Christ; for if it were said the rock signifies Christ, it would seem that the signification of this name rock, and not of this thing the rock, was pointed out.

QUESTION XLIV. Note that above he says, that Ishmael was born according to the flesh; Isaac not according to the flesh, but through promise, but was not Isaac, like Ishmael, born by the intercourse of both sexes? how then was he not born according to nature or according to the flesh? Solution. Ishmael was born by the accustomed law of nature, namely from the concurrence of natural causes; but the generation of Isaac was the operation not of nature, but of divine power, and grace. For to such intercourse, as could be at such an age between old Abraham, and Sara aged and 564Dbarren, nature does not grant children; but what nature denied, grace conferred.

QUESTION XLV. But how then did he, who was born according to the flesh, persecute him who was born according to the spirit, or promise; so also now. It is asked: Where this is found, that Ishmael persecuted Isaac. For in Genesis it is read, that the elder played with the younger (Gen. XXI). What evil then did he do? what did he sin? how by merely playing did he persecute him? Solution. The play of the elder with the younger Sara understood to be a mockery. Whence also, indignant, she said: Cast out the handmaid, and her son. (Ibid.) And the Apostle calls such mockery persecution. So also mockers persecute us more than open persecutors.

QUESTION XLVI. If you be circumcised, Christ 565Ashall profit you nothing. (Gal. V.) Did not the Apostle circumcise Timothy? Then he deceived him, and made [it so] that Christ profited nothing? Solution. He says this of those who sought to be justified from circumcision; and therefore circumcised themselves, and thus fell from grace, which they believed to be insufficient. But to those, who received it out of a certain reverence, yet not putting hope in it, it was not pernicious according to Augustine, but according to Jerome it harmed all who received [it], unless a dispensation were made. Concerning which controversy it has been more fully said above.

QUESTION XLVII. I testify to every man circumcising himself, that he is a debtor to do the whole law. Will he, if he fulfill the whole law, even so be able to obtain justice? Which seems [to follow] from these words, but 565Belsewhere it is manifestly held that justice is not from the law. Likewise, is not every man bound to fulfill the law, at least according to the spirit? What is it then that every man circumcising himself owes this, [and] not another? Likewise: Is not everyone bound to love his neighbor as himself? but he who loves his neighbor fulfills the whole law. Does it not seem from these things, that everyone is bound to fulfill the whole law? What is it then that he says: I testify to every man circumcising himself, etc. Solution. He who seeks to be justified from circumcision or from the law, is bound to this, that, in order to have justice, or be worthy of life, he fulfill whatever is commanded in the law, namely that he covet nothing; and love God with his whole heart, in which two consists perfect justice; which, if anyone had, he would not need the grace 565Cof faith, as neither [do] the angels of God, [a justice] which is granted to no one in the present [life], save only to the Mediator of God and men: whence it is necessary, that if anyone wishes to be justified or beatified, he flee to grace alone; for if he seeks to be justified in the law, that is required of him which cannot be discharged by man.

QUESTION XLVIII. In Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth, nor uncircumcision. The expositor says that for those who are in Christ Jesus vices are to be fled, virtues to be sought; but the middle things [are] neither to be fled, nor to be sought, among which he places circumcision. Whence it seems that it neither profits, nor hurts; but above it was said that circumcision not only does not profit, but even hurts. And the Apostle says: If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing. If then 565Dit takes Christ from us, it hurts much. Solution. Circumcision simply received, in that the cause of salvation is not placed in it, seems to be indifferent, and so neither profits, nor hinders; but if [received] with this intention, and this mind, that from it salvation be sought, [it] hurts [when] received.

QUESTION XLIX. The whole law is fulfilled in one word: Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself. Since there are two precepts of love, namely of God and of neighbor, it is asked how in the love of neighbor the whole law is fulfilled? Solution. In the love of neighbor is contained the love of God; for who can love his neighbor for God's sake, unless he love God? Likewise no one can love his neighbor as himself, unless he love 566Ahimself; but no one loves himself, unless he love God: for what is it to love oneself, but to love one's own good? but the true and highest good is Christ. Otherwise he who loves iniquity, hates his own soul.

QUESTION L. It is asked who is [one's] neighbor? Solution. Every man. We are bound therefore by precept to love every man, and to exhibit the offices of piety to everyone in need.

QUESTION LI. As thyself, etc. It is asked whether we ought to love [our] neighbor as much as ourselves? Which seems [so], since it is said, as thyself. Solution. "As" is not of quantity, but of quality: this indeed we are bound to do to others, which we wish according to reason to be exhibited to us by others. Note: Since each precept of love is contained in 566Beach [other], often one is set down rather than two, for if both were set down together, it would seem that one could be had without the other, or could be had.

QUESTION LII. The flesh lusteth against the spirit. It is asked how the flesh is said to lust, since the soul alone lusts. Solution. What the soul does from the flesh, this is attributed to the flesh, as the ear is said to hear, the eye to see, since the soul does these things through instruments of this kind.

QUESTION LIII. Since therefore the soul and the spirit are the same according to substance, by what does the soul lust against the spirit; is it against itself? Solution. He calls the lusting flesh the carnal delight, which the soul has from the flesh. But by the name of Spirit he signifies the spiritual delight. 566CAnd on account of these two delights the inner man is divided, and obtains diverse names. For according to the lower delight, he is called now flesh, now man, now soul, or animal, or carnal; but according to the higher he is called spirit, or spiritual, or new man.

QUESTION LIV. If you be led by the spirit, you are not under the law. It is asked what it is to be under the law? Solution. To abstain from every evil work by the fear of punishment, not by the love of justice, this is to be under the law. As he is said to be under the law, who seeks to be justified from it, who is a debtor to fulfill the whole law.

QUESTION LV. But manifest are the works of the flesh, which are fornication, etc. It is asked how the Apostle 566Denumerates among the works of the flesh certain things which are not vices of the flesh, but rather of the soul, as anger, envy, etc. Solution. By the name of flesh he signifies the whole man, who by living according to himself has fallen into these things. For to believe that all vices are from the flesh, is an error, lest the devil, who has no flesh, seem immune from these.

QUESTION LVI. But the fruit of the spirit is charity. The expositor says that the Apostle calls the works of the spirit fruits, because they are to be sought for their own sake. But Augustine says that the virtues are to be sought for the sake of beatitude alone, but for their own sake nothing is to be loved, save the highest good, whose fruition makes us blessed. What then is to be said? what is to be held? Solution. The virtues are to be sought for their own sake, because they delight their possessors 567Awith a sincere delight, but not only for their own sake, but also for the sake of beatitude, which is the supreme end.

QUESTION LVII. If a man be overtaken in any fault (Gal. VI), etc. It is asked what it is to be overtaken, and what he calls a fault. Solution. He is overtaken, who falls into some fault, or sin, either because he is ignorant of what is to be done or to be omitted, or when he knows [it], but yet weakness impels [him] to sinning. A fault is the desertion of good, as sin is the perpetration of evil, or a fault is what is done ignorantly; sin what [is done] by one knowing, yet indifferently the one is set for the other.

QUESTION LVIII. Every one shall bear his own burden, etc. It is asked how both are true. 567BBear ye one another's burdens, etc., and this, which he says here: Every one shall bear his own burden? Solution. There are some burdens of the weakness to be shared, of which he treated above; there are others of the account to be rendered to God concerning our acts, of which he treats here. It is true therefore that in the present we ought to help one another; and [that] those who are stronger [ought] to sustain the weaknesses of others; and yet in the future everyone shall bear his own burden, that is, for his own sin and not for the sin of another.

QUESTION LIX. Let us work good to all, etc. It is asked whether we are bound by precept to bestow the offices of piety even on enemies? Which seems [so], since the Apostle says: Let us work good to all; and the Lord 568Ain the Gospel: Love your enemies; do good to them that hate you (Luc. VI). But Augustine says: To love enemies is not of so great a multitude, as I believe to be heard in the Lord's Prayer, where it is said: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matth. VI). And Gregory says: It suffices not to hate enemies, that is, to will their salvation; even if works of mercy be not bestowed on them. Solution. By precept we are bound to will the salvation of all; but to bestow also the offices of piety on enemies is, as regards the weak and less perfect, counsel, [but] as regards the perfect, precept. Diligently therefore is it to be noted what is said according to counsel, [and] what according to precept.

QUESTION LX. Likewise since it is established, that it is good 568Bto do good to the wicked, and to sinners, and to the impious, what is it that Scripture says: Give to the merciful, and receive not the sinner, and to the impious, and to sinners render vengeance, and do good to the humble, and give not to the impious (Eccles. XII). Solution. The sense of the aforesaid authorities is that you do good to no sinner for this reason, because he is a sinner, but because [he is] a man, that is, we ought to foster no one's fault, but [his] nature. In each let us love what God loves, and hate what he hates; but if we cannot help all, both good and bad, we ought to bestow the good things which we can on the servants of God; whence the Apostle: But most of all to those of the household of the faith.

V. IN EPISTOLAM AD EPHESIOS.

  • 567

567C(Ephes. I.) Paulus, apostolus, etc. Hanc Epistolam scribit Ephesiis, quos in fide Paulus non fundavit, sed ab Joanne apostolo fundatos confirmavit, qui firmiter in fide et bonis operibus perstiterunt, quos hortatur ut in bonis proficiant, scribens eis a Roma de carcere. Est itaque materia apostoli in hac epistola status Ephesiorum, in quo tunc erant. Intentio vero, eos in bonis habitis confirmare, adulteriora provocare, nec non ad humilitatem actionemque gratiarum informare. Modus agendi talis est: more suo salutationem praemittit; deinde agit gratias, exponens multiplicia Dei beneficia, tum generi humano, tam ipsis apostolis, tum ipsis Ephesiis per solam gratiam collata. Deinde Christi dignitatem et praelationem ostendit. Postea ad patientiam 567Det charitatem eos invitat, unitatem fidei et Ecclesiae commendans, et dona gratiae enumerans, tandem ad certamen exhortans, contra principes tenebrarum militiae Christianae armaturam describit.

QUAESTIO I. Benedictus Deus, qui benedixit nos, etc. Cum benedici dicatur de Deo et de homine, quaeritur an eodem modo dicatur, et secundum eamdem significationem. Solutio. Aliter, et aliter de utroque. 568CNam Deus ab homine benedicitur, cum dignis laudibus extollitur; homo vero a Deo benedicitur, cum Deus ei munera gratiae suae impertitur.

QUAESTIO II. Dicit expositor quod Apostolus hic ponit duas praeordinationes: unam de praesenti justitia, alteram de futura corona. Sed cum una sit Dei praedestinatio, quae est ipse Deus, quaeritur quomodo duae dicantur? Solutio. Non ideo duae dicuntur, quin una sit; sed quia duos habet effectus, scilicet per praesentem justitiam, et futuram gloriam. Cui solutioni sic objicitur: Si numerus praedestinationum assignandus est secundum numerum effectuum, jam erunt infinitae praedestinationes, cum sint infiniti praedestinationis effectus. Solutio. Omnes justitiae, quia numero et non specie differunt, 568Dunus effectus dicuntur esse, sic et omnes coronae, quia non specie, sed solo numero discernuntur, unus effectus praedestinationis dicuntur. Quoniam vero praesens justitia et futura gloria non solum numero, sed etiam specie differunt, non incongrue duo effectus praedestinationis dicuntur. Notandum quod multa sunt hujusmodi, quae cum sint plura numero, et unum specie, simpliciter non plura, sed 569Aunum secundum usum loquendi dicuntur, ut fides mea et fides illius cum duae sint numero, non tamen duae simpliciter, sed una dicuntur; quia una sunt specie; sic de herba, de voce, de intellectu, visu et multis aliis, littera, figura, elemento, vocali, differendum est.

QUAESTIO III. Sicut elegit nos, ut essemus sancti, etc. Dicit Pelagianus quod eos quos Deus ab aeterno elegit, ideo eos elegit, quia praesciebat eos futuros bonos et per liberae voluntatis arbitrium, non quia eos erat sanctificaturus. Sed hanc ejus haeresim destruit Apostolus cum dicit: Elegit nos, ut essemus sancti, et immaculati; non dicit quia futuri eramus sancti; sed ut essemus. Si enim hoc esset quod dicit Pelagianus, justificatio nostra causa 569Besset divinae electionis, non divina electio causa nostrae justificationis, et sic quod est temporale causa esset ejus quod est aeternum, non e converso: quod non potest esse.

QUAESTIO IV. In quo habemus redemptionem, etc. Quaeritur an idem vocet redemptionem et remissionem peccatorum? si idem videtur, quod alterum superflue positum sit. Solutio. Redemptionem, pretium illud, per quod redempti sumus, vocat, per quod datur facultas nobis redeundi; remissio vero peccatorum, quae nobis confertur in baptismo, effectus est ipsius redemptionis.

QUAESTIO V. Instaurare omnio, quae in coelis sunt, etc. Cum Christus pro angelis non sit mortuus, quaeritur quomodo ea quae sunt in coelis per Christum 569Csint restaurata? Solutio. Ideo hoc dicitur, quia qui per gratiam salvantur, supplent numerum angelorum diminutum; vel per ea quae in coelis sunt, intelligit animas, quae jam sunt in coelo; per ea quae in terris sunt, sanctos adhuc in hac vita degentes.

QUAESTIO VI. Signati estis Spiritu sancto, qui est pignus haereditatis. Quaeritur quomodo Spiritus sanctus dicatur pignus haereditatis nostrae; nonne pignus est illud quod ad tempus pro aliquo pretio datur, et iterum cum pretium solvitur, illud aufertur? nunquid ergo Spiritus a nobis aufertur, cum ipsa haereditas nobis datur? Solutio. Pignus hic ponitur pro arrha, quae est de ipso pretio, nec aufertur cum pretium solvitur; unde quidam codices habent arrham, non pignus.

569DQUAESTIO VII. Constituens ad dexteram suam, etc. Deus spiritus est, nec corporis forma finitur, vel concluditur: quomodo ergo dicitur Filius sedere ad dexteram Patris, cum Pater non habeat latus dextrum vel sinistrum, quia non habet corpus? Solutio. Per dexteram Dei in sacra Scriptura quandoque significatur aeterna beatitudo, quandoque aequalis divinae naturae, quandoque judiciaria potestas. Est enim Christus ad dexteram Patris, quia in Patris majestate manet aequalis, et quia Pater non judicat quemquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio (Joan. V). Per dexteram ergo Dei vel per manum, vel brachium, vel digitum, vel oculum, vel aurem, et similia, nihil corporale debet intelligi, sed totum spiritualiter.

570AQUAESTIO VIII. Supra omne nomen, quod nominatur non solum in hoc saeculo, etc. Nonne novem sunt ordines angelorum? Angeli, archangeli, virtutes, potestates, principatus, dominationes, throni, cherubin, seraphin, et non sunt plures iis, qui in praesenti omnes nominantur. Quomodo ergo dicit: Constitutum super omne quod nominatur non solum in hoc saeculo, sed etiam in futuro, quasi aliqui sint in futuro nominandi, qui in praesenti non nominantur. Solutio. Quorumdam angelorum denominationes datae sunt eis secundum officia quae nobis exhibent in praesenti, ut angeli, archangeli, virtutes, potestates, principatus, dominationes; ideo dicuntur nomina in praesenti, quia hoc modo eorum denominatio spectat ad praesens. 570BUnde in futuro evacuabuntur, quando Christus tradet regnum Deo et Patri, quando Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Quorumdam vero angelorum denominationes ad futurum statum spectant, ut throni, cherubin et seraphin; unde nec in futuro evacuabuntur, sed super omnes hos ordines supercoelestium spirituum sublimata est humanitas Salvatoris.

QUAESTIO IX. Et ipsum dedit caput super omnem Ecclesiam. Quaeritur secundum quam naturam, scilicet divinam an humanam, Christus sit caput Ecclesiae. Solutio. Potest dici quod secundum divinam, secundum quam caput, principium, et auctor est omnium fidelium. Cui solutioni sic objicitur: Eadem ratione potest dici quod sit caput lapidis, et omnis creaturae, quorum est auctor; et nihil diceretur 570Cde Ecclesia. Ideo dicimus, quod Christus proprie secundum humanitatem est caput Ecclesiae.

QUAESTIO X. Quare Christus dicitur caput Ecclesiae. Quare dicitur caput esse, non inconvenienter potest quaeri. Solutio. Ideo Christus caput Ecclesiae dictus est, quia sicut in capite hominis plene sunt omnes sensus carnales, scilicet visus, auditus, odoratus vel olfactus, gustus et tactus; sic in Christo est plenitudo omnium sensuum spiritualium, scilicet plenitudo gratiae, de cujus plenitudine nos omnes accepimus (Joan. I), unde et membra dicimur, quasi aliquem sensum non omnes habentes, sicut caetera membra corporis unum solum sensum habent; nullum habet omnes praeter caput.

QUAESTIO XI. Eramus natura filii irae (Ephes. 570DII), etc. Deus est auctor naturae; si ergo natura sumus filii irae, videtur quod Deo auctore hoc sumus. Solutio. Natura tribus modis accipitur in sacra Scriptura, scilicet pro illo integro et interrupto bono, in quo conditus est homo, secundum quam acceptionem dicitur quod omnis creatura Dei bona est. Dicitur etiam natura corruptio peccati, in qua concipitur, et cum qua nascitur omnis homo, et sic accipitur hic cum dicitur: Eramus natura filii irae. Vitium enim inolevit pro natura: quia ergo pro culpa originalis peccati, cum quo nascimur, digni sumus gehenna, ideo dicimur natura filii irae. Accipitur etiam natura pro reliquiis illius boni naturalis, quae remanserunt in nobis post peccatum, et sic 571Aaccipitur, ubi legitur quod Gentes naturaliter faciunt ea, quae legis sunt (Rom. II).

QUAESTIO XII. Mihi omnium sanctorum minima data est gratia (Ephes. III). Cum Apostolus non esset minimus in numero omnium sanctorum, imo inter apostolos unus de primis esset, quomodo verum dicat se minimum omnium nominando. Solutionem hujus quaestionis quaere super illum locum: Ego sum minimus apostolorum, in prima Epistola ad Corinthios.

QUAESTIO XIII. Investigabiles divitias Christi, etc. Quaeritur quomodo Apostolus intellexit vel evangelizavit, si investigabiles sunt divitiae. Investigabiles enim res dicuntur, quae non possunt comprehendi. Solutio. Quae natura sua investigabiles, per gratiam 571Bet revelationem sancti Spiritus factae sunt vestigabiles non solum Apostolo, sed etiam caeteris fidelibus, quos ipsa unctio docet de omnibus.

QUAESTIO XIV. Sacramenti absconditi, etc. Quaeritur, quae dicantur abscondita. Solutio. In mundo causae absconditae sunt omnium quae naturaliter fiunt. In solo autem Deo absconditae sunt causae omnium, quae per gratiam fiunt. De his duobus generibus causarum jam in superioribus aliquantum dictum est.

QUAESTIO XV. Ut innotescat principibus, et potestatibus in coelestibus per Ecclesiam, etc. Quaeritur an mysterium incarnationis fuerit revelatum super coelestibus essentiis ante ipsius impletionem. In solutione hujus quaestionis videntur contrarii Hieronymus 571Cet Augustinus. Dicit enim beatus Hieronymus, angelicas dignitates ad purum non intellexisse supra memoratum sacramentum; unde sic quaerunt: Quis est iste, qui venit de Edom? (Isa. LXIII.) Et alibi: Quis est iste rex gloriae? (Psal. XXIII.) Beatus vero Augustinus dicit, quod non latuit angelos mysterium regni coelorum; unde littera diversis exponitur modis, Ut innotescat, etc. Haec autem contrarietas, quae videtur esse inter praedictos doctores sic potest solvi: illis, qui majoris dignitatis sunt, revelatum est praedictum sacramentum; aliis vero non ad purum, ut dicit beatus Hieronymus. Quod autem angeli crescant quotidie in cognitione, ex iis quae in mundo fiunt multi consona voce asserunt doctores. 571DUnde nos quasi pro certo hoc habemus, cum canonica Scriptura hoc videatur manifeste innuere.

QUAESTIO XVI. Ex quo omnis paternitas in coelis, et in terra nominatur. Ex hoc loco habemus, quod non solum Deus Pater noster est, sed et angeli, et homines patres nostri dicuntur. Sed alibi dicit Dominus: Unus Pater est vester, qui est in coelis (Matth. XXIII). Si ergo unus est, quomodo plures? vel si plures, quomodo unus? Solutio. Sicut Deus, qui solus vere est, et solus vere bonus est, essentiae et bonitatis suae nomen caeteris impertit, ut ipsa quoque et esse, et bona dicantur; ita et ipse, qui solus vere Pater est omnium creatione, et fidelium regeneratione, paternitatis nomen caeteris concessit. Sciendum est ita, quod Deus Trinitas omnium Pater est 572Acreatione et fidelium regeneratione. Deus vero ingenitus solus Pater est Unigeniti per naturam. Angeli vero patres nostri dicuntur auctoritate exempli, ratione beneficii, cura, et providentia. Homines vero patres et natura, et auctoritate exempli et ratione beneficii; et cura, et providentia.

QUAESTIO XVII. Quae sit latitudo, et longitudo, et sublimitas. Quae sit latitudo dilectionis, quae longitudo aeternitatis; quae sublimitas potentiae, quod profundum scientiae, secundum hoc, quod de Deo exponitur, talis potest esse intelligentia.

QUAESTIO XVIII. Scire etiam supereminentem scientiae charitatem Christi. Si charitas Christi supereminet scientiae, quomodo potest sciri? si non potest sciri, quomodo orat Apostolus, ut eam sciant discipuli? 572BSolutio. Quae scientia humana non potest comprehendi, per gratiam ex parte cognoscitur, quod ut fiat Apostolus orat.

QUAESTIO XIX. Ut impleamini in omnem plenitudinem Dei, etc. Nonne minus habebimus quam ipse Deus? quomodo ergo possumus impleri in omnem plenitudinem Dei? quomodo potest aliquis habere plenitudinem Dei, et non esse plenus Deus et aequalis Deo? Solutio. Sensus est, ut sitis pleni Deo, non plenus Deus. Hoc est in plenitudinem omnem impleri; in praesenti habere plenitudinem virtutum, et in futuro plenitudinem gloriae; non enim optat Paulus alicui plenitudinem divinae naturae conferri, sed ut simus pleni Deo in praesenti et in futuro.

572CQUAESTIO XX. Unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma (Ephes. IV). Quomodo intelligantur? Solutio. Unus Dominus Pater, et Filius, et Spiritus in natura, non in persona. Una fides non in numero, sed genere, quia similis in omnibus, sicut omnium idem volentium dicitur esse eadem voluntas. De fide jam dictum est. Unum baptisma dicitur, quia aequale est, et ejusdem essentiae a quocunque detur, et ideo etiam quia non potest reiterari.

QUAESTIO XXI. Dedit dona hominibus. David dicit? Accepisti dona in hominibus (Psal. LXVII); si dedit, quomodo accepit? vel si accepit, quomodo dedit: Solutio. Tanquam Deus dedit; accepit non solum in semetipso secundum quod est homo, sed etiam in membris suis, in quibus est, de qua acceptione 572Dagit Propheta: unde dicit: Accepisti dona in hominibus.

QUAESTIO XXII. Quae dona dedit ascendens. Quaeritur quae dona dederit ascendens. Solutio. Spiritum sanctum, et dona etiam, quae non sunt Spiritus sanctus, quae cum dat etiam in ipsis dat Spiritum sanctum, non seorsum dat Spiritum sanctum, et dona ejus, quae non sunt ipse, sed dando Spiritum sanctum dat dona; et dando dona Spiritus sancti donat ipsum. Hoc dico propter eos qui nolunt concedere Spiritum sanctum dari, cum sit immutabilis, sed dona ejus tamen. Tunc enim dicitur Spiritus sanctus nobis dari a Patre, et Filio, et etiam a semetipso, cum cordibus nostris per charitatem hanc virtutem 573Ainfundit ad hoc, ut diligamus Deum et proximum.

QUAESTIO XXIII. Cum Christus sit Deus et homo, quaeritur secundum quam naturam dedit dona? Solutio. Secundum eam dedit, ut dicit expositor, secundum quam ascendit, et descendit, et sic secundum quod est homo dedit; quia divinitas, quae est ubique, nec descendit, nec ascendit. Sed hoc videtur esse contrarium praedictis, ubi asserui, quod tanquam Deus dedit, non tanquam homo. Cum ergo legitur, quod tanquam homo vel secundum humanitatem dedit, sic intelligi debet, qui est homo, non quia est homo, sed quia est Deus.

QUAESTIO XXIV. An Deitas descendit, et quomodo. Item dicit alia expositio, quod Christus secundum 573BDeitatem descendit, et secundum humanitatem ascendit, quod videtur contrarium superioribus. Dictum enim quia divinitas quae ubique est, nec descendit, nec ascendit, hic autem dicitur quod Deitas descendit: quid ergo tenendum est? Solutio. Cum dicitur quod Deus descendit, hoc intelligitur de descensione incarnationis, qua Deus factus est homo. Cum dicitur quod homo descendit, hoc debet intelligi de descensione ad inferos, quae fuit tantum secundum animam, non secundum corpus, quod jacuit in sepulcro, nec secundum Deitatem, quae ubique erat.

QUAESTIO XXV. In virum perfectum, etc. Quaeritur qua perfectione. Solutio. Nec perfectio potest intelligi vel de toto Christo, id est corpore et capite, vel 573Cde singulis membris. Christus enim in se consummatus, in aliis crescit et proficit, sed in futuro tandem perficietur, ut nec viribus, nec numero aliquid superaddatur. Unusquisque etiam tunc erit vir perfectus, tam virtutum consummatione quam corporis statura. Unde sequitur: In mensuram aetatis plenitudinis Christi. Unusquisque enim in ea perfectione resurget, in qua erat, vel ad quam perventurus erat, cum esset triginta annorum; non enim omnes erunt ejusdem magnitudinis vel illius, cujus Christus erat de hac vita exiens.

QUAESTIO XXVI. Irascimini, et nolite peccare, etc. Permittit Apostolus irasci, quod non potest vitari, sed Dominus prohibet irasci dicens: Quicunque 573Dirascitur fratri suo, reus est judicio (Matth. V). Unde videtur quod illud quod Dominus prohibet, Apostolus permittat. Item dictum est superius: quod nihil prohibetur in Novo Testamento, quod non possit vitari, sicut nec aliquid praecipitur, quod non possit impleri; quod non videtur esse verum, si Dominus prohibet irasci, et nullus possit vitare irasci. Solutio. Primus motus irae, qui non est in potestate nostra, permittitur ab Apostolo: Dominus autem non prohibet primum motum, qui dicitur propassio, sed voluntatem, et propositum nocendi alteri. Aliud itaque permittitur ab Apostolo, et aliud prohibetur a Domino, quod potest vitari gratia adjuvante.

QUAESTIO XXVII. Quae sint portae mortis et vitae. Nota quod concupiscentia, et timor mundi duae sunt 574Aportae mortis, per quas intrat diabolus; sicut timor et amor Dei sunt portae vitae, per quas intrat Christus. Uterque stat ad ostium; et Christus pulsat, et diabolus: sed hostis expellitur, Christus introducitur.

QUAESTIO. XXVIII. Nolite contristare Spiritum sanctum, etc. Quaeritur quomodo quis possit Spiritum sanctum contristare, cum impassibilis sit nec tristitiae passionem possit in se suscipere. Solutio. Quodam tropo usus est in theologia satis usitato; quo ea, quae Deo auctore in nobis fiunt, ipsi attribuuntur; quia illi ergo, quos implet charitate, sicut gaudent de profectibus aliorum, sic contristantur de lapsibus cadentium, dicit Apostolus: Nolite contristare Spiritum sanctum, id est eos in quibus habitat 574BSpiritus sanctus per charitatem.

QUAESTIO XXIX. Donate invicem, etc. Dicit Scriptura: Nisi dimittamus conservis nostris, quod Deus repetit dimissa; sed quaeritur quomodo Deus repetit? Nunquid iterum puniet Deus pro peccatis pro quibus jam satisfactum est per cordis contritionem, et oris confessionem, et per dignos fructus poenitentiae. Nunquid bis puniet in idipsum? Solutio. Ad hoc, ut aliquis faciat dignos fructus poenitentiae, exigitur ut de caetero non peccet mortaliter; unde quicunque post poenitentiam peccat, inutilem sibi priorem satisfactionem reddit.

QUAESTIO XXX. Quid bis punire in idipsum? Bis autem punire in idipsum est pro peccato per poenitentiam deleto, nec repetito, in alia vita iterum punire, 574Cquod Deus non facit. Si aliquis autem poenitens affligitur pro aliquo peccato et iterum idem repetat; si in hac vita vel in alia pro illo iterum puniatur, hoc non est bis punire in idipsum.

QUAESTIO XXXI. In odorem suavitatis (Ephes. V), etc. Si mors Christi fuit Deo suavis odor, ergo mortem ejus libenter accepit; ergo non peccaverunt Judaei, qui illum crucifixerunt; quia id fecerunt, quod bonum erat, et Deo placuit. Solutio. Actio Judaeorum mala erat, nec Deo placebat id quod fiebat ab eis; sed passio Christi bonum fuit, et salutis nostrae causa.

QUAESTIO XXXII. Dies mali sunt, etc. Nonne dies habent esse ex Deo auctore, sicut scriptum est: Tuus 574Dest dies, et tua est nox? (Psal. LXXIII.) Quomodo ergo dicuntur mali? Solutio. Pro malitia, et miseria hominum dicuntur dies mali; alioquin quantum ad horarum spatia ordinati sunt, et boni.

QUAESTIO XXXIII. Nemo carnem suam odio habuit, etc. Nonne viri sancti carnem oderunt, persequuntur, crucifigunt et mortificant, non nutriunt, nec fovent? quomodo ergo verum est, Nemo carnem suam odio habuit? Solutio. Sancti non carnem, sed carnis vitium oderunt, et persequuntur.

QUAESTIO XXXIV. Propter hoc relinquet homo patrem. Quaeritur quomodo hoc ad Filium Dei pertineat, qui nunquam Patrem deseruit, sed semper cum eo inseparabiliter permansit? Solutio. Quia Filius in forma, qua patri aequalis est, nobis non 575Aapparuit, dictus est Patrem deseruisse vel reliquisse; nunquam tamen ab eo recessit: in mundum venit, et Patrem non deseruit.

QUAESTIO XXXV. Qui uxorem suam diligit. Quaeritur de qua dilectione hic agat; si enim de dilectione, qua diligimus nos mutuo propter Deum, sensus est: Qui diligit uxorem suam, seipsum diligit, id est facit quod sibi utile est: secundum hoc ita posset dicere de quolibet proximo. Solutio. Hoc ideo dicit Apostolus, quia magis instat viro providere uxori quam alii: unde si propter Deum acquirit ei necessaria, et regit, et se diligit, id est, facit quod sibi utile est; quia inde meretur apud Deum.

QUAESTIO XXXVI. Servi, obedite dominis vestris (Ephes. VI). Hic quaeritur an liceat Christiano servum 575Bhabere, cum hoc Apostolus permittat. Catholica quoque, et maxime Gallorum Ecclesia hoc recipit. Solutio. Melius esset hujusmodi servitutem non exigere, nec Ecclesia quasi bonum recipit, sed quasi malum tolerat.

QUAESTIO XXXVII. Filii, obedite parentibus vestris; et vos, patres, nolite ad iracundiam provocare filios. Quaeritur quare Apostolus praecipiat parentibus ut 576Afilios diligant, et filiis ut parentes honorent, cum natura ad se mutuo diligendos compellat. Solutio. Naturalis amor non habet meritum, nisi propter Deum fiat: ideo praecipit ut se propter Deum diligant, et sic meritum habeant.

QUAESTIO XXXVIII. Non est nobis colluctatio contra carnem. Nonne sancti pugnant contra carnem et sanguinem, contra malos homines, vel contra vitia, quae ex carne et sanguine oriuntur? quomodo ergo dicit: Non est nobis colluctatio, etc.? Solutio. Non est nobis colluctatio tantum contra carnem et sanguinem, sed etiam contra daemones.

QUAESTIO XXXIX. Adversus mundi rectores. Nonne Deus, qui mundum condidit, mundum gubernat, et regit, ut idem sit conditor et rector? quomodo ergo 576Bdaemones vocat Apostolus mundi rectores. Solutio. Hic nomine mundi signat mundi amatores. Hic est mundus, qui totus in maligno positus est: hic est mundus, in quo non reperitur nisi concupiscentia carnis, concupiscentia oculorum et superbia vitae: hunc mundum vocat Apostolus tenebras, subjungens harum tenebrarum, et alibi dicens: Fuistis aliquando tenebrae; nunc autem lux in Domino (Ephes. V).

V. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS.

  • 567

567C(Ephes. I.) Paul, an apostle, etc. This Epistle he writes to the Ephesians, whom Paul did not found in the faith, but, having been founded by John the apostle, he confirmed — men who firmly persisted in faith and good works, whom he exhorts to advance in good things, writing to them from Rome, from prison. And so the matter of the apostle in this epistle is the state of the Ephesians, in which they then were. But the intention is to confirm them in the good things they possess, to spur on adulteriora, and also to form them to humility and the giving of thanks. The mode of proceeding is such: after his manner he sends a salutation beforehand; then he gives thanks, setting forth the manifold benefits of God, conferred by grace alone — now upon the human race, now upon the apostles themselves, now upon the Ephesians themselves. Then he shows the dignity and preeminence of Christ. Afterward he invites them to patience 567Dand charity, commending the unity of faith and of the Church, and enumerating the gifts of grace; at last, exhorting them to the contest, he describes the armor of the Christian soldiery against the princes of darkness.

QUESTION I. Blessed be God, who hath blessed us, etc. Since "to be blessed" is said of God and of man, it is asked whether it is said in the same manner, and according to the same signification. Solution. Otherwise and otherwise of each. 568CFor God is blessed by man when he is extolled with worthy praises; but man is blessed by God when God imparts to him the gifts of his grace.

QUESTION II. The expositor says that the Apostle here sets down two preordinations: one concerning present justice, the other concerning the future crown. But since the predestination of God is one, which is God himself, it is asked how they are said to be two? Solution. They are not said to be two as though it were not one; but because it has two effects, namely through present justice and through future glory. To which solution it is thus objected: If the number of predestinations is to be assigned according to the number of effects, then there will be infinite predestinations, since the effects of predestination are infinite. Solution. All instances of justice, because they differ in number and not in species, 568Dare said to be one effect; so also all crowns, because they are distinguished not in species but in number alone, are said to be one effect of predestination. But since present justice and future glory differ not only in number but also in species, they are not incongruously said to be two effects of predestination. It is to be noted that there are many things of this kind which, though they be many in number and one in species, are said to be simply not many, but 569Aone, according to the usage of speaking; as my faith and his faith, though they be two in number, are nevertheless said to be not two simply, but one, because they are one in species; so of grass, of voice, of understanding, of sight, and of many other things — letter, figure, element, vowel — the like distinction is to be made.

QUESTION III. As he chose us, that we should be holy, etc. The Pelagian says that those whom God chose from eternity, he chose them for this reason, because he foreknew that they would be good, and through the choice of free will, not because he was going to sanctify them. But the Apostle destroys this heresy of his when he says: He chose us, that we should be holy and unspotted; he does not say because we were going to be holy, but that we should be. For if it were as the Pelagian says, our justification would be the cause 569Bof the divine election, not the divine election the cause of our justification; and thus that which is temporal would be the cause of that which is eternal, and not conversely: which cannot be.

QUESTION IV. In whom we have redemption, etc. It is asked whether he calls redemption and the remission of sins the same thing? for if they seem the same, then one of them is superfluously set down. Solution. By redemption he calls that price by which we were redeemed, through which the power of returning is given to us; but the remission of sins, which is conferred upon us in baptism, is the effect of that redemption itself.

QUESTION V. To restore omnio, which are in the heavens, etc. Since Christ did not die for the angels, it is asked how the things which are in the heavens were restored through Christ? 569CSolution. This is said for this reason, because those who are saved by grace fill up the diminished number of the angels; or by the things which are in the heavens he understands the souls which are already in heaven; by the things which are on the earth, the saints still dwelling in this life.

QUESTION VI. You are sealed with the Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of the inheritance. It is asked how the Holy Spirit is called the pledge of our inheritance; is not a pledge that which is given for a time for some price, and again, when the price is paid, is taken away? Is the Spirit then taken away from us when the inheritance itself is given to us? Solution. Here "pledge" is set down for "earnest," which is part of the price itself, and is not taken away when the price is paid; whence certain manuscripts have "earnest," not "pledge."

569DQUESTION VII. Setting him at his right hand, etc. God is spirit, and is not bounded or enclosed by the form of a body: how then is the Son said to sit at the right hand of the Father, since the Father has no right or left side, because he has no body? Solution. By the right hand of God in Holy Scripture is sometimes signified eternal beatitude, sometimes the equality of the divine nature, sometimes judiciary power. For Christ is at the right hand of the Father, because in the majesty of the Father he remains equal, and because the Father judgeth no man, but hath given all judgment to the Son (Joan. V). By the right hand of God therefore, or by hand, or arm, or finger, or eye, or ear, and the like, nothing corporeal is to be understood, but the whole spiritually.

570AQUESTION VIII. Above every name, which is named not only in this world, etc. Are there not nine orders of angels? Angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, seraphim — and there are no more than these, which are all named in the present. How then does he say: Set above everything that is named not only in this world, but also in that which is to come, as though there were some to be named in the future who are not named in the present. Solution. The denominations of certain angels are given to them according to the offices which they exhibit toward us in the present, as angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations; therefore they are said to be names in the present, because in this manner their denomination looks to the present. 570BWhence in the future they will be made void, when Christ shall deliver up the kingdom to God and the Father, when God shall be all in all. But the denominations of certain angels look to the future state, as thrones, cherubim, and seraphim; whence they will not be made void even in the future, but above all these orders of the supercelestial spirits the humanity of the Savior has been exalted.

QUESTION IX. And him he gave to be head over all the Church. It is asked according to which nature, namely the divine or the human, Christ is the head of the Church. Solution. It can be said that it is according to the divine, according to which he is the head, the beginning, and the author of all the faithful. To which solution it is thus objected: By the same reasoning it can be said that he is the head of a stone, and of every creature, of which he is the author; and nothing would be said 570Cof the Church. Therefore we say that Christ is properly the head of the Church according to his humanity.

QUESTION X. Why Christ is called the head of the Church. Why he is said to be the head may not unfittingly be asked. Solution. Christ is called the head of the Church for this reason: because as in the head of a man are fully all the carnal senses, namely sight, hearing, smell or scent, taste, and touch; so in Christ is the fullness of all the spiritual senses, namely the fullness of grace, of whose fullness we all have received (Joan. I); whence we are also called members, as not all having some one sense, just as the other members of the body have but a single sense; none has all except the head.

QUESTION XI. We were by nature the children of wrath (Ephes. 570DII), etc. God is the author of nature; if therefore we are by nature children of wrath, it seems that we are this with God as author. Solution. Nature is taken in three ways in Holy Scripture, namely for that whole and interrupted good in which man was created, according to which acceptation it is said that every creature of God is good. Nature is also called the corruption of sin, in which every man is conceived, and with which he is born, and thus it is taken here when it is said: We were by nature children of wrath. For the vice has grown ingrained in place of nature: because therefore, on account of the guilt of original sin, with which we are born, we are worthy of Gehenna, therefore we are called by nature children of wrath. Nature is also taken for the remnants of that natural good which remained in us after sin, and thus 571Ait is taken where it is read that the Gentiles do by nature the things that are of the law (Rom. II).

QUESTION XII. To me the least of all the saints is given this grace (Ephes. III). Since the Apostle was not the least in the number of all the saints, but rather among the apostles was one of the first, how does he speak truly in naming himself the least of all. Seek the solution of this question upon that passage: I am the least of the apostles, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

QUESTION XIII. The unsearchable riches of Christ, etc. It is asked how the Apostle understood or evangelized, if the riches are unsearchable. For those things are called unsearchable which cannot be comprehended. Solution. Those things which are by their nature unsearchable were made searchable, through the grace 571Band revelation of the Holy Spirit, not only to the Apostle, but also to the rest of the faithful, whom the anointing itself teaches concerning all things.

QUESTION XIV. Of the hidden mystery, etc. It is asked, what things are called hidden. Solution. In the world the causes are hidden of all things that come to be naturally. But in God alone are hidden the causes of all things that come to be through grace. Concerning these two kinds of causes something has already been said above.

QUESTION XV. That it may be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places through the Church, etc. It is asked whether the mystery of the incarnation was revealed to the supercelestial essences before its fulfillment. In the solution of this question Jerome 571Cand Augustine seem contrary. For the blessed Jerome says that the angelic dignities did not understand purely the aforesaid mystery; whence they thus ask: Who is this that cometh from Edom? (Isa. LXIII.) And elsewhere: Who is this king of glory? (Psal. XXIII.) But the blessed Augustine says that the mystery of the kingdom of heaven was not hidden from the angels; whence the text is expounded in diverse ways, That it may be made known, etc. But this contrariety, which seems to be between the aforesaid doctors, can be resolved thus: to those who are of greater dignity the aforesaid mystery was revealed; but to others not purely, as the blessed Jerome says. But that the angels grow daily in knowledge, from those things which come to be in the world, many doctors assert with concordant voice. 571DWhence we hold this as if for certain, since canonical Scripture seems manifestly to intimate it.

QUESTION XVI. Of whom all paternity in heaven and in earth is named. From this passage we have that not only is God our Father, but also the angels and men are called our fathers. But elsewhere the Lord says: One is your Father, who is in heaven (Matth. XXIII). If therefore there is one, how are there many? or if many, how one? Solution. As God, who alone truly is, and who alone is truly good, imparts the name of his essence and of his goodness to the rest, so that they too are said both to be and to be good; so also he, who alone is truly Father — of all by creation, and of the faithful by regeneration — has granted the name of paternity to the rest. It is to be known thus, that God the Trinity is the Father of all 572Aby creation and of the faithful by regeneration. But God unbegotten alone is the Father of the Only-begotten by nature. But the angels are called our fathers by the authority of example, by reason of benefit, by care, and by providence. But men are fathers both by nature, and by the authority of example, and by reason of benefit, and by care and providence.

QUESTION XVII. What is the breadth, and length, and height. What is the breadth of love, what the length of eternity, what the height of power, what the depth of knowledge — according to this, which is expounded of God, such can be the understanding.

QUESTION XVIII. To know also the charity of Christ, which surpasseth knowledge. If the charity of Christ surpasses knowledge, how can it be known? if it cannot be known, how does the Apostle pray that the disciples may know it? 572BSolution. That which human knowledge cannot comprehend is known in part through grace, which the Apostle prays may come to pass.

QUESTION XIX. That you may be filled unto all the fullness of God, etc. Shall we not have less than God himself? how then can we be filled unto all the fullness of God? how can anyone have the fullness of God, and not be full God and equal to God? Solution. The sense is, that you may be full of God, not full God. This is to be filled unto all fullness: to have in the present the fullness of virtues, and in the future the fullness of glory; for Paul does not wish that the fullness of the divine nature be conferred upon anyone, but that we be full of God in the present and in the future.

572CQUESTION XX. One Lord, one faith, one baptism (Ephes. IV). How are they to be understood? Solution. One Lord: the Father, and the Son, and the Spirit in nature, not in person. One faith not in number, but in kind, because it is alike in all, just as of all who will the same thing there is said to be the same will. Concerning faith it has already been spoken. It is called one baptism, because it is equal, and of the same essence by whomsoever it is given, and therefore also because it cannot be reiterated.

QUESTION XXI. He gave gifts to men. But does David say: Thou hast received gifts in men (Psal. LXVII)? if he gave, how did he receive? or if he received, how did he give? Solution. As God he gave; he received not only in himself according to that he is man, but also in his members, in which he is, of which receiving 572Dthe Prophet treats: whence he says: Thou hast received gifts in men.

QUESTION XXII. What gifts he gave in ascending. It is asked what gifts he gave in ascending. Solution. The Holy Spirit, and also the gifts which are not the Holy Spirit, which when he gives, in them also he gives the Holy Spirit; he does not give separately the Holy Spirit and his gifts which are not himself, but in giving the Holy Spirit he gives the gifts; and in giving the gifts of the Holy Spirit he gives him. This I say on account of those who will not grant that the Holy Spirit is given, since he is immutable, but grant nevertheless that his gifts are given. For the Holy Spirit is then said to be given to us by the Father, and the Son, and even by himself, when he infuses into our hearts through charity this power, 573Ato the end that we may love God and neighbor.

QUESTION XXIII. Since Christ is God and man, it is asked according to which nature he gave the gifts? Solution. He gave according to that, as the expositor says, according to which he ascended and descended, and thus he gave according to that he is man; because the divinity, which is everywhere, neither descends nor ascends. But this seems to be contrary to the aforesaid, where I asserted that he gave as God, not as man. When therefore it is read that he gave as man or according to his humanity, it ought to be understood thus: he who is man, not because he is man, but because he is God.

QUESTION XXIV. Whether the Deity descended, and how. Likewise another exposition says that Christ descended according to 573Bhis Deity, and ascended according to his humanity, which seems contrary to the foregoing. For it was said that the divinity which is everywhere neither descends nor ascends; but here it is said that the Deity descended: what then is to be held? Solution. When it is said that God descended, this is understood of the descent of the incarnation, by which God was made man. When it is said that man descended, this ought to be understood of the descent to the lower regions, which was only according to the soul, not according to the body, which lay in the sepulcher, nor according to the Deity, which was everywhere.

QUESTION XXV. Unto a perfect man, etc. It is asked, by what perfection. Solution. Perfection can be understood neither of the whole Christ, that is, of body and head, nor 573Cof the individual members. For Christ, consummated in himself, grows and advances in others, but in the future at last he will be perfected, so that nothing be added either in powers or in number. Each one also will then be a perfect man, as much by the consummation of virtues as by the stature of the body. Whence there follows: Unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ. For each one will rise again in that perfection in which he was, or to which he was going to come, when he was thirty years of age; for not all will be of the same magnitude, nor of that of which Christ was when departing from this life.

QUESTION XXVI. Be angry, and sin not, etc. The Apostle permits anger, which cannot be avoided, but the Lord forbids anger, saying: Whosoever 573Dis angry with his brother shall be in danger of the judgment (Matth. V). Whence it seems that what the Lord forbids, the Apostle permits. Likewise it was said above: that nothing is forbidden in the New Testament which cannot be avoided, just as nothing is commanded which cannot be fulfilled; which does not seem to be true, if the Lord forbids anger, and no one can avoid being angry. Solution. The first motion of anger, which is not in our power, is permitted by the Apostle: but the Lord does not forbid the first motion, which is called pro-passion, but the will and the purpose of harming another. And so one thing is permitted by the Apostle, and another is forbidden by the Lord, which can be avoided with grace helping.

QUESTION XXVII. What are the gates of death and of life. Note that concupiscence and the fear of the world are the two 574Agates of death, through which the devil enters; as the fear and love of God are the gates of life, through which Christ enters. Each stands at the door; and both Christ knocks and the devil: but the enemy is driven out, Christ is brought in.

QUESTION XXVIII. Grieve not the Holy Spirit, etc. It is asked how anyone can grieve the Holy Spirit, since he is impassible and cannot receive into himself the passion of sadness. Solution. He has used a certain trope, sufficiently customary in theology, by which those things which come to be in us with God as author are attributed to him; because therefore those whom he fills with charity, as they rejoice over the progress of others, so are grieved over the lapses of those who fall, the Apostle says: Grieve not the Holy Spirit, that is, those in whom 574Bthe Holy Spirit dwells through charity.

QUESTION XXIX. Forgive one another, etc. Scripture says: Unless we forgive our fellow servants, God requires again what was remitted; but it is asked how God requires it again? Will God punish again for sins for which satisfaction has already been made through the contrition of the heart, and the confession of the mouth, and through worthy fruits of penance? Will he punish twice for the same thing? Solution. To the end that anyone may bring forth worthy fruits of penance, it is required that henceforth he sin not mortally; whence whoever sins after penance renders his former satisfaction useless to himself.

QUESTION XXX. What is it to punish twice for the same thing? Now to punish twice for the same thing is to punish again in another life for a sin destroyed by penance and not repeated, 574Cwhich God does not do. But if any penitent is afflicted for some sin and again repeats the same; if in this life or in another he is punished for it again, this is not to punish twice for the same thing.

QUESTION XXXI. For an odor of sweetness (Ephes. V), etc. If the death of Christ was a sweet odor to God, then he willingly accepted his death; then the Jews did not sin, who crucified him; because they did that which was good, and which pleased God. Solution. The action of the Jews was evil, nor did that which was done by them please God; but the passion of Christ was good, and the cause of our salvation.

QUESTION XXXII. The days are evil, etc. Do not the days have their being from God as author, as it is written: Thine 574Dis the day, and thine is the night? (Psal. LXXIII.) How then are they called evil? Solution. On account of the malice and misery of men the days are called evil; otherwise, as to the spaces of the hours, they are ordered, and good.

QUESTION XXXIII. No man ever hated his own flesh, etc. Do not holy men hate the flesh, persecute, crucify, and mortify it, not nourish nor cherish it? how then is it true, No man ever hated his own flesh? Solution. The saints hate and persecute not the flesh, but the vice of the flesh.

QUESTION XXXIV. For this cause shall a man leave his father. It is asked how this pertains to the Son of God, who never forsook the Father, but always remained inseparably with him? Solution. Because the Son did not 575Aappear to us in the form in which he is equal to the Father, he is said to have forsaken or left the Father; yet he never departed from him: he came into the world, and did not forsake the Father.

QUESTION XXXV. He that loveth his wife. It is asked of what love he here treats; for if of the love by which we love one another for the sake of God, the sense is: He that loveth his wife loveth himself, that is, does what is useful to himself: according to this he could say the same of any neighbor whatever. Solution. The Apostle says this for this reason, because it is more incumbent upon a man to provide for his wife than for another: whence if for the sake of God he acquires for her the necessaries, and governs her, he also loves himself, that is, does what is useful to himself; because thereby he merits with God.

QUESTION XXXVI. Servants, obey your masters (Ephes. VI). Here it is asked whether it is lawful for a Christian to have a servant, 575Bsince the Apostle permits this. The Catholic Church too, and especially the Church of the Gauls, receives this. Solution. It would be better not to exact servitude of this kind; nor does the Church receive it as a good, but tolerates it as an evil.

QUESTION XXXVII. Children, obey your parents; and you, fathers, provoke not your children to anger. It is asked why the Apostle commands parents to 576Alove their children, and children to honor their parents, since nature compels them to love one another mutually. Solution. Natural love has no merit unless it be done for the sake of God: therefore he commands that they love one another for the sake of God, and so have merit.

QUESTION XXXVIII. Our wrestling is not against flesh. Do not the saints fight against flesh and blood, against evil men, or against the vices which arise from flesh and blood? how then does he say: Our wrestling is not, etc.? Solution. Our wrestling is not only against flesh and blood, but also against demons.

QUESTION XXXIX. Against the rulers of the world. Does not God, who founded the world, govern and rule the world, so that the same is founder and ruler? how then does 576Bthe Apostle call the demons rulers of the world? Solution. Here by the name of the world he signifies the lovers of the world. This is the world which is wholly set in wickedness: this is the world in which is found nothing but the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life: this world the Apostle calls darkness, adding of this darkness, and elsewhere saying: You were heretofore darkness; but now light in the Lord (Ephes. V).

VI. IN EPISTOLAM AD PHILIPPENSES.

  • 575

575C(Philip. I.) Paulus et Timotheus, etc. Hanc epistolam scribit Apostolus Philippensibus, qui sunt Macedones. Sunt enim Philippi metropolis civitas in Macedonia, quae est quaedam provincia in Graecia, quam aedificavit Philippus pater Alexandri, vocans eam nomine suo. Hi autem accepto verbo praedicationis ab Apostolo firmi in fide fuerunt, nec pseudo receperunt. Hos ergo munit contra duplex bellum, scilicet tribulationum et pseudopraedicatorum. Est itaque intentio Apostoli in hac epistola cohortari Philippenses ad patientiam contra tribulationes, et ad constantiam contra pseudoapostolos. Modus talis: more solito salutem praemittit. Deinde gratias agit pro eis, implorans eis majora bona, ut virtutibus crescentes ad perfectionem perveniant. Deinde 575Dad patientiam tribulationum monet exemplo suo, et Christi. Postea ut sibi caveant a versutiis pseudoapostolorum. Tandem admonitionem mortalem interserit, et prope finem de gratia, quam sibi Romani per Epaphroditum miserant, se gaudere dicit.

QUAESTIO I. Quid enim? dum omni modo sive per occasionem, sive per veritatem Christus annuntietur. Quaeritur quomodo permittat Apostolus malis praedicare evangelicam doctrinam cum alibi scriptum sit: Peccatori dixit Deus: Quare tu enarras justitias meas (Psal. XLIX)? etc. Item: Non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris (Eccli. XV). Item: Cujus vita despicitur, restat ut praedicatio ejus negligatur. Solutio. In hujusmodi praedicator increpatur propter se, non propter alios. Non enim sibi prodest, sed aliis quod praedicat: 576Cunde laus Dei in ore peccatorum non est speciosa. Tolerandi ergo sunt mercenarii. Unde Dominus: Super cathedram Moysi sederunt Scribae et Pharisaei: quae dicunt facite (Matth. XXV), etc. Itaque praedicatores, qui pro veritate praedicant, diligendi sunt; mercenarii, qui ex occasione et temporali commodo veritatem annuntiant, permittendi sunt; fures et latrones, sive lupi cavendi, imo fugiendi sunt.

QUAESTIO II. Quid eligam, ignoro, etc. Quaeritur quomodo Apostolus dubitet utrum eligat, an manere in carne, an dissolvi et esse cum Christo (Philipp. I), cum sciat quod quanto pugna fortior, tanto corona major. Nonne sciebat majoris meriti esse pugnare quam quiescere? Solutio. Affectus ad utrumque trahebat: idcirco dicit se ignorare quid 576Deligat. Dubitat ergo Apostolus ex affectu, non ex ignorantia. Sed tunc quaeritur: Quomodo dicat multo melius esse dissolvi et esse cum Christo. Solutio. Melius, hic ponitur pro suavius et securius.

QUAESTIO III. Vobis donatum est non solum, ut in eum credatis, sed etiam ut pro ipso patiamini, etc. Quaeritur an ipsum pati sit bonum, et an sit donum Dei? quod si est, appetendum est. Solutio. A quo est fides credentium, ab eo est tolerantia patientium. Poena autem ipsa in se non est bona, nec propter se appetenda, nec inter dona Dei debet enumerari. Pati tamen pro Christo bonum est et desiderandum; quia magnum habet meritum. Nec Apostolus dicit simpliciter: Vobis donatum est pati; 577Ased sic: Vobis donatum est pro Christo pati.

QUAESTIO IV. Qui cum in forma Dei esset (Philipp. II). Quaeritur quid hic notet forma. Solutio. Forma aliquando ponitur pro repraesentatione, aliquando pro veritate rei, ut hic: Qui cum in forma Dei esset, id est in veritate divinae essentiae et in aequalitate substantiae; sicut enim homo hominem, canis canem gignit , sic Deus Deum genuit per omnia aequalem, non imparem: unde et Filius dicitur esse hoc, quod Pater est et quoniam hoc potest secundum personam, et naturam intelligi, Augustinus ostendit hujus dicti intelligentiam, dicens: Ideo Filius dicitur id quod Pater est, quia sicut Pater est Deus, sic et Filius, et sicut Pater est omnipotens, sic et Filius, et sicut Pater est immutabilis, sic et 577BFilius. Ideo enim unum, et summe unum sunt Pater et Filius, quorum nulla est diversitas naturae vel voluntatis. Utrumque ergo dicit Scriptura, quod Filius est aequalis Patri, et quod Pater major est Filio, sed hoc secundum formam servi, illud autem secundum formam Dei.

QUAESTIO V. Et habitu inventus est ut homo, etc. Quot modis aliquid habetur? Solutio. Quatuor modis aliquid alicui accedit, ut habeatur, vel sic ut mutet et non mutetur, ut sapientia; vel sic ut mutet et mutetur, ut cibus; vel sic ut nec mutet nec mutetur, ut annulus; vel sic ut non mutet sed mutetur, non a sua natura, sed a quadam priori forma, ut vestis, quando induitur; non mutat hominem, sed mutatur; non a natura sua, sed accipit speciem et formam, quam 577Cdejecta non habuit, secundum quam comparationem et similitudinem intelligitur incarnatio: sic enim forma servi accessit ad formam Dei, ut eam non mutavit vel convertit, sed ipsa forma servi est mutata, non a natura sua, sed in excellentiorem et digniorem statum, quam prius fuerat. Hoc ergo totum, quod Augustinus dicit de habitu, ideo adducit ut ostendat, quod quando Verbum caro factum est non est mutatum vel conversum in hominem; sicut nec homo mutatur in vestem, quando ea induitur. Hoc autem, quod quidam addunt de suo, quod sicut homo quando induitur veste sua, non fit aliquid; sic nec Deus, quando formam servi accepit, factus est aliquid: hoc, inquam, non habent ex verbis Augustini, 577Dnec alterius sancti, cum sit falsum: si enim in omnibus volunt tenere similitudinem adductam de veste, oportet eos concedere, quod sicut homo non fit vestis, quando ea induitur; ita nec Deus homo, quando forma se servi induit, factus sit. Si enim Christus non est nisi id quod fuit ab aeterno, nullum esse habuit commune cum matre: ergo non consubstantialis matri; quia nullum substantiale dicitur de utroque. Dum enim dicitur: Christus est homo, et Virgo mater Domini est homo, non idem significatur, hoc nomine, homo, secundum hos novos haereticos. De his plenius dictum super Epistolam ad Romanos.

578AQUAESTIO VI. Qui humiliavit semetipsum factus obediens, etc. Quaeritur an Christus aliquid meruit. Solutio. Nobis, non sibi meruit. Nos enim per ejus meritum facti sumus digni vita aeterna; ipse vero per mortem suam sibi non acquisivit aliquid, quo prius dignus non erat. Dici tamen potest: Vere per humilitatem passionis meruit claritatem resurrectionis, scilicet impassibilitatem et immortalitatem.
