Caeterum licet pars hujus definitionis aliis virtutibus assignari videatur, non tota tamen; sola enim fides est argumentum non apparentium, per quam solam certi sumus de aeternis, quod sunt; per spem vero, quod ea nos sumus habituri, confidimus. Et ideo proprie fides substantia futurorum dicitur, quia per eam scimus quod sunt. fides etiam de praesentibus, vel praeteritis potest dici substantia rerum sperandarum, id est causa quae 630Afacit quandoque ea quae speramus subsistere in nobis, quia per fidem passionis venitur ad futura bona, et est argumentum non apparentium, adeo quod illi qui viderunt eum pati aliquid crediderunt, scilicet Christum esse Deum, qui in cruce pendebat.

QUAESTIO XCIV. Ut ex invisibilibus, etc. Quaeritur quid vocet invisibilia? Solutio. Vel informem et invisibilem materiam quatuor elementorum, quae Graece chaos dicitur; vel invisibilem mundum, qui archetypus dicitur, qui in mente Dei erat juxta cujus exemplar factus est iste sensibilis et visibilis mundus.

QUAESTIO XCV. Abel fide adhuc defunctus loquitur, etc. Quaeritur quomodo ille, qui non vivit, loquatur? 630BSolutio. Loquitur, id est materia est loquendi; loquitur quia suo exemplo nos monet ut simus justi.

QUAESTIO XCVI. Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo, etc. Quaeritur de qua fide hoc dicat; nunquid de fide incarnationis? Solutio. Dicitur quod sine ea nullus ab initio placuit Deo.

QUAESTIO XCVII. Credere oportet accedentem ad Deum quoniam est, etc. Quaeritur de qua fide agat, an de perfecta, an de imperfecta? Si de imperfecta, quomodo per eam potuit aliquis Deo placere; si de perfecta, quomodo hoc potest sufficere ad salutem, credere quia est, et quia inquirentibus se remunerator sit? his enim non sunt omnes articuli contenti, qui sunt necessarii ad salutem. Solutio. Videtur 630Chic fidei habendae ponere ordinem, id est ostendere quid in primis credere oportet, non fidei sufficientiam assignare.

QUAESTIO XCVIII. Utrum vero aliquod tempus fuerit in quo hoc credere tantum, scilicet, quia Deus est, et quia remunerator, etc., suffecerit, quaeri potest. Quod non videtur.

QUAESTIO XCIX. Fide et de futuris benedixit Isaac Jacob, etc. Nunquid cum benediceret ei, intellexit quod ibi significabatur per hoc, quod minorem benedicebat? Si intelligebat, tunc sciebat quod diceret Jacob, quod nequaquam historia patitur. Nam et manus contrectavit, ut probaret an esset Esau, et postea veniente Esau ait: Quis fuit, qui venit fraudulenter: cui benedixi, et erit benedictus? Solutio. 630DLicet tunc non intellexit, tamen post intellexit, et ejus rei fidem habuit, quod major populus serviet minori.

QUAESTIO C. Item quaeritur unde Isaac in benedicendo deceptus est? Solutio. Non fuit deceptus, quin sciret quem effectum haberet benedictio in illo quem benedicebat; nondum tamen quod Jacob esse sciebat, quem benedicebat. Solet autem proprie deceptio in iis, quae non debent fieri, accipi. Nunquid decipi dicendus est, qui pro aurichalco emit aurum, vel pro stanno argentum? Si vero large deceptio accipiatur, pro omnibus quae aliter fiant quam existimantur, et hic deceptio quaedam fuit.

QUAESTIO CI. Et adoravit fastigium virgae ejus; 631Avel ut alia habet littera, super fastigium, etc. Quaeritur quid est quod Jacob adoravit super cacumen virgae Joseph. Solutio. Forte tulerat a filio virgam, quando idem filius jurabat, et dum eam tenet post verba jurantis, nondum illa reddita, mox adoravit Deum: sic solvit Augustinus. Vel potest dici quod adoravit fastigium virgae ejus, id est regnum Christi futurum in gentibus: quod per illud significabatur, ut nomine signi signatum intelligatur.

QUAESTIO CII. Jephthe, etc. De hoc quaeritur an rationale fecerit votum, et an peccaverit implendo illud, unicam filiam offerendo Domino. Nunquid si canis occurrisset ei, obtulisset eum Deo? Solutio. Videtur, quod stulte egerit vovendo, stultius votum implendo: 631Btamen si occulto monitu sancti Spiritus hoc fecerit, excusatur, sicut Samson, qui secum Philisthaeos compressit, quia non licet sibi manum inferre. Unde et Jonas dixit: Mittite me in mare.

QUAESTIO CIII. Quaeritur cur in recordatione mortis illius puellae, Hebreae virgines singulis annis planctus faciunt? Solutio. Exempli causa, ne quis iterum sic stulte aliquid voveat, vel faciat, unde talis dolor sequi possit.

QUAESTIO. CIV. Quaeritur an Abraham voluntate peccaverit, volendo immolare filium suum, cum, secundum quosdam, imo revera Jephthe peccaverit occidendo filiam, nisi hoc factum sit instinctu divino. Solutio. Abraham non solum non culpatur crudelitatis crimine, verum etiam laudatur pietatis 631Cnomine, quod filium suum non scelerate, sed obedienter, voluit occidere.

QUAESTIO CV. Deinde patres quidemcarnis nostrae eruditores habuimus, et reverebamur eos: nonne multo magis obtemperabimus Patri spirituum, et vivemus? (Hebr. XII.) Si quaeratur, utrum animae humanae sint ex traduce, nota diligenter hanc auctoritatem, per quam manifeste probatur, quod animae non sunt ex traduce sicut caro; si enim hoc esset, nequaquam distingueret Apostolus inter patres carnis nostrae, et Patrem spirituum.

QUAESTIO CVI. Contemplantes ne quis desit gratiae Dei, etc. Quaeritur quid sit deesse gratiae Dei? Solutio. Gratiae oblatae oculos mentis claudere, et gratiam respuere, quemadmodum radio solis oculis 631Dmeis apertis eos claudere, vel apertos tenere, pro libitu possum, quod est ex libero arbitrio; et sic gratia non excludit liberum arbitrium, nec ipsum arbitrium excludit gratiam.

QUAESTIO CVII. Vendidit primogenita sua, etc. Quaeritur quid Apostolus vocet primogenita Esau. Solutio. Primogenita hic vocat honorem et dignitatem sacerdotii: quia ante sacerdotium Aaron omnes primogeniti sacerdotes erant, sicut fuit Sem. Et haec erat magna dignitas, quia de substantia et haereditate paterna majorem portionem sumebat, vestiumque ornatu locupletiorum splendebat, eique benedictio dabatur.

QUAESTIO CVIII. Quaeritur an peccatum Esau erat 632Airremissibile, cum Apostolus dicat quod non invenit poenitentiae locum. Nonne poenituit? imo lacrymatus est: quomodo ergo verum est, non invenit locum poenitentiae? Solutio. Non invenit locum poenitentiae, id est veniae, et locum benedictionis per poenitentiam non quod non poenituerit, sed quia non poenituit uti debuit. Lacrymae enim illae potius fuerunt ex indignatione contra fratrem, et ex dolore amissi honoris, quam ex humilitate veraque poenitentia.

QUAESTIO CIX. Testamenti novi mediatorem Jesum, et sanguinis aspersionem melius loquentem quam Abel. Quaeritur in quo sanguis Christi melius loquatur quam sanguis Abel? Solutio. Dicit glossa ideo melius, quia iste, id est Christi, petebat veniam, 632Bille vindictam; iste salutem, ille damnationem. Sed dicet quis: Nonne effusores sanguinis Christi perierunt, sicut effusores sanguinis Abel? Ergo sanguis Christi vindictam loquitur, sicut sanguis Abel. Quomodo ergo melius loquitur iste quam ille? Solutio. Sanguis Christi non solum vindictam clamat contemnentibus, sed etiam veniam omnibus, etiam persecutoribus, si ipsi volunt poenitere. Sanguis vero Abel tantum vindictam, et nulli veniam loquitur. Vel melius loquitur sanguis Christi quam Abel, id est melius nos loqui facit, scilicet, quod Jesus sit Filius Dei, a quo redempti sumus; quam sanguis Abel, qui facit nos loqui Abel fuisse virum justum in figura Christi immolatum. Nota quod Abel, qui primus injuste occisus fuit, positus est pro omnibus 632Caliis quorum sanguis nullam veniam facere potuit.

QUAESTIO CX. Per hanc quidem placuerunt Deo, etc. Quaeritur an Abraham et Lot cognoverunt eos esse angelos. Si cognoverunt, quomodo officia humanitatis praebuerunt, quae non sunt necessaria, nisi infirmitati hominum? Item si non cognoverunt angelos esse, sed homines tantum arbitrati sunt, quomodo plusquam homines venerati sunt eos? Solutio. Primo homines arbitrati sunt divinitus missos, et in quibus Deus esset; postea vero compererunt angelos esse.

QUAESTIO CXI. Quaeritur quomodo angeli in sumptis corporibus comedere potuerunt? Non enim sic illa corpora unita habebant, ut animae hominum habent 632Dsibi unita corpora, unde nec animata erant, nec sensibilia illa corpora; nec laedi poterant in illis corporibus angeli. Solutio. Non comederunt angeli more animalium, sed sicut ignis quod ipsi apponitur consumit, et in nihilum redigit; sic et cibus ille consumptus est operatione illorum, vel ipsi inde fecerunt quod volebant.

QUAESTIO CXII. Item quaeritur quomodo cum angeli essent tres visi, unum eorum in fide Trinitatis et unitatis adorare potuerit Abraham? Solutio. Divina revelatione cognovit in illis mysterium Trinitatis et unitatis.

QUAESTIO CXIII. Quorum enim animalium, etc. Dicit expositor, quod per duplicem allegoriam probat, 633Aquod corpus Christi non est comedendum ab iis qui tabernaculo deserviunt; sed cum unus sit sensus utriusque historiae, quomodo per duplicem allegoriam probat hoc? Quid est allegoria? Nonne spiritalis sensus? Ergo ubi est unus sensus, quomodo duplex est allegoria? Solutio. Dicit per duplicem allegoriam, 634Aid est per allegoriam de duplici historia surgentem. Vel allegoria dicitur significans et significatum; hic autem pro significante ponitur: Quid est autem per duplicem allegoriam nisi per duplicem historiam, scilicet unam Veteris, alteram Novi Testamenti?

XIV. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS.

  • 607

607CIn many ways (Hebr. I), etc. Paul, the excellent doctor, the Apostle of the Gentiles, wishing to honor his ministry. According to which he says in the Epistle to the Romans: As long as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry, trying if by any means I may provoke to emulation my own flesh (Rom. XI). To the churches of the Hebrews he writes this epistle, treating of the eminence of Christ according to both natures, and of the uselessness of the Mosaic law; building up in many ways that the faith of Jesus Christ, without the legal observances, suffices for justice and salvation. But that the legal observances, after Christ's passion, 608Cnot only do not profit, but even hinder, excluding the estimation of certain Hebrews, who, confessing Christ, thought that the legal observances were to be kept; and by their authority had led into this error even some who had come to Christ from heathenism; therefore the Apostle, providing for the Gentiles, lest thenceforth they be drawn into this error by the authority of the Hebrews, provoking the Jews also to emulation, commends the grace of God made to the faithful in this time through Christ the true high priest, showing the law to be reprobated. The intention, therefore, of the Apostle 609Ain this epistle is to show the eminence of Christ, and the sufficiency of faith, as well as the insufficiency and uselessness of the law.

The manner of treating is such. First he proposes that the words of Christ are to be heard as those of the prophets, and further, by comparing him with the prophets, and preferring him; because in him God spoke as in the prophets, and he is greater than they. Then he commends him alternately according to both natures, namely the human and the divine, afterward he compares him with the angels, and prefers him, interweaving many things about his excellence according to both natures. Then he compares him with Moses and prefers him. Then by many reasons and authorities he declares that the grace of faith is to be carried through for the shadow of the law; and the priesthood of Christ to the Levitical 609Bpriesthood, and the New Testament to the Old; and he shows that its one sacrifice is to be set before the many sacrifices of that; because there is the shadow, here the truth. Finally he sets down a description of faith, commending it by many testimonies. But toward the end he adds a moral instruction.

QUESTION I. First it is asked, why to this epistle, as to the others, he did not prefix his own name, which is Paul; why also he was silent about the name of dignity, which is Apostle? Solution. Because he was odious to the Hebrews, to whom he seemed a destroyer of the law, he kept silent his name, odious to them, lest the ill-will toward his name, prefixed, should exclude the usefulness of the reading that follows; knowing also their pride, and showing his own humility, he was unwilling to put forward the dignity of his order by naming 609Chimself Apostle, but, keeping silent the merit of his office, himself humble toward the proud, he did not name himself apostle, lest the proud be indignant. But someone will say: Does not the Apostle write to the faithful who were at Jerusalem, to whom the name of Paul was not odious, nor did they envy his dignity as though he were proud; how then is it true that he kept silent his proper name or the name of dignity because it was odious to the Hebrews, since to those to whom he wrote he was not odious, but beloved? Solution. Among those to whom, as an excellent preacher of grace, he was much pleasing, there were certain zealots of the law, who thought and preached that the law was to be kept together with grace, and to these the name of Paul was odious. For they found no one so contrary to their false opinion as Paul, whence they persecuted 609Dhim as much as they could. It is to be noted that there were some saying that this epistle was by no means the apostle Paul's, because his name is not prefixed to it as in all the others, and also because it shines with a more splendid and more eloquent style than the others; but that it was either Luke's, or Barnabas's, or Clement's. To whom Jerome thus responds: If it is therefore not to be called Paul's, because it is not inscribed with his name, then neither is it any of theirs, nay of no one at all, since it has no one's name in the title, which was done for the aforesaid cause already given. But that it shines with greater eloquence than the others is not to be wondered at, since it is natural for each one to be more capable in his own language than in a foreign one; since therefore he wrote this one 610Aalone in the Hebrew language, but the others in Greek, what wonder if it shines with greater eloquence?

QUESTION II. In these days. It is asked what days he calls them. Solution. The Apostle calls the time of grace "days" on account of the eminent doctrine of faith and the knowledge of salvation, whence elsewhere: Behold, now is the day of salvation (II Cor. VI).

QUESTION III. Whom he hath appointed heir of all things, etc. It is asked, according to which nature Christ is here called heir of all things. Solution. It can well be said that according to the divine nature he is here called heir, that is, possessor, and Lord of all things, that is, of all nature. Or according to his humanity he is called heir of all things, namely of those to be saved, or of Jews and Gentiles. For this is the heir of the world, that seed in which all nations are blessed, 610Bto whom the Father speaks, saying: Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance (Psal. II).

QUESTION IV. By whom also he made the ages. Did not God the Father make all things through the Son, visible and invisible, mutable and immutable? Why then does the Apostle not say: By whom he made all things, but "by whom he made also the ages"! Solution. These visible and mutable things are more known to us; and therefore in these we more admire the power of God than in those which are unknown; and this is the reason why he rather named the ages specially.

QUESTION V. Who, being the brightness of glory, etc. It is asked why he uses this likeness, and elsewhere another? Solution. The Apostle, wishing to show that, although the Son is from the Father, yet he is coeternal with him, 610Cuses a proportional likeness of temporal things, saying: who, being the brightness of glory, as if he were to say: as the brightness of fire, although it be from the fire, yet is coeval with the fire, and would be coeternal with it, if it were eternal; for the fire was never without brightness; so the Son, although he be from the Father, yet is coeternal with him, because the Father was never without the Son. Likewise, wishing to show the identity of nature which the Son has with the Father, he uses a proportional likeness of other things, calling the Son the figure of the substance, because he could not demonstrate both in the same things. For in creatures nothing is found which has being from another, and is of the same nature or substance, and which is not preceded by it. But the Son so has being from the Father, that he is coeternal with him; as the brightness 610Dis coeval with the fire, and is of the same essence or nature with the Father. As the man begetting, and the man begotten of him — for as a man cannot beget except that which he himself is, that is, because a man begets a man, so God begets nothing other than what he himself is, that is, God begets God. Reader, diligently observe these words of the Apostle, and the exposition of the holy ones upon them; and thou wilt notice how both the Sabellian heresy and the Arian is here manifestly destroyed.

QUESTION VI. And upholding all things by the word of his power. It is asked how God is said to uphold all things by the word, since to uphold does not pertain to the property of the Word. Likewise, whether he is beneath all things, and not rather over and above them, that he should be said to uphold them. Solution. 611AHe is said to uphold all things by the word rather than by power for this reason, that in upholding — that is, in containing, and governing, and preserving — he may be understood to sustain no labor or difficulty, he who is more inward than every thing, because all things are in him; and higher than every thing, because he is above all; and more ancient than every thing, because he is before all; and newer than every thing, because he is after all, that is, after the beginnings of all things.

QUESTION VII. He sitteth at the right hand, etc. The expositor says that the man assumed was exalted even to equality with the Father, which is understood by the "right hand": therefore it is asked whether it is to be granted that the man assumed is equal to the Father; but since the Son says: The Father is greater than I (Joan. XIV): which is to be understood 611Baccording to that which is assumed, how is the same equal to the Father, since the Son according to it is less than the Father? Solution. That man, inasmuch as he is man, is less than the Father, and not equal: but inasmuch as the man assumed is God, the Son of God, he is not less than the Father, but equal. It is therefore to be seen what is said of what, and in respect of what, as often as discourse occurs about Christ; yet there are many who do not grant that the man assumed is God, as has already been said above.

QUESTION VIII. Being made so much better than the angels. It is asked according to which nature he here speaks of Christ: that according to divinity he is better than the angels, there is no question; but yet he was not made better than the angels, but rather born. By this therefore, 611Cthat he says "made," we are compelled here to understand of Christ according to his humanity, namely that he was made better than the angels. But to this seems contrary what is found in the Psalm: Thou hast lessened him below the angels (Psalm. VIII). How, according to the same nature, can he be better, and less? Solution. He was made less than the angels by the mortality and passion of the flesh; and he is greater and better than the same by the fullness of grace, from which the angels themselves also receive.

QUESTION IX. I have this day begotten thee, etc. It is asked of what day he speaks. Solution. Augustine says that this can be understood of that day on which Christ was born according to the flesh. Yet it can be understood more divinely of his eternal generation: whence he says "I begot," 611Dlest it be understood as new; for "today" is said of a past begetting; and thus it is intimated to be eternal, in which nothing is past, as though it had ceased to be, nor future, as though it were not yet.

QUESTION X. But again it can be asked how this can be expounded of the temporal generation of Christ, since God the Father did not beget Christ according to human nature? For as Christ has no mother according to his Deity, so neither a father according to his humanity. Since therefore he is not his father according to this nature, how can it be said that he begot him according to it? Solution. To beget does not always denote a natural generation, but sometimes a gratuitous one, as to thee: Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth (Jac. I). Because, therefore, the temporal generation of Christ 612Awas the work of the whole Trinity, it can not unfittingly be said that the Father begot him even according to his humanity. But someone will say: Therefore Christ is a son of grace, and so adoptive? Solution. It is not true: by grace indeed that man was made a son, not of grace, but of nature.

QUESTION XI. And again he says: Therefore to him for a father, and he himself shall be to me for a son, etc. It is asked concerning this authority how it pertains to Christ, since neither the things preceding nor the things following that place, whence this authority is taken, seem to admit this. For in the book of Kings God the Father is brought in speaking to David: Thou shalt not build me a house, because thou art a man of blood; but thy son, who shall reign after thee: 612Bwho if he shall have done wickedly, I will correct him with the rod of men, and in the blows [stripes] of the sons of men, and I will establish his kingdom for ever and ever, and I will be to him for a father, and he himself shall be to me for a son (II Reg. VII), etc. All these things can be fitted neither to Solomon nor to Christ. Solution. In divine Scripture often in the same series certain things are set down which refer to the history alone; certain things to the mystical sense alone; certain things also which can be taken both ways, as in the aforesaid; certain things refer to Solomon, certain to Christ.

QUESTION XII. Likewise it happens in many others. For if anyone, following the history, considering the things preceding and following, where it is written: Behold a virgin shall conceive, and shall bear a son (Isa. VII): it will seem to him 612Crather that this authority refers to that young woman of Isaiah than to the Virgin, since there are there certain things which can in no way agree with the mother of our Emmanuel, which pertain to the history alone, although a certain mode of speech and property of relation sufficiently indicate that all things refer to the same person: Thy son, he says, who shall reign after thee, etc. Solution. It is to be known that there are three kinds of relations: for one is personal, as Saul, who is also Paul; another general and simple, as the woman who condemned, saved; another vocal, as my hands, which made you, are fastened with nails.

QUESTION XIII. Likewise it is asked according to which 612Dnature the Father says: I will be to him for a father. For according to the human he is not father; according to the divine he was father from eternity; how then does he say: I will be father to him? Solution. Then a thing is said to be made, when it begins to be known; because therefore through the resurrection it was made plain to all the faithful, and in the future will be made plain even to the unbelieving, that he himself is Father, and that one Son, therefore he says: I will be to him for a father. Or thus: I will be to him, that is to the man assumed, for a father, and that man himself shall be to me for a son, yet not according to humanity, but according to divinity.

QUESTION XIV. And when again he bringeth in the first-begotten, etc. It is asked how the Apostle calls "entrance" that coming which the Lord himself calls "going forth," saying: I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world (Joan. XVI), calling it entrance 613Awhen he says, And again when he bringeth in (Hebr. I). Solution. As regards the Father, who was within, the coming of the Lord is called a going forth; but as regards us, who were without, it is called an entrance, or conversely.

QUESTION XV. And let all the angels of God adore him, etc. Concerning the man assumed it is wont to be asked whether he is to be adored with that adoration which is called latria: for latria is exhibited to God alone, and not to a creature; but the man assumed is a creature, and thus it seems that latria is not to be exhibited to him. Solution. Latria is exhibited to that man not because he is man, but because he is God; concerning this it has already been said above; but that adoration which is exhibited to men or to angels is called dulia.

613BQUESTION XVI. Who maketh his angels spirits, etc. It is asked how he does this? Solution. "Spirit" is the name of a nature, as "man"; "angel" is the name of an office, as "soldier": therefore of spirits are made angels, as of men are made soldiers; not of angels are made spirits, just as neither of soldiers are made men.

QUESTION XVII. And his ministers a flame of fire, etc. It is asked how he makes a flame of fire, that is, the seraphim, his ministers, since the seraphim always stand by: how then is that order said to minister, if it always stands by? For they are not said to minister except from the fact that they minister. Solution. It can be said that the seraph receives immediately from God that which he reveals to an inferior, who is sent to us: whence also the inferior 613Cis reckoned by the name of the superior, whose office he bears, or rather from whom he receives the office. Whence Isaiah says: One of the seraphim flew to me, and touched my lips (Isa. VI). Or it can be said that, when some great things are to be done or announced, then those superiors are sent, whose office nevertheless is not to minister, but rather to stand by. Note that nothing is done which is not done either by God commanding or by God permitting: by which words it is intimated that not everything which is done is a work of God: for what he only permits, he does not do. This I say on account of those who say that whatever is, in that which it is, is from God. If this be so, the aforesaid distinction is null, that some things finnt by God commanding, others are done by God permitting.

613DQUESTION XVIII. Therefore he anointed thee, etc. The expositor says that Christ was anointed for this, that he might love justice. But did he not, from the moment he existed, love justice, nor was he anointed before he was full of love? how then is he said to be anointed for this, that he might love justice? Solution. By the oil of anointing is understood grace itself, and virtue: by "to love" he insinuates the very act proceeding from virtue. Causally therefore the anointing precedes the act of loving, and not in time. Or pursue another exposition.

QUESTION XIX. Therefore he anointed, that is, therefore because thou hast loved justice, he anointed thee. But did he not from his very cognition have the fullness of anointing? what anointing then did he receive as it were in reward, because he loved justice? Solution. By the oil of gladness, 614Aas it were anointed by the merit of love, according to certain men is understood the stole of the mature resurrection.

QUESTION XX. God, thy God, hath anointed thee, etc.— the other, that is the former, is the vocative case, as if he should say: O Son, God, thy God hath anointed thee. But what God has a God? what God is anointed? Solution. Christ is God, and has a God, not inasmuch as he is God, but inasmuch as he is man, and according to that he is anointed.

QUESTION XXI. They shall perish, etc. It is asked concerning which heavens he says that they are to perish. Solution. Concerning the airy heavens, as the expositor says, which perished through the flood, and are to perish by fire. Whence it is asked, if they already perished through the flood, how are they again to perish through 614Bfire? If they have already perished, have they not ceased to be? and if they have already ceased, how shall they again perish by fire? Solution. They perished through the flood, that is, they were changed for the worse; and those same are to perish by fire, that is, they are to be changed into a better state. But concerning the earth and the higher heavens there is no question but that they are to be changed for the better: whence Peter says: We look for new heavens and a new earth (II Pet. III). Concerning water and air it is doubted whether they are to be changed into a better state, like earth and heaven, because in the Apocalypse it is written: And the sea was now no more (Apoc. XXI). And here concerning the airy heavens it is written: They shall perish. Whence it seems to some that water and air will lose those properties from which these names belong to them, 614Cand with them will lose also the names, yet they will not be wholly annihilated; but neither water nor air will they any longer be called, these things being taken away and annihilated whence before they were so called.

QUESTION XXII. They are all ministering spirits, etc. It was said above that it is not the office of the superiors to minister, how then are they all ministering? Solution. It can be said that all spirits minister to us either immediately, as the inferiors; or through the mediation of others, as the superiors and the middle ones; or by "all" he gathers only those who are of the lowest order, who are properly called angels, whose office it especially is to minister, and therefore they alone are properly ministering.

QUESTION XXIII. What is man, that thou art mindful 614Dof him (Hebr. II), etc. It is asked how this is to be expounded. The solution is expounded in three ways. First thus: That by "man" is understood the old man, by "the son of man" the new man is understood. Secondly thus: That by "man" is understood any good man, by "the son of man" Christ. Thirdly thus: That by "man" and "the son of man" the same is understood, namely Christ.

QUESTION XXIV. Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, etc. Above he said that he was made better than the angels: here he says that he was made less than they: and we have said in what way both are true. But here it is asked whether it is to be granted absolutely that Christ is less than the angels. Which certain men wish thus to prove: Christ is all that he was made, but 615Ahe was made less: therefore he is less than the angels. Solution. It is not to be said absolutely that he is less than the angels; but that "a little less" he was made less, is thus understood, that is, according to something he was made less, namely according to the infirmity of the flesh and the passion of death, as the authority says: nor is it consequent that, if he is less according to something, he is therefore absolutely less.

QUESTION XXV. Thou hast subjected all things under his feet (Psal. VIII). "All" sometimes gathers the whole, as all the angels of heaven are just. Sometimes by determination it is reduced to a part, as all mine are thine (Joan. XVII), for this God the Father says to the elder son, that is to the Jewish people: therefore by "all" here it behooves to understand, not those things which belong to God according to 615Bnature, but only those which are necessary for salvation. Sometimes also "all" has the force of a negation, as all things which I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you (Joan. XV), that is, none except those which I have heard. Whence it can be asked how this is to be taken when it is said, thou hast subjected all things. Solution. Some say that it is reduced to a part, and by "all" they understand only angels and men. But if the more excellent things are subjected to Christ, how not the lesser? Since Ambrose says that just as nothing is excepted from the work of God, so neither from the power of Christ. And Augustine says: No creature will be not subject, to whom the chief angels are subjected. And the Apostle himself shows that nothing is excepted, when he subjoins: For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing not subject to him.

615CQUESTION XXVI. But now we see not yet all things subject to him, etc. The prophet says, thou hast subjected all things to him: which the Apostle, expounding, subjoined, he left nothing not subject to him; how then does he say here: We see not yet all things subject to him? Solution. David, after his manner, uses the past for the future out of certitude, saying: Thou hast subjected all things to him. The Apostle, understanding this, said above that the world was to be subjected to him: and here he says: We see not yet all things subject to him; as if he should say: already in part the prophecy is fulfilled, in part still to be fulfilled. But someone will say: do not all things serve the divine dispensation, whose will nothing can resist? and thus already, willing or unwilling, all things are subjected to him. How then does the Apostle say, We see not yet all things subject to him? Solution. Subjection 615Dis one kind general, another special. Likewise one hidden, another necessary, another voluntary. According to the general, and the hidden, and the necessary, all things are already subject to God; according to the voluntary, not yet are all things subject which shall be subjected. Not yet does every tongue of things heavenly, earthly and infernal confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of the Father (Philipp. II). Not yet are all enemies made the footstool of his feet (Psal. CIX). All which indeed shall wholly come to pass in the future; therefore the Apostle says: We see not yet all things, namely voluntarily, or openly, subject to him. Note that only God is greater than the human mind, not any of the angels. Angels indeed can be greater divine ones than men as regards the body and the mind 616Aweighed down by the corruption of the body (Sap. IX): but not as regards the very purity of the mind, in which it was assumed by the Word.

QUESTION XXVII. That by the grace of God he might taste death for all, etc. The death of Christ did not profit all; how then did he taste death for all? Solution. The whole is here reduced to a part: namely, for all the predestined he tasted death. Or it is therefore said that he tasted death for all, because, as far as in him lies, the death of Christ suffices for all.

QUESTION XXVIII. It became him for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, etc. It is asked how it became God the Father to perfect the author of the salvation of the faithful through the passion of death. Wherein consists this 616Bfittingness, since it rather seems unfitting that the Lord of glory should die? Solution. If Christ did not die, man would perish: and if this were so, God would not be glorified by the whole; and this would be unfitting, since all things were made for God to be glorified. Likewise, if Christ did not die, man would not be saved, and thus the divine predestination would not be fulfilled, and this would be unfitting, that it should be made void. Nor was it unfitting that the author of salvation should die for us, since he is our neighbor, and brother, and it befits a neighbor to provide for the advantage of his neighbors as much as he can; whence it follows:

QUESTION XXIX. For which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren, etc. It is asked whether Christ is therefore called our brother, because he was made a partaker of our nature, 616Ctaking the form of a servant (Philipp. II). But since the nature assumed by God is common to good and bad, it seems that Christ is not only the brother of the faithful but also of the unfaithful. Solution. Christ is not called our brother only because he shares in our nature, but also because we have received of the fullness of his grace. Therefore, for anyone to be called a brother of Christ, it behooves that he be joined to him by nature and by grace.

QUESTION XXX. And he himself, namely Christ, in like manner partook of the same, namely of the children, or of flesh and blood. But it is asked how Christ partook of the children? Solution. That is, he was made a child consisting of soul and flesh, as the expositor says. Or he partook of flesh and blood, that is, he was made 616Dman, and this "in like manner," that is, passible and mortal.

QUESTION XXXI. That he might destroy him who had the empire of death. Since death is a punishment justly inflicted by God, and thus is not unfittingly said to be from God, it is asked how the devil is said to be the author of death. For the same thing does not seem able to be from God and from the devil. Solution. Because death happened from sin, which the devil persuaded, therefore he has the empire of death, or is said to have it; because he was the cause of death, therefore he was called its author: whence it is said that God does not make death, that is, its cause has not its being from God. Note that this is the justice by which we were redeemed. For because the devil shed the blood of one who was not a debtor, 617Ahe was commanded to give back the debtors; and because he shed the blood of the innocent, in whom he found nothing, he was commanded to withdraw from the guilty, whom by a certain right he seemed to possess.

QUESTION XXXII. The expositor says that unless it were a man who conquered the devil, not justly, but by violence would man be taken from him. But had not the devil done injury to God, who first fraudulently deceived the servant, and afterward violently possessed him? What injustice then would God do, if by the sole word of his power he should snatch man from the hand of the most unjust invader? Solution. All the works of God are just, but in some there is also manifest power, and justice lies hidden; in some also hidden power lies, and justice is manifest. If therefore Christ in our liberation had used 617Bmanifest power and hidden justice, it might seem to some less discerning that man was taken from the devil not justly, but by violence: but that all iniquity might stop its mouth (Psal. CVI), our Lord used in our redemption manifest justice and hidden power.

QUESTION XXXIII. That he might deliver them, who through the fear of death, etc. It is asked to whose servitude they were subject, whom the Lord delivered? Solution. The devil, before the coming of Christ, obtained the effect of his wickedness through death: by the fear of which he cast down those whom in no other way he could cast down. For they gave all things for their life. Whence in Job it is read: Skin for skin; all that a man hath he will give for his life (Job I). And so, conquered by the fear of death, they yielded, and succumbed to temptation, 617Cuntil Christ came, who by dying and rising took away the fear of death from their midst. Whence the saints deride death, and desire to be dissolved, and to be with Christ (Philipp. I). Or it can be understood of the fear of punishment, whereby the Jews served under the law, whom Christ, the law being emptied, through grace liberated from the burden of the law and from servile fear.

QUESTION XXXIV. For nowhere doth he take hold of the angels, etc. It is asked whether God could have assumed the angelic nature into the unity of the person as he did the human? Solution. It seems to us that he could, but would not; wherein the dignity of our race is understood: for to man, who had received less than the angels in his creation, more was conferred in his glorification through 617Dgrace. For human nature does not adore the angelic nature above it, but rather conversely.

QUESTION XXXV. Wherefore he ought in all things to be made like unto his brethren. Was he not by grace alone made like unto his brethren in this, that he was born man, that he was reared, suffered, died? how then does the Apostle say that this "ought" to be, since this is not a debt, but a gratuitous gift of God? Solution. He does not say simply "ought," but added, that he might be merciful (Hebr. II): for by dying he could not have mercy on us, unless he first became passible and mortal. Or he therefore says "ought," that is, it was fitting for him to be made like unto his brethren. For by this, that he bore our infirmities and death for us, he provoked us to humility, and kindled charity in us.

618AQUESTION XXXVI. For in that he himself hath suffered and been tempted, he is able, etc. Was he not before his passion, nay before his incarnation, able to help the tempted? for his power was not augmented through the passion; what then is it, "in that he himself hath suffered, he is able to help those who are tempted"? Solution. After the passion he well knows even by experience what that temptation is, and the tribulation of those who suffer: whence with much alacrity he stretches out his hand to compassionate; therefore he is said to be able to do these things, and perfectly to know them. For he knows who they are who suffer for him, he knows when and how and to whom he ought to stretch out his hand. Whence the Prophet: The Lord is become a refuge for the poor in his opportunities, in tribulation (Psal. IX).

618BQUESTION XXXVII. By so much hath he greater honor than the house who framed it (Hebr. III), etc. Does not often he who dispenses in the house have greater glory in it than he who framed it? how then does the Apostle say: By so much greater, etc. Solution. This is to be understood of the spiritual house, as if he should say: Christ as Lord and Creator is greater than Moses the servant and minister.

QUESTION XXXVIII. According to the day of temptation, etc. It is asked by whom temptation is made. Solution. Man tempts, that he may know what he is ignorant of, according to which acceptation temptation is a certain soothing foretaste of the mind, running before, for the recognizing of something which before was unknown. God tempts, that he may prove through affliction and tribulation, that he may crown the proved. 618CThe devil tempts, that he may cast someone down into sin: whence it is said: And lead us not into temptation (Matth. VI), that is, suffer us not to be cast down into sin. The flesh tempts, when we feel its inordinate motions. The world tempts, when it provokes us through vanity to the love of itself.

QUESTION XXXIX. Wherefore I was offended, etc. Another translation has "I was near." How then, if offended, was he near; and if near, how offended? and if both readings cannot stand, which rather is to be held? Solution. He was near by applying the scourges of correction; because it is the part of a neighbor to correct his neighbor. He was offended and angry, because even through the scourges they would not repent. Or toward the good for forty 618Dyears he can be understood angry in this; because for so long a time he did not bring them into the land of promise: this opinion nevertheless the following text does not seem to approve. But toward the wicked he can be understood near for forty years in this, that for so long a time he bore with them, nor wholly destroyed them.

QUESTION XL. If they shall enter into my rest. It is asked by what figure this is said. Solution. It is the figure which is called aposiopesis, and the sense is: If this shall be, anything impossible will be, or let me no longer be believed in anything. Note that there are four Sabbaths, or rests. The first rest is that of God, of which it is written in Genesis: And God rested on the seventh day (Gen. II); the second rest is the land of promise; the third, the quiet of the mind; the fourth is the eternal. The first and 619Afourth are of God; the second and third of man. The first is a figure of the fourth, the second of the third.

QUESTION XLI. As I swore in my wrath, etc. It is asked what here is called the wrath of God: for it is agreed that such a passion does not fall upon God. Solution. He calls the wrath of God the immovable sentence of eternal justice, by the figure which is called anthropopathos: which occurs whenever those things which, said of men, signify passion, are figuratively attributed to God. God therefore swears in wrath, when he firmly determines to punish for the obstinacy of sin. Note that there are four kinds of symbols, that is of signs, that is of those things which are figuratively said of God. For some symbols are like, and are taken from corporeal things, as fire, light, sun and others of this kind. Others are like and taken from incorporeal things, 619Bas reason, intellect, spirit and the like. Others are unlike and taken from corporeal things, as lion, bear, worm and such like. Others are unlike, and taken from incorporeal things, as wrath, fury, grief, repentance and the like.

QUESTION XLII. That none of you be hardened by the fallacy of sin, etc. It is asked what he calls the fallacy of sin. Solution. The fallacy of sin is when one presumes upon the grace of God: and secure in this confidence lies in sins. Or when one promises that in the coming year he will amend, that in the present he may sin more securely, which is done at the instigation of the devil. There can also be a threefold fallacy noted here, so that the first is when we consent to a depraved motion; the second, when we break forth into an evil work; the third, when in the habit of sin 619Cwe take delight.

QUESTION XLIII. But with whom was he offended for forty years, etc. It is asked how this is to be understood. Solution. The number forty indicates the entirety of years: therefore he is said to be offended with them for those forty years, because he is angry with sinners even to the end of their life.

QUESTION XLIV. And indeed the works from the foundation of the world (Hebr. IV), etc. It is asked where mention is made of that eternal rest, which is signified by the land of promise: for the rest of the Sabbath is there treated of: And God rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had done. But of the rest of the land of Palestine mention seems to be made there, where it is said: If they shall enter into my rest 619D. Solution. Where the rest of the Sabbath, or the rest of the land of Palestine according to the letter, is treated of, there also the true rest is treated of anagogically, which is signified by those two.

QUESTION XLV. God rested on the seventh day, etc. Scripture says that in six days God made all his works, so that he made nothing new afterward; but does he not daily create new souls? how then does he make nothing new? Solution. God makes nothing except from matter made in the first condition, as any corporeal thing: or after the likeness of things then already made, as incorporeal spirits, namely human souls.

QUESTION XLVI. Again he determineth a certain day, To-day, etc. It is asked how, by that which the Apostle here 620Abrings in, he compels the Jews to understand a rest other than the other, which was that of the land of promise, saying: To-day if you shall hear his voice, etc. Solution. Those to whom he wrote had faith, and believed David to be a prophet: according to which it was necessary to understand another day, and another rest than that rest of the land of promise, from the words of the prophet there set down: and thus the proof of the Apostle proceeds:

QUESTION XLVII. For the word is living, etc. The expositor says that the Son of God sees how reason and sensuality agree in their differences: but do they not differ in their differences? how then do they agree in their differences? can any things agree and differ in the same? Solution. He does not say that in the differences by which reason differs from sensuality, 620Bor conversely, these two agree, but that reason has differences by which it is distinguished from itself, while it gazes upon God, thinking of the divine usia, or lower, considering the heavenly things, it contemplates the natures of invisible spirits, or on earth it deals with the things of the world rightly to be handled. Likewise sensuality too has differences by which it is divided from itself, while, more given to the lowest things, it is lower, or, called back from them, it is worthier. So then the Son of God sees how the superior difference of sensuality, by consenting, agrees with the differences of reason; or the inferior difference of reason, pressed and captive, sometimes consents to the inferior difference of sensuality. Note that "soul" is put either for sensuality, or for carnal sins, or for carnal 620Cthoughts: so also "spirit" for reason, or for spiritual sins, or for good thoughts. When it is said that the word of God reaches even to the division of the soul and the spirit (Hebr. IV), whence thou wilt find a threefold exposition in the gloss on account of the threefold acceptation of soul and spirit.

QUESTION XLVIII. Tempted in all things for the likeness, without sin. In that he was tempted, he knows how to compassionate. In that he is without sin, he is able to deliver. The expositor says that it is impossible for a man to know afflictions, unless he has experienced them. But do not many from sight alone know the afflictions of others, which they have nowhere suffered: so much even that they compassionate them? how then is it true, it is impossible for a man, etc.? Solution. He who has not experienced does not know so perfectly 620Das he who knows by experiment: which manner of knowing the Apostle notes, saying: We have not a high priest who [cannot compassionate, that is, has known.

QUESTION XLIX. Neither doth any man take the honor to himself (Hebr. V), etc. Do not many very great men in this time thrust themselves forward: and, not called, sometimes even by violence take the honor to themselves? how then is it true: Neither doth any man take the honor to himself? Solution. No one acting piously and religiously thrusts himself forward. Neither did Christ glorify himself, etc., since this glorification of the Father was made concerning the Son according to the human nature.

QUESTION L. It is asked how this authority: 621AThis day have I begotten thee, which according to Augustine is expounded of the eternal generation, is in this place brought in by the Apostle: how does the Father, saying, This day have I begotten thee, testify that Christ, according as he is man, is his Son, and the redeemer of the world? Solution. Jerome says that this authority is thus understood of the human generation of Christ: This day, that is in the time of grace and light, have I begotten thee, that is, I have incarnated thee: or "I have begotten," that is, I have shown thee to be begotten: according to which this authority is well brought in.

QUESTION LI. According to the order of Melchisedech, etc. The expositor says that Melchisedech was not temporal: but was he not only a man, and thus temporal, because every man is temporal? Solution. It is therefore said that he is not temporal: because Scripture 621Bwas silent as to the beginning and end of his life, in figure of Christ, who lacks beginning and end. Or he can be said a priest not temporal on account of his priesthood, which remains in Christ for ever.

QUESTION LII. He was heard for his reverence, etc. It is asked what it is that Christ was heard for his reverence. Was not Stephen likewise heard for his reverence, and the other saints? What then is great concerning Christ if he was heard for his reverence? Solution. It is no wonder if certain things are said of Christ common to the martyrs, since certain things also common to the legal priests are here set down. Yet it can be said that Stephen was heard for the reverence of Christ rather than for his own: for Christ entered by himself, others through him: 621Cwhence also of his fullness we all have received (Joan. I). And thus something special is said of Christ when it is read that he was heard for his reverence: which is noted in this, that without sin and by charity alone he died and suffered.

QUESTION LIII. He learned obedience by the things which he suffered, etc. We learn those things which we do not know: since therefore Christ knew all things as God, how did he learn what he was not ignorant of? Solution. This question has already been sufficiently discussed above. For it was said that cognition is twofold, one of comprehension, the other of experience: that which is of comprehension he had from eternity, but the other he learned in time.

QUESTION LIV. Which are the elements of the beginning of the words of God, etc. It is asked what is the difference between these 621Dthree: elements, beginning, word of God? Solution. He calls the word of God the evangelical doctrine; the beginning, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer: the elements are the matter which the Creed contains, as the nativity, the passion, and the other articles of faith.

QUESTION LV. Every one that is a partaker of milk, etc. The expositor says: He who does not grasp, The Word was made flesh (Joan. I): how will he grasp, In the beginning was the Word (ibid.)? It is asked therefore how it is lighter to understand, The Word was made flesh, than that, In the beginning was the Word, since that concerning the incarnation of the Word is against human reason: but the former are higher, and concerning the Trinity of persons, and the unity of essence, investigated by reason, as from the prophets 622Ait appears? Solution: those things concerning the incarnation are therefore said lighter, because they were visibly exhibited: but these more difficult, because comprehended by the intellect alone of few.

QUESTION LVI. Likewise it is asked how those to whom the Apostle here speaks needed to be taught what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God. Were they not faithful? how were they ignorant of the nativity, the passion, and the other articles of faith: since without these no one is faithful? Solution. They knew these things, but not fully.

QUESTION LVII. Wherefore, leaving the word (Hebr. VI), etc. Since the word of beginning seems necessary to them, how does he say, leaving the word of beginning? Solution. The sense is: 622Byou ought not always to tarry in those things which pertain to the beginning, but to tend to perfection.

QUESTION LVIII. Not again laying the foundation, etc. This seems contrary to the aforesaid. For if they still needed the doctrine of the elements, the foundation was necessary to them. Solution. The glosses suffice for this question, expounding how "not again" is to be understood.

QUESTION LIX. From dead works, etc. He calls dead works either mortal sins, or good works which have been mortified by an ensuing evil: it is asked therefore how it is true, that no good is unrewarded, as no evil unpunished. Solution. Such goods are therefore called dead, because they 622Cdo not profit unto eternal life: and yet in this they shall be rewarded, because they who did them shall be less punished in the future. Or perhaps a temporal advantage was given for them. Likewise such goods are called dead, because through penance they can revive according to certain men: not that they be any more rewarded for them: but because from goods before done they will more easily attain grace. But it seems to us that, the sin being blotted out by penance, through which they were mortified, they are, as before, before they were mortified, worthy of eternal life.

QUESTION LX. Of baptisms, etc. It is asked how he here says in the plural "of baptisms," since elsewhere he says: One Lord, one faith, one baptism (Ephes. IV), etc. If one, how many? Solution. 622DAs faith is said to be one not in number, but in kind, as the authority teaches, so baptism can be said to be one not in number, but in kind, because it is one form: nor can it be repeated: and because there is there one operation of the three persons, many are spoken of as regards the several washings. Or he therefore says "baptisms" in the plural, because there is baptism in power, in blood: and not for this reason, that the sacrament of baptism is celebrated except in water: but because the shedding of blood, faith, and penance supply the place of baptism: there only where the moment of necessity, not contempt of religion, excludes the sacrament of baptism. To which solution it is thus objected: Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven (Joan. III). 623AAccording to this authority it seems that no one is worthy of salvation without the reception of this sacrament. Solution. The doctors thus expound the aforesaid words of the Lord, Unless a man be born again of water, etc., that is, unless a man be born again by that spirit and regeneration by which are reborn those who are reborn of water, and by the Holy Spirit he can be saved. But by this spirit men are reborn in diverse ways. Some are reborn through penance, others through the shedding of blood, others through baptism. Note that the foundation of the Christian religion is divided into six, which are here set down by the apostles, namely penance, faith, baptism, imposition of hands, resurrection, future judgment: which pertain to the instruction of neophytes.

623BQUESTION LXI. It is impossible for those who were once illuminated, etc. Here the Apostle seems to deny penance to those gravely fallen, as in the following, where he says: To those who sin voluntarily there is now left no sacrifice for sin. Solution. It seems to us that in both places he describes the sin against the Holy Spirit, into whose pit whoever once falls, it is impossible that he attain penance or salvation. But the doctors say that this "impossible," etc., does not deny all renovation, but only the repetition of baptism. Or it can be understood of the future state: to which opinion certain glosses are of service.

QUESTION LXII. The expositor says that baptism avails even against subsequent sins. But it is asked how sins which are not yet done are already 623Cforgiven. Solution. Some say that baptism is therefore said to avail against subsequent sins, because through the grace conferred in baptism future sins are avoided. But according to this solution what is this, which in the same gloss follows, "if penance be done concerning them"? It seems to us to be thus understood, that baptism avails against subsequent sins: because by the virtue of baptism they can be blotted out with less satisfaction: so that if it happen that a faithful man and an unfaithful commit the same sin, the penance which suffices for the reborn unto salvation, the same does not suffice for the unfaithful or not yet reborn. This I say without prejudice to a better opinion.

QUESTION LXIII. The Lord entered in by himself, etc. Since the Lord says in the Gospel: Let your speech 623Dbe: Yea, yea; No, no: and that which over and above is, is of evil (Matth. V), it is asked how the Lord then swore to Abraham. Would not Abraham believe, or would he believe more slowly, God, if he promised without an oath? Solution. Not on account of Abraham did the Lord swear, since without an oath he firmly believed him: but on account of those who were to come after him, who would either not at all believe, or would more slowly believe, the promise made to Abraham, unless it were confirmed by an oath, and thus that oath was not from the evil of Abraham, but of those who were to come.

QUESTION LXIV. If it be asked: Why did the Lord swear by himself? Solution. Because men are wont to swear by one greater than themselves, but God had not 624Aa greater: whence it is agreed that they sin who swear by something inferior. For that by which they swear they in a manner constitute above themselves.

QUESTION LXV. And an oath for confirmation is the end of all their controversy. What then shall we say of the judgment of fire, or of water, or of others of this kind, which the Church seems to receive? Is not in those also the end of controversy? Solution. These are not judgments of the Church: whence also the guilty are many times thereby absolved, and the not-guilty are sometimes condemned: which would by no means happen, if mother Church held these. Whence in certain places she rather tolerates these than commends them. But someone will say: The same judgment ought to be made concerning an oath. This we grant. For the Church did not institute that, just as neither the aforesaid.

624BQUESTION LXVI. According to the order of Melchisedech (Hebr. VII), etc. It is asked how? Solution. Christ is said to be a high priest according to the order of Melchisedech in many ways. Both because that man was king and priest alone, so is Christ; both because he was instituted not with visible oil, as Moses, but was anointed with the oil of gladness and the purity of faith; nor did he immolate animals, but in bread and wine offered dedicated the sacrifice of Christ; so also Christ was anointed by the Father with the Holy Spirit; who offered himself on the altar of the cross to God the Father; and because he gave his true body and blood to his disciples at the supper, and because his priesthood remains for ever according to rite and dignity.

QUESTION LXVII. It is asked what that oblation of Melchisedech in bread and wine profited those who received it? Solution. 624CSome say that it profited those who received with faith as much as now the body of Christ profits. Which does not seem to us to be true: for the sacraments of the natural law, or of the written law, did not profit, nor could profit, as much as the sacraments of grace.

QUESTION LXVIII. That which is less is blessed without any contradiction by the better. Is not often a holy man blessed by one who is of less sanctity: as when a monk is blessed by some secular priest, how then is it true, that which is less is blessed by the greater? Solution. Someone can be less than another in excellence of merits, and greater than the same in dignity: but here it is treated of the majority and minority which consists according to dignity. That therefore which 624Dis less in dignity is blessed by that which is greater in excellence of dignity. Nor is it here treated of any blessing whatever, but only of that which belongs to the consecrated.

QUESTION LXIX. Through Abraham, even Levi, who received tithes, was tithed, etc. Augustine says that just as, Adam sinning, those who were in his loins sinned; so, Abraham giving tithes, those who were in his loins were tithed. But did Christ either sin, Adam sinning; or was he tithed, Abraham giving tithes, since he was in the loins of both, according to the flesh? Since therefore Levi and Christ were alike in the loins of Abraham, how was Levi tithed, and not Christ? Or 625Aif Christ was tithed like Levi, how does the Apostle prove the priesthood of Christ to be greater than the levitical priesthood: by this, that the levitical order in Levi was tithed in Abraham? Solution. There were some, and perhaps still are, saying that the flesh of Christ from Adam even to the Virgin was kept entire and incorrupt, who are not to be heard. Levi therefore was tithed, and not Christ, although both were there, because Levi contracted thence that whereby he lay subject to tithing, that is, fault. But Christ contracted nothing thence whereby he might be subject to tithing, whose flesh contracted thence not a wound, but the medicament of a wound. To which solution it is thus objected: All the flesh which was in Isaac descended from Abraham according to the common law, namely through concupiscence; 625Bbut the flesh of Christ was in Isaac: therefore the flesh of Christ descended through concupiscence from Abraham. Solution. It is not to be granted absolutely that the flesh of Christ so descended thence through concupiscence: for this would be, that the flesh of Christ was made through concupiscence; yet it can be granted by division: a certain flesh, which afterward was Christ's, descended thence according to the common law, which from the first man even to Mary was under original sin.

QUESTION LXX. The priesthood being translated, it is necessary that a translation also be made of the law. It can be asked how, upon the translation of the priesthood, the translation of the law necessarily follows. Solution. Because both were given at once by the same one under 625Cthe same promise: what is asserted of the one is necessarily understood also of the other. Or therefore, the priesthood being translated, the law is necessarily translated; because the translation of the priesthood is made for this, that by its ministry no one was justified, and thus on account of its insufficiency and infirmity it was translated; but the law is equally insufficient and infirm. Whence the Apostle: The law brought nothing to perfection (Hebr. ). By the same necessity therefore is it translated. Because neither therefore could consummate, of both is made a translation: which was figured in the priest and levite, the languishing man, who fell among robbers, passing by and not conferring the mercy of healing (Luc. X).

QUESTION LXXI. For it is manifest that our Lord sprang 625Dout of Juda. It is asked therefore whether his mother also? Solution. Call back to memory that question which we set down above upon the Epistle to Timothy, which the words of Origen make, saying that Mary was only of the tribe of Levi, and on account of Joseph only was the Lord said to be of the tribe of Juda. But, as I said, two tribes were intermingled, the royal and the sacerdotal, and the Virgin was on the father's side, of her father, of the tribe of Juda, and on the mother's side of the tribe of Levi.

QUESTION LXXII. The law brought nothing to perfection, etc. Were not certain men perfect in the time of the law, as David, and many others; and had they not that justice, since they were just, from obedience to the divine law? how then were they not just from the law? Solution. The just of that time had justice not from the law, but from faith in him who was to come: 626Afor the law showed sins, it did not take them away.

QUESTION LXXIII. To make intercession for us, etc. It is asked how Christ makes intercession for us? Solution. The expositor says that it is by the representation of himself, which is thus to be understood, that the merit of his passion, which he exhibited in his humanity, reconciles us believers to the Father.

QUESTION LXXIV. Who hath not daily necessity (Hebr. VIII). It is asked concerning the sacrifices of the law what utility they conferred: perhaps the remission of sins? Solution. For certain sins the sinners were forbidden entrance, and through the sacrifices they were so reconciled that it was permitted them to enter into the temple: but not through such remission were they made 626Bworthy of eternal life.

QUESTION LXXV. If then he were upon earth, he would not be a priest, etc. It is asked how these things are to be understood. Solution. The text of this chapter is less coherent, and cut off: and therefore brings in obscurity. Whence it is expounded in five ways, as is had in the glosses. Note that in every sacrifice four things are considered: namely, to whom it is offered, and by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered. The same one mediator of both, reconciling us to God through the sacrifice of peace, would remain one with him to whom he offered, would make one in himself those for whom he offered; he himself would be one who offered and what he offered.

QUESTION LXXVI. Who serve the exemplar and shadow, 626Cetc. It is asked what is here called "exemplar." Solution. The truth shown on the mount to Moses is called the exemplar of the figures made according to it. Likewise the figures themselves are called the exemplar of the truth, which was afterward fulfilled: and thus the figures themselves, in a different respect, can be called both example and exemplar. "Exemplar" onim is properly said that to whose likeness something is made; "example," that which is drawn from it.

QUESTION LXXVII. For if that former had been without fault, etc. Is not the law good, holy and given by God? how then is it not without fault? Solution. For that reason the Old Testament is said not to be without fault, for which the law is said to work wrath, namely, because it does not justify, and because it commands what cannot be done without grace.

626DQUESTION LXXVIII. It is asked why we do not worship God with that rite with which the Hebrew fathers worshiped him? Solution. Because God commanded us another thing through the fathers of the New Testament: nor are these things which we observe against the Old Testament, but foretold and pre-announced in it.

QUESTION LXXIX. Likewise, why do we hold the authority of that testament? Solution. Lest we extinguish the prophets, and take away the testimony of truth from our midst. When therefore something is read which is not observed by us, we must only ask what it signifies, not reprehend it; because by the very fact that it is now not observed, it is proved not condemned, but fulfilled.

QUESTION LXXX. Likewise it is asked whence that is called the Old Testament, this the New, since the law is fulfilled 627Athrough the New Testament? Solution. The Old Testament is called "old" for the old harm, which is not healed through the letter commanding and threatening. But this is called "new" on account of the newness of spirit, which heals a man from the vice of oldness. Note diligently what is the difference between the two testaments: that old, this new. There the letter, which alone kills, here the spirit giving life. That is written on tables of stone, this on minds and hearts. That promises earthly things, this heavenly. That has sacraments signifying salvation, not conferring it; this has sacraments conferring salvation. Likewise note that "testament" is said both of the promise itself, temporal or eternal, and of the writing containing the promise itself. The Old Testament therefore contains the promise 627Bpertaining to the old man. But the New Testament, which contains the promise of the eternal inheritance which belongs to the new man.

QUESTION LXXXI. For if the ashes vitulaeaspersus sanctify the defiled (Hebr. IX), etc. It is asked what he calls the defilement, from which the sprinkled ashes of a heifer sanctify? Solution. He so calls the touch of the dead; or leprosy, from which those ashes cleanse, that is, from the punishment which according to the law was due to such uncleanness: by which touch is signified the consent of sin.

QUESTION LXXXII. And as it is appointed unto men once to die. The expositor says that Christ died by the same necessity and right of nature by which necessity, and in fact, other men die. 627CWhence it is asked whether Christ died by necessity, and whether he had the necessity of dying? Which seems manifest according to the aforesaid authority. But if by necessity, how did he die by will alone, as it is written: He was offered because he willed it? (Isa. LIII.) Solution. Some say that among the other penalties which the Lord took up with our nature without fault, he took up also this penalty, namely the necessity of dying, voluntarily: which does not exclude the will, nor is excluded by it. Nor yet is it to be understood but that Christ could by the power of divinity lay aside this penalty without the dissolution of soul and body, and clothe over the nature assumed with the stole of immortality; but if he conferred no more 627Dthan was conferred on it before death, he would necessarily die.

QUESTION LXXXIII. To them that expect him unto salvation, etc. Upon this place the expositor says that Christ died not by necessity, but by will for the sin of those expecting him unto salvation: but above it was said that he died by necessity: which seems to be contrary. Solution. What he says here, understand thus. Christ died not by necessity, that is, in him there was no sin for which it was necessary that he die: whence, as it were expounding what he had said, he subjoins: but he died for their sin, namely of those who expected him unto salvation.

QUESTION LXXXIV. Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered (Hebr. X), etc. The legal victims, as the Apostle says, if 628Athey made perfect would cease to be offered: whence it is asked why the salutary victim of the New Testament, since it perfects, and consummates the sanctified, is more often offered, and does not cease to be offered? Solution. Once indeed it was offered through the passion of death on the altar of the cross in human form; nor is it again so offered through death, but yet in the sacrament it is more often offered, not by reason of its own infirmity, but rather of ours, who daily sin: and especially for the remembrance of the death of Christ, that his love may be more deeply fixed in our hearts through this, that we are mindful of so great a benefit.

QUESTION LXXXV. But a body thou hast fitted to me, etc. It is asked in what he fitted the body of Christ? Solution. This fitness consists in two things, namely in cleanness and in mortality: for unless it were clean, through 628Bit the unclean could not be redeemed, unless it were mortal it could not be immolated; it is necessary therefore that the body of the Lord be clean through immunity from sin, and mortal.

QUESTION LXXXVI. Not forsaking your assembly. It is asked whether the Apostle here condemns what the Lord permits, saying: If they shall persecute you in one city, flee into another (Matth. X), of which thing he himself also gave an example by fleeing into Egypt. And Paul likewise is found many times to have done the same: what is it then that here he blames those who forsake the assembly? Solution. The Apostle in this place blames those who, as it were for the cause of their own sanctity, cannot dwell among other infirm or imperfect ones: and therefore by forsaking the assembly they rend unity, and thus 628Csin unto death. When some are specially sought by persecutors, then it is lawful to decline the rage of the persecutors, if it can be done without detriment to the assembly.

QUESTION LXXXVII. To those who sin voluntarily, etc. It is asked who are those who sin voluntarily, to whom there is left no sacrifice for sin. Solution. The gloss says that he calls those who sin voluntarily those remaining in sin out of the will of sinning: to whom Christ, who is the sacrifice for sin, does not profit, who profits only the penitent.

QUESTION LXXXVIII. But again it is asked why the Apostle says after having received the knowledge of the truth, since Christ does not profit those remaining in the will 628Dof sinning even before the knowledge of the truth? Perhaps someone will say that such can be profited through the grace of baptism, so that no punishment even of satisfaction is enjoined, whereas after the grace of regeneration he cannot be renewed even through penance. Saying this we do not exclude penance, as certain men wish, taking occasion from these words of the Apostle: to those who sin voluntarily, etc. But to certain men it seems that he calls those "sinning voluntarily" who, knowingly assailing the truth out of envy, or hatred, or some such cause, sin against the Holy Spirit, and therefore sin irremissibly; because this sin has remission neither in the present nor in the future, as the Lord says. Which also seems to be intimated above, where the Apostle says: It is impossible for those who were once illuminated 629A(Matth. XII), etc. And subsequently in this place he supposes: Who hath trodden underfoot the Son of God, and hath esteemed the blood of the testament polluted, and hath offered an affront to the spirit of grace. By which words the sin against the Holy Spirit seems manifestly to be signified.

QUESTION LXXXIX. It is asked why baptism cannot be repeated: whose repetition is here denied by the Apostle, according to certain men? Solution. Because baptism at once takes away both fault and punishment. Whence if it were repeated, not only would it become cheap, but would even invite to sin. But someone will say: by the same reasoning neither ought penance to be repeated, lest it become cheap or provoke to sinning. Solution. There is another judgment concerning penance, which by the infliction of punishment restrains from sin, 629Bthan concerning baptism, by which both fault and punishment are wholly remitted.

QUESTION XC. And a certain jealousy of fire. It is asked what punishment he here signifies through fire? Solution. The vehemence of eternal punishment here the fire signifies, because no element has such efficacy as fire.

QUESTION XCI. Which shall consume the adversaries, etc. Shall the fire reduce Christ's enemies to nothing? Solution. Therefore it is said that the jealousy of fire shall consume the adversaries, because no part of the body or soul shall be free from punishment, but shall be tortured by the fire.

QUESTION XCII. Revenge to me, and I will repay, saith the Lord. It is asked whether vengeance is always to be reserved to the Lord; is it not lawful for a man 629Cto take vengeance? Are not robbers lawfully hanged? Solution. It is not lawful for a man to take vengeance for himself, nor ought he to desire it; but if it is necessary to take it, let God alone be in the cause, and the zeal of justice; but he who takes it otherwise, sins mortally. According to that: He that shall take the sword, shall perish by the sword (Matth. XXVI).

QUESTION XCIII. Faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things that appear not (Hebr. XI). Concerning this definition of faith it is asked whether it fits all faith, and whether it can also be fitted to faith alone. But it seems that this definition fits only faith which is concerning future things; but since faith is concerning present and past things, as concerning the nativity and the passion, how is the faith of the passion the substance of things to be hoped for? 629DLikewise, is not hope and charity the substance, that is the thing and cause, which makes the things to be hoped for subsist in us? how then is faith alone the substance of things to be hoped for? Solution. According as the gloss expounds this definition, it seems that it does not fit faith alone. But although part of this definition seems to be assigned to other virtues, yet not the whole; for faith alone is the evidence of things that appear not, through which alone we are certain concerning things eternal, that they are; but through hope we are confident that we shall have them. And therefore properly faith is called the substance of future things, because through it we know that they are. Faith also, concerning present or past things, can be called the substance of things to be hoped for, that is, the cause which 630Asometimes makes those things which we hope for subsist in us, because through faith in the passion one comes to the future goods, and it is the evidence of things that appear not, so much that those who saw him suffer believed something, namely that Christ, who hung on the cross, was God.

QUESTION XCIV. That from invisible things, etc. It is asked what he calls invisible things? Solution. Either the unformed and invisible matter of the four elements, which in Greek is called chaos; or the invisible world, which is called the archetype, which was in the mind of God, according to whose exemplar this sensible and visible world was made.

QUESTION XCV. Abel by faith being dead yet speaketh, etc. It is asked how he who does not live, speaks? 630BSolution. He speaks, that is, is matter of speaking; he speaks because by his example he admonishes us to be just.

QUESTION XCVI. Without faith it is impossible to please God, etc. It is asked of what faith he says this; is it of the faith of the incarnation? Solution. It is said that without it no one from the beginning pleased God.

QUESTION XCVII. He that cometh to God must believe that he is, etc. It is asked of what faith he treats, whether of perfect, or of imperfect?
